text: [warm] Mike and the robot that listened.
description: The title of the story "Mike and the robot that listened", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Mike was six when his uncle brought the robot in a shoebox. It was the size of a mug, red with two round eyes, and it had four arrow buttons on its back. Mike pressed every button at once, and the robot did nothing at all. It just blinked at him, like it was waiting for something.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] His uncle laughed. It cannot see you, and it cannot hear you, he said. It only knows what you press. The buttons tell it, and its wheels and its beep show you what it heard. Tell first, and then it shows you.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] So Mike pressed up. The robot rolled forward one square on the kitchen tiles and stopped. He pressed up, up, up, and it rolled three squares and bumped the table leg. Every press was one step, and it did the steps in the order he pressed them, nothing more and nothing less.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Mike wanted the robot to carry a crayon to his uncle across the room. He pressed a long line of arrows without thinking, and the robot wandered off under a chair. Plan the steps first, his uncle said, and press them after. So Mike drew the path on paper: up, up, right, right, up.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 4 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] He pressed the five arrows and let go. The robot rolled up two squares, went right for two, then up one more, and stopped at his uncle's feet with the crayon. First, next, then, last, his uncle said. That is a plan a robot can follow. Mike called it his robot list.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 5 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] The next job was longer. The kitchen was twelve squares wide, and pressing up twelve times made Mike's thumb tired. His uncle showed him the little loop button. Press up, then the loop, then the number twelve, and the robot does that one step twelve times. Three presses instead of twelve.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 6 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Then the robot bumped a cup and stopped. Mike did not press every button again. He looked at his list, found the one step that was wrong, and changed just that one. The robot rolled the rest of the way. Fixing one wrong step, his uncle said, is how every robot gets fixed.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 7 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] That night the robot sat on Mike's shelf, blinking and waiting. Mike knew now that it was not being lazy. It was listening for the next list. A robot only does what it is told, one step at a time, so the telling has to be right. He fell asleep planning tomorrow's path.
description: "Mike and the robot that listened", paragraph 8 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Miss Park's kindergarten class had a circle rug with twenty spots. One week in October, the circle learned five things, one each day. Miss Park said the rug was a good place to learn how to talk and how to listen.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Monday was listening with your brain and body. Miss Park said, show me listening. Jonah turned and looked right at her. Lily looked down at her shoes, because that is how she listens best. Then Miss Park played a game where she said things once, softly. Jonah heard her say touch your nose, and Lily heard her say hop one time. Both of them had their brains on her words.
description: "The circle that learned to listen", paragraph 2 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Tuesday was steps. Miss Park gave three of them. First, get a cup, and then put in the soil, and last, push in a seed with one finger. The class said them back together. Cup, soil, seed. Eli said soil first, and Miss Park fixed it before any soil was out. That is why you say the steps back, she said. Then everyone did it in order, and twenty cups had seeds in them.
description: "The circle that learned to listen", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Wednesday was the clear voice. Each child told about one thing from home. Miss Park sat in the back, on purpose. Talk to me, she said, and if I can hear you, everyone can. Jonah said, this is my truck, it is red, and I like it because it is fast. He said every word slowly, right to its end. Miss Park heard every word.
description: "The circle that learned to listen", paragraph 4 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Thursday was turns. Twenty children had twenty ideas, all at once, and nobody could hear any of them. So Miss Park brought out a stick. Whoever holds it talks, and everyone else listens. It went around the circle, and every idea got heard. Lily had the last turn, and she had been quiet all year. She said the class should plant flowers by the door, and everyone agreed.
description: "The circle that learned to listen", paragraph 5 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Friday another class came to visit, and Miss Park's children knew just what to do. Hello, my name is Lily, said Lily. Hello, my name is Omar, said Omar. Please and thank you went around the rug the way the stick had, and the visitors learned the stick rule in one try.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] It rained for five days straight in October, and the kindergarten class could not go outside once. Miss Okafor called it the rainy day club, and every afternoon the club learned one thing about the mind.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Monday was the five reporters. Miss Okafor hid a lemon, a bell, a rose, an ice cube and a feather around the room, and the children found each one with a different sense. Jonah checked the rack three times that day and it stayed a rack.
description: "The rainy day club", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Wednesday was the song. The class song had four lines, and nobody could keep it in their heads. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Thursday was the feelings chart, and it was needed. Being inside for four days had made everyone loud. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] The fight came at the end of Thursday, over the one umbrella that had a working handle. Two children pulled on it and yelled. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Every Wednesday the kindergarten class sat on the blue rug for wondering time. The rule was simple. Miss Ruth asked one question, and the class thought about it out loud, one voice at a time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] The first question was whether a stick is a toy. Half the class said yes and half said no, so Miss Ruth asked what a toy was. A thing you play with, said Jonah. But what about a spoon, said Ana, because her baby brother played with spoons all day. The class fixed the idea three times before the bell, and nobody minded, because fixing an idea felt like building something.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] The next Wednesday was the because game. Miss Ruth held up a picture of the playground and asked why they should go out. Jonah said because the sun is out, Ana said because I want to, and Theo said because his shoes were new. Only one of those was a reason, the class decided, and it was the one about the sun.
description: "The wondering rug", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] They found the rule together. A reason comes after because, but it has to be about the thing, and it has to be true. A wish is not a reason and an order is not a reason. When nobody knew whether it would rain, Miss Ruth asked how do you know, and the class walked to the window to look.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] By the third Wednesday the class had a talking stick, painted with stars by the class itself. Whoever held it talked. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Saying it back was the hard part. Before you could answer a friend, you had to say their idea back until they said yes, that is it. Jonah got Ana's idea wrong twice and right the third time, and by then they were almost agreeing.

text: [warm] The lemonade stand on Maple Street.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Nadia and Ben wanted the same thing, a kite with a long red tail from the shop on Maple Street. The kite cost twenty coins, and between them they had three. So on the first hot Saturday of summer they set up a lemonade stand at the end of Nadia's driveway, with a pitcher, paper cups and a sign.
description: "The lemonade stand on Maple Street", paragraph 1 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] The first thing they learned was that a stand has needs of its own. Lemons, sugar and cups had to be bought before a single cup could be sold. Ben wanted to buy a fancy tablecloth too. That is a want, Nadia said, and the lemons come first. They bought the lemons with their three coins and borrowed the sugar from Ben's kitchen.
description: "The lemonade stand on Maple Street", paragraph 2 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] By noon they had sold nine cups at one coin each, and the jar on the table held nine coins. That was income, money they had earned by squeezing and pouring. When Miss Alvarez dropped in two coins and did not take a cup, Nadia set those apart. That is a gift, she said. It is kind, but we did not work for it.
description: "The lemonade stand on Maple Street", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] A boy named Theo came by with a plate of cookies and no coins at all. He wanted lemonade; they wanted cookies. Two cookies for one cup, Ben offered, and Theo agreed. That was a trade, a swap with no money in it, and it only worked because each side wanted what the other had.
description: "The lemonade stand on Maple Street", paragraph 4 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] In the afternoon the line got longer, and Ben had an idea. He raised the price to two coins a cup. Three people paid it, and four walked on. Nadia lowered the price back to one coin, and the line came back. The price, they decided, is what people will pay, not what you wish they would.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] At the end of the day the jar held twenty-one coins, and Ben wanted to spend them all on ice cream. Nadia counted out what the next Saturday would need: coins for lemons, sugar and cups. Spending is now, she said, and the stand needs some of this later. They put six coins in a second jar and labeled it lemons.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] That left fifteen coins for the kite, and a decision. Ice cream now would eat the whole kite. They chose two cones instead of four, spent two coins, and put the rest away. Giving up the other two cones was the price of the kite, and they paid it gladly.

text: [warm] Ella's farm year.
description: The title of the story "Ella's farm year", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Ella spent a whole year helping on her grandpa's farm. The farm had a garden, a field of corn, and three brown cows. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] In spring, they planted seeds. Ella pushed each corn seed into the soil a hand apart, so every plant would have room. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Summer was hot and dry. By afternoon the corn leaves curled in the heat, so Ella and Grandpa watered every evening. The cows stood under the trees, where the shade was cool. They drank so much water that Ella helped fill the trough twice a day. Ella learned that plants and cows both need water to grow.
description: "Ella's farm year", paragraph 3 of 8: told calm and unhurried to a young child, with a voice of its own for each character who speaks, the same each time.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] In the fall, it was time to pick. Ella pulled up carrots, which are roots, and cut lettuce, which is leaves. text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Winter was cold and gray. The garden rested under a blanket of straw, and the animals spent cold nights in the snug barn. Its walls kept out the wind and the rain. Grandpa gave the cows hay every morning, because the grass had stopped growing.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] Every morning, Ella gathered eggs from the hens. In summer there were often six eggs, but in winter there were only two or three. Grandpa said hens lay fewer eggs when the days are short and dark. Ella counted the eggs and wrote each number on the barn wall with chalk.

text: [calm and unhurried, a voice for each character] When spring came around again, one of the cows had a calf. The calf wobbled on long legs, and soon she was drinking her mother's milk. text: [warm] The broken cups.
description: The title of the story "The broken cups", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The morning of the harvest fair, Maya was baking a lemon cake for the whole street. The kitchen smelled of butter. She reached for her measuring cups and knocked the set off the shelf. Clink, clink, crack. Every cup broke but one: the smallest, marked one quarter.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The recipe asked for three quarters of a cup of sugar and one whole cup of milk. Maya had one tiny cup and forty neighbors expecting cake. Her little brother held up a coffee mug. Just fill this most of the way, he said.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] But where is three quarters of a mug? This one was fatter at the top than the bottom, and nobody had cut it into four equal parts. A guess could make the cake too sweet, or not sweet enough.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then Maya looked at the little cup again. Four of these, all the same size, fill one whole cup. The bottom number, four, told her how many equal parts make a whole. The top number, three, told her how many to use.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She filled the little cup and leveled it with a knife. Pour. Fill. Pour. Fill. Pour. Three quarters of a cup, exactly. The milk was the same trick: four quarters make one whole cup.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A fraction is not a strange kind of number. It is an instruction: cut the whole into equal parts, and take this many. The parts must be equal, or the counting means nothing. Maya's cake was gone by noon.
description: "The broken cups", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two pizzas.
description: The title of the story "Two pizzas", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Leo and his sister Ava ordered two pizzas the same size. One came cut into two big pieces, the other into four smaller ones. Leo took one big piece. Ava took two small ones and said she had more, because two is more than one.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Leo was sure she was wrong, but he could not say why. Two pieces did look like more. The box smelled of oregano, and the cheese was going cold. Prove it, their dad said. Do not shout it.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So they laid Ava's two pieces beside Leo's one and lined up the crusts. The edges matched exactly. Two quarters covered the very same pizza as one half.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The pizza had not changed. Only the cuts had. Cutting each half in two doubled the bottom number, from two to four. Taking twice as many pieces doubled the top, from one to two. Double both and nothing changes.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next Friday, a pizza came cut into eight thin slices. Ava grabbed two. Same as last week, she said. Leo laughed, because two eighths was a skinny strip. She had changed the bottom number and not the top.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] To match one half, she needed four of the eight slices, because one times four is four and two times four is eight. She took two more, and the crusts lined up again.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is an equivalent fraction. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number, and the amount stays put. Change only one, and the amount changes.
description: "Two pizzas", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Which slice is bigger?
description: The title of the story "Which slice is bigger?", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] At Maya's birthday party, her uncle held a knife over the chocolate cake and offered her a choice. One third of the cake, or one eighth. Maya loved big numbers, and eight is much bigger than three. She chose the eighth.
description: "Which slice is bigger?", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her cousin Ben got one third. His slice was a thick wedge with frosting piled on the edge. Hers was a thin sliver she could almost see through. She had picked the bigger number and gotten the smaller cake. How?

text: [warm and friendly] Her uncle drew two circles on a napkin, both the same size. He cut one into three pieces and the other into eight. Cut a cake into three and each piece is big. Cut the same cake into eight and each piece is small.
description: "Which slice is bigger?", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The bottom number counts how many pieces the whole was cut into. More pieces means thinner slices. So when the top numbers match, one and one, the smaller bottom wins. One third beats one eighth.
description: "Which slice is bigger?", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Later he cut a second cake into eight equal slices for the guests to take home. Ben took three. Maya took five. This time there was no trick. Every slice was an eighth, the same size, so more slices meant more cake. Five eighths beat three eighths.
description: "Which slice is bigger?", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is how to compare fractions. Same bottom, the bigger top wins. Same top, the smaller bottom wins. When neither matches, rename them so the bottoms match, then look again. And never trust a big number until you know what it counts.
description: "Which slice is bigger?", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Marks on the ruler.
description: The title of the story "Marks on the ruler", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam was building a model grasshopper for the science fair. Its legs were bits of drinking straw, and each one had to be three quarters of an inch long. His ruler showed 0 and 1. Between them sat three little marks with no numbers at all. Where was three quarters?
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He guessed and cut. Too short. He guessed again. Too long. The pile of straw bits grew, and the glue was drying in its cap. Six legs to make, and not one was right. Those little marks had to mean something. But what?
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher put a green bead at 0 and slid it along. The three marks cut the space from 0 to 1 into four equal steps. Four steps made one whole inch, so each step was one quarter.
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Step: one quarter. Step: two quarters. Step: three quarters. The bead stopped on the third mark. The bottom number, four, told Sam how many steps make a whole. The top number, three, told him how many steps to walk.
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam cut all six legs at the third mark, and every one matched. Then he noticed the middle mark. Two steps out of four, exactly halfway. Two quarters and one half were the same spot on the road.
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A number line is a road with signposts. Cut 0 to 1 into equal steps, and every fraction is a place on that road. The bottom number sets the size of each step. The top number says how far to walk.
description: "Marks on the ruler", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Blocks of a fifth.
description: The title of the story "Blocks of a fifth", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Nadia had five wooden blocks that fit together into one long bar. The bar was one whole. Her little brother Omar asked her to show him three fifths. She stared at the blocks. A fraction was a thing you wrote, not a thing you built. Or was it?
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She wrote it on paper. Three over five. Omar shrugged. He wanted to see it, not read it. The blocks smelled of pine and clicked as she pushed them around, and then she saw it.
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Each block was one fifth of the bar. She pulled three forward. One fifth, one fifth, one fifth. Three fifths, sitting on the table where anyone could count them.
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Omar pushed two of the three blocks together and left one apart. Was that still three fifths? It was: two fifths and one fifth, the same three blocks in two piles. Push all five together and it was five fifths, the whole bar again.
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At snack time their mom brought two granola bars for three kids: Nadia, Omar and a friend. Nadia cut each bar into three equal pieces, thirds, just like her blocks. Each kid took one piece from each bar. Two bars shared by three people is two thirds apiece.
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A fraction is built from unit pieces, one fifth or one third at a time. It can be taken apart in more than one way. It is also a sharing that has not been finished yet. Once you can build it, you can see it.
description: "Blocks of a fifth", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The pizza that fed the whole street.
description: The title of the story "The pizza that fed the whole street", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The pizzas arrived at noon: three of them, all the same size, for a street with more mouths than slices. The air smelled of cut grass and charcoal. Mrs. Okafor from number twelve picked up the knife. Somebody had to cut them, she said, and cutting is where fractions live.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first pizza went into two equal pieces, halves, and Malik's sister took one. The second went into four equal pieces, fourths, and Malik took two. Equal pieces are the whole rule. Cut a pizza into four lopsided chunks, and the word fourth stops meaning anything.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the arguments started. Malik said his two fourths were less than his sister's one half, because a half was one big slice and he had two little ones. Mrs. Okafor laid the slices on one plate, crust to crust. Two fourths covered exactly the same space as one half. Same pizza, different cuts.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third pizza had to reach everyone else, so it went into eighths. Wren got one and was sure it beat one of Malik's fourths, because eight is bigger than four. They held the slices side by side. Her eighth was half the size of his fourth. The bottom number counts the cuts, and more cuts make smaller pieces.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Wren's little brother took his eighths one at a time, grinning with sauce on his chin. One eighth, two eighths, three eighths. A fraction is built from unit pieces like that, and three eighths is simply three of them.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then three latecomers ran up, and only two fourths were left. Mrs. Okafor did not flip a coin. She cut each slice into three equal pieces and gave every latecomer one piece of each. Two slices shared by three people is two thirds of a slice apiece. Nobody argued, which was a first for the afternoon.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When the pizzas were gone, Wren drew a chalk line on the sidewalk from 0 to 1 and cut it into eight equal steps. Her friends hopped behind her as she walked it: one eighth, two eighths, three eighths, four eighths. Four eighths landed exactly halfway, right where one half would be.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A fraction is a share of one whole, cut into equal parts. The bottom number says how many parts, the top says how many you have, and every fraction has its own spot on the line from 0 to 1. The street had eaten the lesson.
description: "The pizza that fed the whole street", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The movie in one sentence.
description: The title of the story "The movie in one sentence", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mateo came home from the movies bursting. His abuela had stayed home with a sore knee, so she asked him what the film was about. He sat on the porch step and took a big breath.
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He told her about the boat, the storm, the dog, the lighthouse going dark, the girl with the lantern and the ending. It took eleven minutes. She nodded through all of it. Then she said, "Yes, but what was it about?"
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mateo frowned. He had just told her. Every piece of it had happened. He started again, faster, and she held up a hand. Not what happened, she said. What was it about?
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He thought about it. The boat, the dog and the storm were all pointing at one thing, the way the spokes of a bike wheel point at the middle. It was about a girl who would not give up until everyone was safe, he said.
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His abuela smiled. "Now I have seen it." One sentence had done what eleven minutes could not.
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next day his teacher handed out a paragraph about bees. Bees carry pollen from flower to flower. They make honey. Without them, apple trees grow far fewer apples. Mateo asked his abuela's question: what is the whole thing about? Bees help people. The rest were details holding that up.
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every story, every paragraph, every page has one idea its details are working for. Look first at the first and last sentences. Find the sentence the others lean on, and you have the main idea.
description: "The movie in one sentence", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Happy, unhappy, happily.
description: The title of the story "Happy, unhappy, happily", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Diego had a spelling list with happy, unhappy and happily on it. Three long words to learn, he thought, and there were fifteen more below them. He groaned and put his head on the table. The paper smelled like fresh printer ink.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His big sister slid a finger over the first two letters of unhappy. What was left? Happy. Then she covered the last two letters of happily. Happy again. Diego sat up. Were these even three words?
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They were one word wearing costumes. Un goes on the front and means not, so unhappy means not happy. A piece on the front is a prefix. Ly goes on the end and turns happy into a way of doing something. A piece on the end is a suffix.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Take the costume off, his sister said, and the small word is still standing there.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Diego went down the list hunting for costumes. Hopeful: hope, plus ful, which means full of. Full of hope. Hopeless: hope, plus less, which means without. Without hope. Reread: re, which means again, plus read. Read it again. The long list was shrinking into short words he already knew.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He finished in ten minutes and spelled every word right the next morning.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Half the long words you will ever meet are short words in costume. Find the front piece, find the end piece, and read the middle. Once you can see the seams, long words stop being scary.
description: "Happy, unhappy, happily", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Check it or argue it.
description: The title of the story "Check it or argue it", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] At the county dog show, Priya was writing for the school paper. Her neighbor lifted his fluffy dog, Biscuit, and told her two things. Biscuit weighs thirty pounds. Biscuit is the best dog here. Priya wrote both down.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next morning her teacher circled the second sentence in red. Priya had heard it with her own ears. Wasn't that enough to make it true?
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She went back to prove it and could not. A boy by the next pen was sure his beagle was the best. A woman with a poodle was sure hers was. Nobody changed anybody's mind.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first sentence was different. Priya put Biscuit on the scale, and the needle stopped at thirty. Anyone could check it and get the same answer. That is a fact. The second sentence could only be argued, because it was what her neighbor felt. That is an opinion.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her the clue words: best, worst, beautiful, boring. They tell you how somebody feels, not what is true. Opinions are fine to print, she said, as long as you say whose they are.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya fixed her story. Biscuit weighs thirty pounds. His owner thinks he is the best dog at the show. Both sentences were true now.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every sentence you read is one or the other. Ask, could I check this with a scale, a map or a clock? If yes, it is a fact. If all you can do is argue, it is an opinion, and it belongs to the person who said it.
description: "Check it or argue it", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Because and so.
description: The title of the story "Because and so", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam came home to a trail of muddy paw prints across the kitchen floor. His mom stood in the doorway, keys still in her hand. What happened here? she asked. Sam knew. He had seen all of it. But when he tried to say it, the words came out in a tangle.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The dog. The rain. The door. The mud. His mom shook her head. That told her what, but not in what order, and not why. The dog looked guilty, and the mop was dripping.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So Sam tried the order words. First, it started to rain. Next, the dog rolled in the yard. Then I opened the door. Finally, the dog ran across the floor. Now his mom could see it happen, one step at a time.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] But she still wanted to know why. Sam tried a small word. The floor is muddy because the dog came in from the rain. Because pointed backward, at the reason.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Or the other way around. The dog was soaked, so the floor got muddy. So pointed forward, at what happened next. The rain was the cause. The muddy floor was the effect.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His mom handed him the mop. And the effect of that, she said, is that you are cleaning it.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A cause is why. An effect is what happened. Because looks back at the cause, so looks ahead to the effect, and first and then tell the order. Pick the right little word, and a tangle turns into a story.
description: "Because and so", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The friends it came with.
description: The title of the story "The friends it came with", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ava was reading a story about a mountain climb when she hit a word she had never seen. Frigid. She stopped. The whole page seemed to lock behind that one word, the way a door locks when you do not know the code.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She could have skipped it. She could have asked her dad. The dictionary was across the room, and the couch was warm under the blanket. So she read the sentence again, slowly, and something caught her eye.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The frigid wind made the climbers shiver and pull their hoods tight. Shiver. Hoods. The new word had come to the party with friends, and the friends gave it away. Frigid meant very cold.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Two pages later came another stranger. The climbers reached the summit, or the very top of the mountain. This time the clue came right after the word, holding the door open. The little word or was saying: here is what it means.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then came a word with no friends at all. On the ridge, a ptarmigan watched them pass. Nothing around it helped. Was it a rock? A person? Ava finally got off the couch and opened the dictionary. A ptarmigan is a bird whose feathers turn white in winter.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Most new words arrive with clues: the words beside them, the sentence before, the picture on the page. Read around the stranger first, and you will guess right more often than not. When the friends stay quiet, the dictionary does the introducing.
description: "The friends it came with", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] What she did at recess.
description: The title of the story "What she did at recess", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Jonah's teacher asked the class to describe the new girl, Lina, after her first day. Almost everybody wrote the same thing. She is shy. That was what Lina had said about herself that morning, in a voice so small the back row missed it.
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] One boy wrote that she was tall. The teacher shook her head. Tall is how someone looks, she said. I asked what she is like. A trait is a way of being: brave, honest, kind, shy.
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Jonah started to write shy, then stopped. At recess he had seen something. A first grader was crying because every swing was taken. Lina got off her swing without a word and gave it to him. Shy people did not do that. Or did they?
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He wrote it carefully. The where was the playground. The when was recess, under a hot sun with the swing chains creaking. Those two were the setting. And who Lina was did not come from what she said about herself. It came from what she did. She was kind.
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On Friday, Lina raised her hand and read her poem out loud to the whole class. Her voice shook a little, but she finished. The girl who called herself shy had just been brave. Jonah wrote that down too. Characters can change.
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is how characters work in every story. Setting is the where and the when. Characters show who they are by what they say and do, and when the two disagree, believe what they do.
description: "What she did at recess", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The day the newspaper came to school.
description: The title of the story "The day the newspaper came to school", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The class was going to make a newspaper. One page, real stories, printed for the whole school, with real bylines. Ms. Reyes handed out red pens and made one rule: every reader must understand every story on the first try.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first job was headlines. A headline is the main idea in a few words. The story about the leaky gym roof had twelve facts in it, from the drip on the free-throw line to the bucket everyone called Gerald. The headline was four words long. Gym Roof Leaks Again.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second job was hard words. The sports report called the fifth grade team unbeatable, and half the class stopped reading. So they took the word apart. Un means not. Able means can be. Unbeatable: cannot be beaten. Once you can see the pieces, a long word opens like a door.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Another story said the rain had been torrential. Nobody knew that word either, but the next sentence helped: the gutters overflowed, and the parking lot turned into a lake. Torrential rain is very heavy rain. The words around a stranger usually give it away, so the class left it in.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The lunch review was the trickiest. It said the Friday pizza was the best in the world. Fact or opinion? Nobody could check every pizza in the world, so it was an opinion. It stayed in the paper, but now it said whose opinion it was: the writer's.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The field trip story had its events in a jumble, like a puzzle dumped on a table. So the writers put them in order and showed the causes. The bus was late because of the rain, so lunch moved indoors, and then the sun came out just in time for the walk home.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The best story of all was a profile of Mr. Bell, the custodian. The writer never called him kind. She wrote what he did: he dried the gym floor with his own towels before the big game, and he knew every kid's name by October. Readers could see who he was from what he did.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When the page was printed, every reader in the school found the main ideas and opened the long words. They knew what was checked and what was only felt, followed each story in order and met Mr. Bell. That is reading to understand, and the class had learned it by working from the other side of the page.
description: "The day the newspaper came to school", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three states in the kitchen.
description: The title of the story "Three states in the kitchen", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] On Saturday morning, Theo dropped an ice cube on a plate and left it on the counter. He poured water into a glass. His mother put the kettle on the stove. Three different things, he thought. Ice, water and steam.
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When he came back, the ice cube was gone. In its place was a puddle, spreading across the plate. The kettle was whistling, and the kitchen window had gone foggy. Where did the ice go? And where did that fog come from?
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His mother tapped the plate. The ice cube kept its square shape until it warmed. That is a solid. Then it melted and spread out flat, taking the shape of the plate. That is a liquid. Pour it into a glass and it becomes glass-shaped.
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The kettle was the next step. Heat the water enough and it boils. It turns into steam, a gas that spreads to fill the whole kitchen. You cannot hold a gas or pour it. It goes wherever there is room.
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo touched the foggy window. It was cold and wet. The steam had cooled on the glass and turned back into tiny drops of water. He filled the ice tray and put it in the freezer. By lunch the water was solid again.
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Everything around you is a solid, a liquid or a gas. A solid keeps its shape. A liquid takes the shape of its container. A gas fills whatever holds it. Heat moves matter up that list, and cooling brings it back down. Same water, the whole way through.
description: "Three states in the kitchen", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Pushes and pulls.
description: The title of the story "Pushes and pulls", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The red wagon sat at the bottom of the hill, loaded with three pumpkins for the fall sale at the top. Jamal stood beside it and waited. Nothing happened. Wagons, it turns out, do not move by themselves.
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He grabbed the handle and pulled, and the wagon rolled, squeaking, up the sidewalk. Then his sister steered it onto the grass to take a shortcut. The wagon slowed and stopped, even though Jamal was still pulling hard. The grass was fighting him. Why?
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His dad knelt by the wheels. A force is a push or a pull, he said, and nothing starts or stops without one. Jamal's pull was one force. The grass was another. It rubbed against the wheels and slowed them. That rubbing is called friction.
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So Jamal pulled and his sister pushed from behind. Two forces in the same direction. The wagon crawled up the grass and reached the top, and the pumpkins sold in an hour.
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the top, Jamal let go of the empty wagon for one second. It rolled straight back down the hill without anyone touching it. Gravity had pulled it, the same pull that makes a dropped ball fall. At the bottom, the grass rubbed it slower and slower until it stopped.
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nothing moves without a force. A push or a pull gets things going, friction slows moving things down, and gravity pulls everything toward the ground. Watch anything roll, slide or fall, and ask which force did that.
description: "Pushes and pulls", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The jar of eggs.
description: The title of the story "The jar of eggs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa scooped a clump of clear jelly from the pond into a jar on the classroom windowsill. Inside the jelly were hundreds of little black dots. Her brother said they were dirt. She said they were eggs. Nobody could tell.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] About a week later the dots had wriggled free. They had tails and swam in quick, jerky circles. They were tadpoles. Rosa fed them boiled lettuce and drew them every Friday.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] After about six weeks, two tiny back legs appeared. A few weeks after that came front legs, and the tails began to shrink. Every time Rosa looked, the thing in the jar was different. Was it even the same animal?
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It was. Her teacher drew a circle on the board: egg, tadpole, tadpole with legs, frog. Each stage leads to the next. And a grown frog lays eggs, which starts the circle again. That circle is called a life cycle.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A bean does it too, her teacher said. Seed, sprout, plant, flower, and the flower makes new seeds. A butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. The stages look nothing alike, but each one makes the next.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In June, Rosa carried the little frogs back to the pond and let them go at the muddy edge. The next spring she went back to look. Floating by the reeds was a fresh clump of clear jelly, full of black dots.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every living thing goes around its own circle of stages. A frog, a bean, a butterfly and you. The shapes change, but the circle keeps turning.
description: "The jar of eggs", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Cold in July.
description: The title of the story "Cold in July", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Every morning in July, Ava checked the weather station in her Texas backyard. The thermometer read a hundred degrees by noon. The rain gauge had been dry for three weeks. Weather is what the sky is doing today, and today it was baking.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then a letter came from her pen pal, Jack, who lives in the mountains of Australia. He wrote about snow. He had built a snowman in the yard and could not feel his fingers. In July.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ava read it twice. Same month, same planet. How could she be sweating while he wore a scarf? Was the Sun closer to Texas?
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher held up a globe and tilted it. The Earth leans. As it travels around the Sun, one half leans toward the light and gets long days and high sun. That is summer. The other half leans away and gets short days and low sun. That is winter.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In July, the northern half leans in, and Texas bakes. The southern half leans out, and Australia shivers. In January they swap. The Earth is even a little farther from the Sun in July, which surprised Ava most.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The pattern comes back every year, in the same order. Spring warms, summer is hottest, fall cools, winter is coldest. Jack's seasons run the same circle, just half a year apart.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Weather is today, and you measure it with tools. Seasons are the pattern, and you can plan for them. They are not about how close the Sun is. They are about which way you are leaning.
description: "Cold in July", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.
