text: [warm and friendly] Owen was building a guitar for music class out of a paper cup and a rubber band. He stretched the band over the cup and plucked it. Twang. He plucked it again and, while it was still buzzing, touched it with one finger. It tickled. The sound stopped the moment he touched it.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That was strange. Why would a finger stop a sound? He tried again and again. Every time the band shook, there was a sound. Every time he held it still, silence. The sound and the shaking seemed to be the same thing.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They were. Sound is a vibration: something shaking fast enough to shake the air. The shaking air travels to your ear, and your ear feels it as sound.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen plucked harder, and the band shook wider. The sound got louder. He stretched the band tighter, and it shook faster. The sound went higher. He loosened it, and the note dropped low. Bigger shake, louder. Faster shake, higher. Slower shake, lower.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he put his ear flat on his desk and tapped the far end with a pencil. The tap came through the wood, louder than it came through the air. Sound can travel through air, water or wood. With nothing at all to travel through, like in outer space, there is no sound.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every sound you have ever heard is something vibrating, from a guitar string to a drum skin to your own voice. Put a hand on your throat and hum. That buzz is you, shaking the air.
description: "The rubber band", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The jar.
description: The title of the story "The jar", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya's tomato plants were drooping, and her grandpa said the trouble was in the dirt. Dirt was just dirt, she thought. She scooped some into a jar of water and shook it until the whole thing turned brown. Then she went to bed.
description: "The jar", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In the morning the jar had sorted itself into stripes. Gritty sand lay at the bottom, fine silt above it. The water was still cloudy with clay, and dark bits of old leaves floated near the top. One scoop of dirt had become four things. How?
description: "The jar", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Because soil was never one thing. Most of it is rock, cracked apart over thousands of years by rain, ice and roots, then ground smaller and smaller. The rest is rotted leaves and roots of things that once lived. Heavy sand sank first. Tiny clay took longest to settle.
description: "The jar", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandpa showed her the squeeze test. He wet a handful of each. Clay made a sticky ball that held its shape. Sand fell apart in his fingers. The good garden soil held together a little and crumbled a little. That mix is called loam.
description: "The jar", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya's garden bed was mostly clay. Clay packs tight and holds water, so her tomato roots were sitting in a puddle. They dug in rotted leaves from the compost pile, and by summer the plants stood tall.
description: "The jar", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The ground under your feet is a slow recipe of rock and rotted life. Clay holds water, sand drains fast, and loam is the mix that gardens love. A jar of water reads the recipe out.
description: "The jar", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The bucket line.
description: The title of the story "The bucket line", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] At summer camp, Kenji stood at the bottom of a line of kids passing a bucket of water up the hill. He filled it to the brim at the creek. Every hand spilled a little. By the time it reached the top, only a splash sloshed at the bottom.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That night the counselor asked a strange question. Why are there so many blades of grass in the meadow and so few hawks above it? The kids guessed hawks were shy, or fast, or hiding. Nobody guessed the bucket.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every food chain starts with the sun. Grass catches sunlight and makes its own food, so grass is a producer. A grasshopper eats the grass, a bird eats the grasshopper, and a hawk eats the bird. Each eater is a consumer, and each one uses up most of the energy it gets, like a spill.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By the hawk, only a splash is left. It takes a whole meadow of grass to feed one hawk, which is why the hawk sits at the top of this chain.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next morning Kenji found a rotting log covered in mushrooms. The counselor said those were decomposers. They break down dead things and turn them back into soil, and the soil feeds the grass. The chain was really a circle.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Late that summer the creek ran low and the meadow went brown. The grasshoppers thinned out, then the birds, and the hawk flew off to hunt somewhere else.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every link depends on the one below it. Take away the grass, and the whole line goes dry.
description: "The bucket line", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The storm that came to the science fair.
description: The title of the story "The storm that came to the science fair", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The science fair was set up outside on the lawn, which everyone later agreed was a mistake. Table one had an ice cube melting on a plate, a glass of water and a thermos of hot water puffing steam: solid, liquid, gas. Table two had a wagon on a wooden ramp for pushes and pulls.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Table three had a jar of tadpoles with tiny back legs, halfway to being frogs. Table four had a rain gauge that had never seen rain. Table five had a jar of garden dirt settled into layers, sand at the bottom, and table six had a poster of a food chain: grass, grasshopper, bird, hawk.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the sky went dark, and thunder rumbled far off. The principal did not wait. When thunder roars, she called, go indoors! Everyone grabbed a poster and ran for the gym, because thunder means lightning is close enough to be dangerous.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They watched the rest through the gym windows. The wind shoved the wagon down its ramp with nobody touching it, and gravity pulled it faster down the slope. It was the best demonstration of a force anyone gave all day. Out on the grass, the rubbing of friction slowed it until it stopped by the flagpole.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The rain came down so hard that the gauge filled past its first line in ten minutes. Nobody had ever seen the gauge move that fast. On table one, the ice cube had melted into a puddle, and the thermos had stopped steaming. Rain on the windows ran together into little streams.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When the thunder cracked close, the gym windows buzzed under a boy's hand. He felt it and heard it at the same moment. Sound is a vibration, and a big one can shake the glass it passes through.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The storm moved on in half an hour. The posters were soaked, but the tadpoles did not mind at all. A tadpole lives in water and was on its way to becoming a frog either way. A robin hopped onto the wet grass to hunt for insects, the food chain from the poster back at work.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The judges gave every table a ribbon. In one afternoon they had seen matter change state, forces move things, a life cycle turning, weather arriving and sound shaking a window. The weather had done the demonstrating, and the judges had the good sense to watch it from indoors.
description: "The storm that came to the science fair", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The shape of it.
description: The title of the story "The shape of it", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Lily had to write a paragraph about her dog, Pepper, and she had a hundred things to say. He brings in the newspaper. He finds her lost shoes. He once ate a whole birthday cake. She wrote it all in one heap, and it sounded like a shopping list.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher asked one question. What is this paragraph about? My dog, said Lily. Yes, said the teacher, but what about him? Every sentence in the heap was true. Not one of them said the big thing.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So she wrote the big thing first. Pepper is the best helper in our house. That was the idea, and it went in the first sentence. Then the heap became proof. He brings in the newspaper. He finds my lost shoes.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she read each sentence and asked the test question: is this about the same idea? The newspaper, yes. The shoes, yes. The birthday cake? That was not helping. That was stealing.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The cake did not get thrown away. It got a paragraph of its own, with its own first sentence. Pepper is also a thief. Now Lily had two paragraphs, two ideas, and nothing in the wrong place.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher drew it as a table. The first sentence is the tabletop, the idea everything rests on. The details are the legs, and a leg from a different table makes it wobble.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is the shape of a paragraph. One idea in the first sentence, details after it holding it up, and a new paragraph for every new idea.
description: "The shape of it", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The paper boat.
description: The title of the story "The paper boat", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus could fold a paper boat with his eyes closed. His friend Eli could not, so Marcus wrote the steps on a card for him. Fold the paper in half. Fold the top corners down. Fold the bottom strips up. Pull it open. Easy.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Eli tried it at the kitchen table. He got a paper hat, and then he got stuck. Pull what open? Every way he pulled, the hat tore. He brought Marcus the ripped hat and the card.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus read his card and frowned. Every step on it was right, but his hands did more than it said. After the hat, you open it at the bottom and flatten it into a diamond. Then you fold the bottom corners up and flatten it again. He had skipped what he no longer noticed doing.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he folded one slowly and wrote down every move as his hands made it. What you need: one sheet of paper. Then seven steps, in the order they really happen. Seven, not four.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Eli followed the new card without asking a single question. Hat. Diamond. Smaller diamond. Pull the top corners apart. The boat popped open, and it floated in the sink.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Explaining how to do something has two parts: say what is needed, then give every step in order. The test is to picture a stranger following your words. A missing step leaves them stuck, and steps out of order leave them with a mess.
description: "The paper boat", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] I think, because.
description: The title of the story "I think, because", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mia's class wanted a pet. When the teacher asked why, twelve kids shouted at once. Because pets are cool! Because! Just because! The teacher waited for the noise to stop. That is not a reason, she said. That is a wish.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mia wanted the pet more than anyone. But she could hear that the shouting was not working. Wanting something was not the same as making a case for it. What did a case even look like?
description: "I think, because", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then Leo stood up for a hamster. I think we should get a hamster, because hamsters are fun. The class clapped. The teacher nodded and asked him for a second reason. Leo opened his mouth, closed it and sat down.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mia put up her hand and said it in order. I think our class should get a fish. Because a fish would teach us to take care of something every day. Because a fish is quiet and will not bother the class next door.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she said it again, in new words. A fish would be the perfect classmate. The teacher wrote it on the board in four lines: what I think, a reason, a reason, and what I think again.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They voted, and the fish won. It got a name, Captain Bubbles, and a job chart.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is how to give a reason. Say what you think. Say because, with two real reasons. Then say it again at the end in fresh words. A wish only gets clapped for. A reason gets a fish.
description: "I think, because", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Georgette and the letter.
description: The title of the story "Georgette and the letter", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] When Georgette was small, she read everything and had never written a real letter. Her grandmother lived a day's drive away and wrote every week in handwriting like lace. Georgette wanted to answer with something worth reading. Her first try was a page of loose facts that wandered like a lost cat. She had a lot to say and no idea where to put it.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her the shape of a paragraph. Say the big idea in the first sentence. Then give details that hold it up. Georgette started over. Our new house is small, but it is perfect. My room has a window seat. The kitchen smells like toast. The yard has a tree made for climbing.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she read each sentence and asked the test question: is this about the same idea? The neighbor's dog barks at the mailman. That one was about the dog, not the house. It moved to a paragraph of its own, with its own first sentence.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her second letter explained how to fold a paper boat. Fold in half, corners down, strips up, pull it open. Two weeks later her grandmother wrote back that she had made a very nice paper hat and worn it to the grocery store. Georgette laughed until her stomach hurt. She had skipped the steps her hands did without thinking.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So she folded a boat slowly and wrote down every move. What you need: one sheet of paper. Then all seven steps, in order, from the first fold to pulling the top corners apart. The next letter from her grandmother had a photo inside: a paper boat floating in her kitchen sink.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third letter was a case. Georgette thought the family should visit at Christmas instead of summer. I think we should come at Christmas, she wrote, because the whole family is off school and work at once, and because you have never seen me in the Christmas play.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she said it again in new words, the way her teacher had shown her. Christmas is the one time we can all be at your table. Her grandmother read it twice and said yes the same afternoon.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Georgette kept every letter her grandmother sent in a shoebox under her bed. Some of them had paper boats tucked inside. Years later, when she was the grandmother people wrote to, she still had them, and she still answered every one in paragraphs.
description: "Georgette and the letter", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three bags.
description: The title of the story "Three bags", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ben was helping at his aunt's apple stall at the farmers market. A customer pointed at three paper bags, five apples in each, and asked how many apples that was. Ben counted every apple with his finger. One, two, three. The customer sighed. Ben lost his place and started over.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His aunt could say the answer before he opened the second bag. Fifteen. Every time. Was she guessing? The apples smelled sweet, and the line was getting longer.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She tipped the apples onto the table in three rows of five. Five, ten, fifteen, she said, tapping one row at a time. Three groups of five is three fives added together: five plus five plus five. That is all multiplying is. Three times five is fifteen.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Rows and columns like that have a name, she said. An array. Count the rows, count how many are in each row, and multiply.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next customer wanted four bags with three apples in each. Ben made four rows of three. Twelve. Then he turned the tray sideways, and the rows became three rows of four. Still twelve. Four groups of three and three groups of four were the same apples, seen from a new side.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first number says how many groups. The second says how many are in each one. Whenever things come in equal groups, you do not have to count them one by one. Groups times how many in each group, and the counting is already done.
description: "Three bags", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Seven times eight.
description: The title of the story "Seven times eight", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Every fact in the times table stuck for Lena except one. Seven times eight. She learned it every night and lost it every morning, like a sock that kept vanishing in the wash.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandfather asked what seven times eight even meant. Fifty-six, she said. No, he said, what does it mean? Lena did not know. She had been memorizing a sound, not a thing.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He drew a rectangle of dots on a napkin, seven across and eight down. Then he turned the napkin sideways. Eight across and seven down. Seven eights and eight sevens were one rectangle, looked at two ways. Every fact works both ways, so learning half the table gets you the whole thing.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he showed her how to build the hard fact from easy ones. She already knew her fives: every fact ends in five or zero. Five eights are forty. She knew her twos, because twos just double. Two eights are sixteen. Forty and sixteen make fifty-six.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The rectangle split right down the middle to prove it: five columns on one side, two on the other, seven columns in all.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He had one more trick: say five, six, seven, eight, and there it is, because fifty-six is seven times eight. The numbers march in order, and Lena said it all the way to school.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The facts up to ten times ten are the tools every bigger problem uses. Practice a few at a time, a little each day. A fact you can picture, and build from facts you know, is a fact you keep.
description: "Seven times eight", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Deal them out.
description: The title of the story "Deal them out", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Twelve cookies, four friends, and nobody wanted to be the one who got fewer. Everyone grabbed. Somebody got five, somebody got just two, and the arguing started before anyone took a bite.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Grace took the plate back. There had to be a fair way. Twelve was too many to split by just looking. She could feel the warm cookies through the plate, and everyone was staring at her.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She dealt them out like cards. One for each friend, around the table. Then another round, and another. No favorites, no grabbing, no arguing. The plate was empty, and every plate had three. Twelve divided by four is three.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She could check it backward, too. Three cookies on each of four plates is three times four, and three times four is twelve. Dividing undoes multiplying. The same three numbers make both facts.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the doorbell rang. Two more friends, and now there were six. Nobody grabbed this time. Everyone looked at Grace. She asked herself the backward question: what times six makes twelve? Two. So each of the first four gave one cookie back, and all six had two.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Dividing is sharing out equally, one round at a time, like dealing cards. When a division looks hard, flip it around and ask the multiplying question: what times the divisor makes the total? The answer to that is the answer to this. Twelve divided by six is two, because six times two is twelve.
description: "Deal them out", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Column by column.
description: The title of the story "Column by column", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Hugo had 256 marbles in one jar and 378 in another, and he wanted one number for the whole collection. He added them in his head and got a different answer every time.
description: "Column by column", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The trouble was the ones. Six and eight make fourteen, and fourteen will not fit in one column. He wrote the whole 14 there anyway, and the answer came out enormous and wrong. Where was the extra ten supposed to go?
description: "Column by column", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher showed him to go column by column, ones first. Six and eight is fourteen. Write the 4, and carry the ten to the tens column. Tens: five and seven and the carried one make thirteen. Write the 3, and carry the hundred. Hundreds: two and three and one make six. 634 marbles.
description: "Column by column", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every number up to a thousand is built the same way, from hundreds, tens and ones. 634 is six hundreds, three tens and four ones. Each column holds one kind, and a ten that spills over belongs next door.
description: "Column by column", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then his cousin asked for 125 marbles. Two steps: put the jars together, then give some away. Ones first again. Four ones are not enough to take away five, so Hugo borrowed a ten, and fourteen take away five is nine. Two tens take away two is zero. Six hundreds take away one is five. 509 left.
description: "Column by column", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Adding and subtracting big numbers is small columns, in order. Carry when a column makes ten or more. Borrow when a column runs short. And read a two-step problem all the way through before you start.
description: "Column by column", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three ways to measure a puppy.
description: The title of the story "Three ways to measure a puppy", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The shelter sent Ellie home with a new puppy named Noodle and a chart to fill in. How long is she? How heavy is she? How much water does she drink in a day? Ellie grabbed a ruler and started with the puppy, who did not want to be measured at all.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fourteen inches, nose to tail, after four tries. Twelve inches make a foot, so Noodle was one foot and two inches long. Then Ellie held the ruler against the puppy again for the second question and stopped. A ruler cannot tell you how heavy something is.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She needed a different tool. The kitchen scale was too small, so her mom stood on the bathroom scale holding Noodle, then without her. The difference was six pounds. Pounds answer how heavy.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] For the water, Ellie poured two cups into the bowl with a measuring cup in the morning. At bedtime she poured what was left back into the cup. One cup. So Noodle drank one cup that day. Cups answer how much liquid.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her dad pointed at the gallon jug in the garage. Sixteen cups fill a gallon, he said, so that jug holds sixteen days of Noodle's water.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Three questions, three tools. A ruler for how long, a scale for how heavy, a measuring cup for how much. Every measurement starts with the question. Pick the unit that answers it, and the tool comes with it. A ruler on a puppy only ever answers one of the three.
description: "Three ways to measure a puppy", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The cars.
description: The title of the story "The cars", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Kai said most cars on their street were red. His sister Ana said blue. They sat on the porch for ten minutes to settle it and called out colors as cars went by. Red, blue, blue, white, red, blue. By the end, neither could remember the count.
description: "The cars", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So they tried again. Ana drew a line for every car under its color, and when a color reached five, she drew the fifth line across the other four. Bundles of five. Counting a bundle takes one look.

text: [warm] Frederick and the ants.
description: The title of the story "Frederick and the ants", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Frederick had an ant farm on his windowsill, a birthday present from his dad, next to the digital microscope he was still not allowed to touch without help. Twenty-four harvester ants came in a tube. His dad said they had come without a queen, so the farm would not grow, but it would be busy.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On the third morning the ants had dug four tunnels, and they would not hold still to be counted. So Frederick stopped counting ants and counted groups. Four tunnels, six ants resting in each. Four groups of six. Twenty-four, without touching a single ant.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By the second week he had the times tables to ten taped above the farm, and he used them the way other kids used a calculator. Six groups of four was the same twenty-four ants seen sideways, because every fact works both ways. His sister asked what seven eights were. Fifty-six, he said, before she finished asking.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When his dad brought home a second, bigger farm, Frederick split the colony fairly. Twenty-four ants, two farms, twelve in each. Dividing was sharing out equally, and it undid the multiplying exactly: two groups of twelve made twenty-four again.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every morning he held a ruler against the glass and measured the longest tunnel in inches. One morning the bigger farm's longest tunnel reached seven inches. He kept a tally chart of which farm dug farther each day, in bundles of five, and turned it into a bar graph. The bigger farm won by a lot. More room, more digging.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he read that a wild harvester ant colony can hold thousands of ants, and he wanted real numbers. He and his sister sat a careful step back from two anthills in the backyard, because harvester ants sting, and tallied every ant that went in for ten minutes at each hill. The first hill got 256. The second got 378.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He added them in columns, ones first. Six and eight is fourteen, so write the 4 and carry the ten. Five and seven and the carried one is thirteen, so write the 3 and carry the hundred. Two and three and one is six. 634 trips into the two hills in twenty minutes.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His dad found the sums penciled on the side of the farm and did not erase them. Frederick would be a biology professor one day. It grew on a windowsill, one tally at a time.
description: "Frederick and the ants", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The talking toaster.
description: The title of the story "The talking toaster", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Arjun's uncle had a toaster that talked. When the toast was ready, it said, done, and the bread popped up. Arjun wanted to know how it decided what to say. His uncle said the toaster only knew three things, and those three explained every computer in the world.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first thing was inputs. The lever going down, the dial set to four, the little button for bagels. Each one tells the toaster something. You do the telling.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second thing was outputs. The heat, the ding, the toast popping up, the voice saying done. Each one shows you something. The toaster does the showing.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In between was a program, a list of steps the toaster follows exactly, in order. Dial at four means this much heat for this long. Then pop, then ding, then done.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Arjun turned the dial all the way to nine to see what would happen. The toaster did exactly what it was told, and the bread came out black. It never wondered whether he meant it. A program cannot guess. It follows the steps it is given, with the inputs it is given.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then Arjun looked at his tablet. Touching the screen was an input. The picture on the screen and the sound from the speaker were outputs. The games were programs. It was the same toaster with more buttons.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Inputs tell a computer. Outputs show you. A program is the steps in between. Watch, car or toaster, every computer runs on those three.
description: "The talking toaster", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Exactly what she was told.
description: The title of the story "Exactly what she was told", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Nina wrote instructions for a jam sandwich and handed them to her big sister, who promised to follow them exactly and add nothing. Step one: put jam on the bread. Her sister picked up the whole loaf, still in its bag, and smeared jam on the outside.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nina shrieked. That was not what she meant! Her sister shrugged. It was what she wrote. Nina had never said to open the bag, or take out a slice, or open the jar. Every step she skipped, her sister skipped too.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second try was longer. Open the bag. Take out two slices. Lay them flat. Open the jar. Spread jam on one slice. But Nina put the slices together before the jam step, and her sister spread jam on the top of a closed, empty sandwich.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Two steps in the wrong order, and the whole sandwich went wrong. Nina swapped them back.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third try had eleven steps, every one in its place. Her sister followed them without making a single decision, and out came a perfect sandwich. Nina had written an algorithm: a list of steps, in order, that gets something done.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A computer follows an algorithm the way her sister did. It never guesses what you meant. If a step is missing, it skips it. If two steps are swapped, it swaps them.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] An algorithm is steps in order. The order matters, and every small step must be there, because whoever follows it will do exactly what it says and nothing else.
description: "Exactly what she was told", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] One instruction, repeated.
description: The title of the story "One instruction, repeated", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Felix wrote instructions for a bead necklace: red bead, blue bead, red bead, blue bead. Eighty lines for eighty beads. His hand ached, and somewhere in the middle he had written blue twice in a row.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher asked what all those lines had in common. Felix looked. Every pair was the same, red then blue, over and over. Eighty lines were really one pair of lines, forty times.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he rewrote the whole thing in two lines. Repeat forty times: red bead, blue bead. That is a loop, a set of steps that runs again and again. Two lines instead of eighty, and no place for a mistake to hide.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then his little sister wanted a bracelet: red, red, yellow, red, red, yellow. Felix hunted for the part that repeats. Not red, red. Not red, yellow. The part was three beads long: red, red, yellow. Repeat it six times, and she had eighteen beads.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A loop is also easy to change. When his sister wanted a longer bracelet, Felix did not rewrite anything. He changed six to eight, and the bracelet grew to twenty-four beads.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Loops are everywhere once you look. A song writes its chorus once and marks it to repeat. A staircase is one step, repeated. Even a clap, stomp, clap, stomp dance is a loop of two moves. Programs use loops to do a lot with very little.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Find the part that repeats. Write it once. Say how many times. That is a loop.
description: "One instruction, repeated", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The robot birthday.
description: The title of the story "The robot birthday", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The robot came in a box on the morning of June's birthday party. It was small and white, with two blue lights for eyes, and her aunt had built it. The first thing it did was nothing at all. Nobody had told it anything. It sat on the table like a guest who had forgotten why it came.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] June's aunt, who built robots for a living, showed her the three parts. The buttons on its back were inputs: you press them to tell the robot something. The little screen and the beep were outputs: that is how it shows you something. In between, a program waits for steps. No steps, no robot.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] June wrote her first program on an index card and typed it in with the buttons. Forward two. Turn left. Beep. The robot rolled two squares across the checkered tablecloth, turned, beeped and stopped dead, because that was the end of the card. It did exactly what it was told, and not one thing more.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Serving the cake needed more steps than anyone expected. Pick up a plate. Put a slice on it. Drive to the next guest. Hand it over. Four steps, in order, once for every guest, and there were ten guests. Written out, that was forty lines, and June's hand hurt by line twelve.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her cousin noticed that the same four steps kept repeating. So June wrote them once, inside a loop: repeat ten times. Forty lines became five. The robot served ten plates without a single mistake, and the whole program fit on a card small enough for a pocket.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The only disaster was the juice. The card said pour the juice, and nobody had said take the cap off first. The robot tipped the bottle over every cup, very politely, and not a drop came out. Everyone laughed so hard that June's grandpa had to sit down.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] June added one line above the pour: take off the cap. The juice poured, and the robot beeped once, which was the closest it could get to singing. Her aunt said June had just debugged her first program: she found the missing step and fixed it.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every computer works like that robot. Inputs tell it, outputs show you, and a program is the steps in between. The order matters, every step must be there, and a loop lets a few lines do a lot of work.
description: "The robot birthday", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three levels.
description: The title of the story "Three levels", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] On Saturday, Tomas hit a pothole on his bike, rode past a crew fixing the highway overpass and mailed a birthday card to his grandmother. Three ordinary things. Then his uncle asked him who fixes the pothole, who fixes the highway and who delivers the card.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The government, Tomas said. His uncle asked, which one? Tomas did not know there was more than one. It felt like a trick question, and the pothole was still there.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] There are three, his uncle said, stacked like floors in a building. The ground floor is local: your city, led by a mayor and a city council. It fixes streets, runs the library and sends the fire truck. The pothole belongs to them.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The middle floor is the state: Texas, led by a governor and a legislature in Austin. It builds the highways, runs the state parks and gives out driver's licenses. The top floor is national: the United States, led by a president and Congress in Washington, D.C. It prints the money and delivers the mail.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Tomas wanted the pothole gone, so his uncle took him to a city council meeting. Tomas stood up and described the hole, how deep it was and where. A council member wrote it down. Two weeks later, a city truck filled it.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Local, state and national. Three levels, three leaders, three sets of jobs. The closer the level, the easier it is to walk in and be heard, even when you are nine.
description: "Three levels", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Rule or law?
description: The title of the story "Rule or law?", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Noah got told off twice in one day. Once at school for running in the hall, and once on the way home for stepping into the street before the walk signal came on. His dad said one of those was a rule and one was a law. Noah said they felt exactly the same.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They both told him what to do. They both had someone watching. But would a police officer ever stop a kid for running down a school hallway? Noah laughed. Of course not. So what made them different?
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Who they cover, his dad said. A rule is for one group: a family, a class, a team. The school made the hall rule, and it stops at the school door. A law is for everyone in a city, a state or the whole country, and breaking it has a set punishment.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The walk signal law covers everyone in Texas. The state legislature in Austin made it. Laws for the whole country come from Congress. The President carries them out, and the courts decide what they mean when people disagree.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next day, Noah's class voted on a field trip. Fourteen kids chose the zoo and ten chose the museum. More than half picked the zoo, so the zoo won by four. That is majority rule.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The museum kids groaned, but they still got to go, and they still get a vote next time. That is the deal that makes voting work.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Rule or law, ask who it covers.
description: "Rule or law?", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The eleven dollars.
description: The title of the story "The eleven dollars", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Hana had eleven dollars. Six came from chores and five from a birthday card. At the store she found the book she wanted for eight dollars and the ball she wanted for seven. She counted her money twice. It did not get any bigger.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She tried every trick. Maybe the ball was on sale. It was not. Maybe she could pay the rest next week. The cashier smiled and shook her head. Eight and seven make fifteen, and eleven is not fifteen.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is scarcity. There is never enough for everything, so every choice gives something up. Hana chose the book. The ball stayed on the shelf, and the ball was the real cost of the book. The thing you give up has a name: the opportunity cost.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She still had three dollars, and she still wanted that ball. So on Saturday she set up a lemonade stand at the end of the driveway. Anyone in the country is free to start a business like that. It is called free enterprise.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She sold twelve cups at fifty cents each, six dollars in all, and paid her mom back one dollar for the sugar and cups. Now she had eight. She bought the ball for seven and dropped the last dollar into her savings jar.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every time you spend money, time or attention, you are not spending it on something else. The trick is not to avoid that. It is to know what you are giving up, and to choose on purpose.
description: "The eleven dollars", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Mike and the crosswalk.
description: The title of the story "Mike and the crosswalk", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike was eight and walked to school past a corner where cars did not stop. There were no stripes and no light, just a sign nobody seemed to see. His big brother had been clipped there by a car's side mirror, and his arm was bruised for a week.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike did what nobody in his house had ever done. He went to a city council meeting in a shirt his mom ironed, stood at the microphone and held up a map he had drawn of the corner. His voice shook on the first sentence and steadied by the third. The corner needs a crosswalk, he said. The mayor listened from the long table.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The street belonged to the city, so the city could paint the stripes. The council talked it over for an hour and took a vote. Five hands went up for the crosswalk and two against. Five is more than half of seven, so the crosswalk won. That is majority rule, and the two who voted no still had to help make it happen.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The light was harder. The corner sat on a state highway, and a traffic light there needed the state's permission. That meant Texas, with its governor and its legislature in Austin. The city wrote to the state highway office, and then everyone waited.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When the answer came, Mike noticed the stamp on the envelope. The mail is run by the national government, the United States, led by a president and Congress in Washington, D.C. Three levels of government, three sets of jobs, and it took all three to fix one corner.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] While he waited, Mike did chores and saved eleven dollars. At the store he wanted a book for eight dollars and a ball for seven. Eleven was not fifteen. He chose the book, and the ball was its real cost, the thing he gave up. That is called the opportunity cost.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He was learning early that there is never enough for everything. His teacher called that scarcity. Even eleven dollars had to choose. He was also learning that things get fixed by the people who show up, and that one did not have a fancy name.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The crosswalk went in the next spring, stripes first and the light a few months after. Mike watched the painters from the sidewalk. His brother crossed it first. Mike crossed it second, holding the new book. Nobody had to run.
description: "Mike and the crosswalk", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] A cup, seven ways.
description: The title of the story "A cup, seven ways", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ines drew a cup, and her art teacher said, again. Ines drew it again. Again, said the teacher, but this time only lines. Then only a flat shape. By the fourth cup, Ines was sure she was being punished.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She was not. Each cup was built from just one of the seven elements of art, the pieces every picture is made of. The teacher lined them up across the table so Ines could see them side by side.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Line was just the edges, a mark traveling around the cup. Shape was the outline filled in flat, like a paper cutout. Form was shaded on one side, so the cup looked round enough to pick up.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Color turned it red. Texture made it rough, dragged on with a dry brush. Space put the cup small and far away, with a whole empty table around it. Value used no color at all, only light, dark and every gray between.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the teacher took the line cup and drew it twice more. Once with a thick, heavy line, and the cup looked loud and sure of itself. Once with a thin, wobbly line, and the same cup looked nervous. Ines laughed. One element had changed the mood.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Seven cups, and none looked like the others. Ines had thought art was talent. It turned out to be ingredients.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The elements of art are line, shape, form, color, texture, space and value. Look for them in any picture, from a scribble to a masterpiece, and you will see how it was built.
description: "A cup, seven ways", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three jars.
description: The title of the story "Three jars", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ravi had three jars of paint, red, yellow and blue, and a picture in his head that needed orange, green and purple. He asked for more jars. His art teacher said the three jars already held everything.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He did not believe her until he mixed. Red and yellow made orange. Yellow and blue made green. Blue and red made purple. Three primary colors had made three secondary colors, and he had not opened a new jar.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he mixed blue with a little green and got blue-green, a color between the two. That kind is called tertiary: a primary mixed with the secondary beside it.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher had him set the colors in a circle. One half glowed: red, orange and yellow, the warm colors, like fire and sun. The other half sat back: green, blue and purple, the cool colors, like water and shade.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ravi painted a sunset with the warm half and a calm sea with the cool half. Then he put a small orange boat on the blue water, and it jumped off the page. Orange and blue sit across the wheel from each other. Complementary colors make each other look brighter.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] For the sky he added white to red and got pink, a tint. For the night coming in at the edges he added black to blue, a shade.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Red, yellow and blue are the primaries, and every other color on the wheel can be mixed from them. Three jars hold the whole wheel.
description: "Three jars", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Four looks.
description: The title of the story "Four looks", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Zoe looked at the painting for three seconds and said she did not like it. Her teacher said that was step four, and asked her to go back to step one.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Step one: describe. Say only what is there. A woman at a window. A letter in her hands. Gray light. A red chair. Zoe was not allowed to say whether any of it was good. Just what was there.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Step two: analyze. How is it made? The light comes in from the left and lands brightest on the letter. The chair is the only warm color in a room full of gray and blue.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Where did your eye go first, the teacher asked. To the letter. That is the focus, she said, and the painter put it there on purpose, with the brightest light in the whole picture.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Step three: interpret. What does it mean, and why do you think so? The letter matters to her. The red chair says the room is not as cold as it looks. Zoe had to point at the painting to prove each idea.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Step four: judge. Now the judging had something under it. Zoe still did not love the painting. But she could say what it was doing and how, and that the red chair was a small, smart choice.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Describe, analyze, interpret, then judge. Most people start at judging, the least interesting step, and stop there. Three looks before the verdict, and the verdict gets better.
description: "Four looks", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Chloe looks at a picture.
description: The title of the story "Chloe looks at a picture", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe always wore the brightest thing in any room, and that day it was a yellow raincoat on a dry afternoon. Her grandmother had brought her to the museum for her birthday. In front of a big painting of a boat in a storm, Chloe said, before anyone asked, that she liked it.
description: "Chloe looks at a picture", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandmother, who was not Georgette but might as well have been, smiled and said that liking it was the last thing to say, not the first. Then she made Chloe look four times, one look at a time.
description: "Chloe looks at a picture", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] First look: what is in it? Chloe was only allowed to name what was there, like a detective taking notes. A small boat. Two people. A tall mast. Dark waves, a gray-green sea, a black sky and one bright red sail. No opinions yet. Just the list.
description: "Chloe looks at a picture", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Second look: how is it built? The mast made a diagonal line, and diagonal lines feel like motion, which is why the boat seemed to tip. The waves were thick paint you could almost feel, which is texture. The red sail was the brightest color in the painting, the only warm one against all that cool gray-green. That was why her eye had gone there first. The painter had made it the focus on purpose.
description: "Chloe looks at a picture", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Third look: what might it mean? Chloe thought about the two tiny people and the one bright sail. Hope in a storm, she said. Her grandmother asked why, and Chloe pointed. Because the only warm color in the painting is the thing that keeps them going. Her grandmother nodded slowly.

text: [warm] Chloe and the worry jar.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe was fourteen the summer she looked after her cousin Nico for a week, and she had been told he was easy. He was eight, he was funny, and on the first night he cried for an hour about a spelling test that was five days away.

text: [warm and friendly] She did not know what to do, so she did what her mother did and asked what the feeling was called. Scared, he said, after a while. description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next morning she found the spelling list, twenty words, and Nico's plan to read it a hundred times on Thursday. Chloe knew that slide from her own tests. Four words a day, she said, at the kitchen table with the tablet off, and every day say yesterday's out loud first. Reading feels like remembering and is not.
description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She found a jar in the pantry and called it the worry jar. description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The friend was Leo, who had said Nico ruined a game of tag. Nico wanted to say Leo was a liar. Chloe gave him the sentence her class had practiced: what you felt, when, and what you want. I felt bad when you said I ruined it, and I want to play again. Nico practiced it on the dog, and then on Leo, who said okay.
description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By Wednesday she had noticed the pattern under everything. Nico was sleeping seven hours, because his parents were away and the house was strange. description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thursday night the jar held one slip. It said, what if I get one wrong. Chloe wrote under it, then you got nineteen right, and put it back, and in the morning Nico read both lines and laughed.
description: "Chloe and the worry jar", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He got twenty on Friday, and when his mother called that night Chloe told her all of it: the fours, the four words a day, the jar, the sentence, the bedtime. description: The title of the story "Can a robot be your friend", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The robot vacuum arrived in Room 8 on a Monday, and by Tuesday the class had named it Bolt and Rosa had asked the question that took the rest of the week. Can Bolt be our friend?

text: [warm and friendly] Miss Okafor did not answer, and instead she wrote two questions on the board, one above the other. How many legs does a spider have? Can a robot be your friend? text: [warm and friendly] So what is a friend, she asked, and the class tried. Someone who is kind to you, said Rosa. text: [warm and friendly] On Friday Miss Okafor told them about a man named Socrates, who had lived long ago in a city called Athens. He spent his days asking people what their words meant. text: [warm and friendly] Sam wanted recess before lunch instead of after, and at the class meeting he said so, and Miss Okafor asked the question she always asked. Why?

text: [warm and friendly] Because everybody wants it, said Sam, and Miss Okafor said that was a headcount and not a reason. Because I said so, said Sam, grinning, and she said that was an order. Because I want to, he tried, and she said that was a wish, and Sam ran out of becauses and sat down.

text: [warm and friendly] Recess moved before lunch in October. Sam kept the tray count on the wall, next to the words Miss Okafor had written when he first stood up: how do you know?

text: [warm] The rabbit and the fish.

text: [warm and friendly] The class pet vote was supposed to take five minutes and had already taken twenty when Miss Okafor stopped it with a rule. Nobody could speak until they had said the other person's idea back, and the other person had said that is it.
description: "The rabbit and the fish", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three boxes and a fence.
description: The title of the story "Three boxes and a fence", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The parade came down Main Street every October, and every October the fence by the bakery was the best place to watch it, if you could see over it.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya could see over it. Ben could see over it on tiptoe. Tomas, who was smallest, could see the fence. The bakery had three boxes, and Priya's first plan was one box each, which was equal, and Tomas stood on his box and saw a little more fence.

text: [warm and friendly] Ben said the plan was fair because everyone got the same. Priya looked at Tomas, who was not complaining, and said that fair had to mean everyone could see the parade, or what was the point. She gave Tomas her box. Now Tomas had two, Ben had one, and Priya had none, and all three of them could see the drums come around the corner.

text: [warm and friendly] That was the day Priya learned that fair is not always equal. Equal gives everyone the same thing. description: "Three boxes and a fence", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The rest of the day kept teaching. text: [warm and friendly] Fair by need at the fence, a rule with a reason at the drill, and cut-and-choose at the bakery. Priya went home with no box and the best view on Main Street, which was the strangest fair of all.
description: "Three boxes and a fence", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Georgette and the wondering jar.
description: The title of the story "Georgette and the wondering jar", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] History had fascinated Georgette since her grandmother's stories, and she worked her way up from teacher's aide to a history classroom of her own, where she taught for forty years. When she retired she took one thing home, a glass jar with a slot in the lid. On Thursdays at the library she set it on a table, and any child in the wonder club could drop a question in.
description: "Georgette and the wondering jar", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first rule of the club was that she would not answer. Every question was read aloud, and the club decided which kind it was. How far is the moon? A look-up question, and Dev looked it up. Is it wrong to lie to be kind? A wonder question, and nobody could look that up.

text: [warm and friendly] The second rule was what do you mean. When Lila said a lie was any untrue thing you said, Georgette asked whether an actor on a stage was lying. Lila thought and said no, because the audience knew. Then a lie needs more than untrue, said Georgette, and Lila added it on purpose, to fool someone, and the meaning got better.
description: "Georgette and the wondering jar", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third rule was because. Nobody could say what they thought without a because, and Georgette sorted the becauses out loud as they came: a headcount, an order, a wish, a real one. text: [warm and friendly] The week the club nearly broke up, two boys wanted the jar's last question to be theirs, and the argument went on until Georgette made each one say the other's idea back. description: "Georgette and the wondering jar", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fairness came up every Thursday, because a jar of questions is a jar of turns. The child who had wanted equal turns most was the one who suggested it.
description: "Georgette and the wondering jar", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The last cookie on the plate was settled the old way, one child cutting and another choosing, and the halves were so even that Georgette kept one on the table as a reminder.

text: [warm and friendly] In June a parent asked what the club was for, since it never reached an answer. text: [warm] The blade sharpener.
description: The title of the story "The blade sharpener", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya and her cousin Jonah both mowed lawns on Elm Street that summer, and both charged the same: six dollars an hour. By July, Jonah had noticed something that did not seem fair. Priya was earning almost twice as much as he was.
description: "The blade sharpener", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The difference was not the mowing. It was what Priya had learned from her grandfather the winter before, on the workbench in his garage. She could take a mower blade off, sharpen it on the grinder, and balance it so the mower did not shake. Nobody else on Elm Street could do that.

text: [warm and friendly] So the neighbors paid her for two things. Six dollars an hour to mow, and eight dollars for every blade she sharpened, which took her fifteen minutes. text: [warm and friendly] In August a windstorm came through and knocked down half the branches on the street. Everyone needed a chainsaw blade at once, and the hardware store had twelve. text: [warm and friendly] Priya understood it before Jonah did. When something is scarce and wanted, it costs more; when the truck refills the shelf, the price comes back down. She did not raise her own prices for the neighbors, but she understood why the store had.
description: "The blade sharpener", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That winter Jonah spent his Saturdays in the garage, learning the grinder. Skills are human capital, his grandfather said, and human capital is the only thing you carry to every job you will ever have. By the next summer, Elm Street had two blade sharpeners, and both of them earned for two things.
description: "The blade sharpener", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The bike that cost forty-four dollars.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus had planned the bike for a month. He knew the model, the color, and the price: sixty dollars, marked down from eighty for one week in June. He had forty dollars in his jar, and the week would end on Saturday.
description: "The bike that cost forty-four dollars", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister Dani, who was in high school and had a job, offered him a loan. Twenty dollars, she said, and you pay me back twenty-four by the end of summer. text: [warm and friendly] His friend Theo went to the same store that Saturday with thirty dollars and no plan. He came out with a remote-control car that had been by the register, a bag of candy, and three dollars. The car broke on Tuesday. The bike Theo had been talking about since April was still sixty dollars, and he had three.
description: "The bike that cost forty-four dollars", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus rode home. Every Saturday in July he mowed Miss Okafor's yard for six dollars, and every Saturday he handed Dani a share. By the middle of August he had paid back all twenty-four, and the bike was his with nothing owed on it.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo asked how it had worked. Marcus explained the two halves of it. The plan had told him what he wanted and what it cost before he walked in, so the register had no power over him. And the loan had been for something planned that he could pay back, with the interest counted before he said yes.
description: "The bike that cost forty-four dollars", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Credit is a tool, Dani told them both. Used for a plan, it gets you the bike. Used in the aisle, it turns a want into a debt, and the debt outlives the want. Theo wrote a list before his next trip to the store.

text: [warm and friendly] Ana signed up for a table at the spring fair to sell cookies, and the first thing she learned was that the table itself cost money. Five dollars for the day, whether she sold one cookie or a hundred. Her mother called it a fixed expense: it did not move.
description: "The cookie table", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The flour, sugar, butter and chocolate chips were different. Every dozen cookies she baked used up more of them, so the more she planned to sell, the more they cost. Those were variable expenses, and they grew with the batch. Four dozen cookies cost her twelve dollars in ingredients.
description: "The cookie table", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She priced the cookies at one dollar each and set out forty-eight of them under a sign. By two o'clock she had sold thirty-one. description: "The cookie table", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the kitchen table that night she did the arithmetic on a napkin. Money in: thirty-one dollars plus seven dollars and fifty cents, thirty-eight fifty. Expenses: five for the table, twelve for ingredients, seventeen. Profit: twenty-one dollars and fifty cents. Her mother made her do it twice, and it came out the same.
description: "The cookie table", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ana divided the profit the way she divided her allowance, before it could disappear: ten to spend, eight to save, and three fifty for the animal shelter jar. The deciding took a minute and the money stayed where she had put it.
description: "The cookie table", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Next year, she said, she would bake five dozen and skip the cousin. Fixed expenses stay the same, variable ones grow with what you sell, and profit is what is left when both are paid. A napkin and a pencil are enough to run a table.
description: "The cookie table", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The paycheck with a hole in it.
