text: [warm and friendly] And yet, farther down the beach, a fresh bank of sand had piled up where none had been. Where the water slowed down, it dropped what it was carrying. Dropping the pieces somewhere new is called deposition.
description: "The sandcastle", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sofia pressed a shell into the new sand bank. Her castle had not vanished. It had moved.
description: "The sandcastle", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Break, carry, drop. Weathering, erosion and deposition shape every hill, canyon and beach on Earth. A sandcastle shows in one week what a mountain shows in a million years.
description: "The sandcastle", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The right tools.
description: The title of the story "The right tools", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] At the zoo, Ravi watched a duck paddle across the pond and then walked into the desert house, where a cactus stood covered in spines. He thought both looked ridiculous. Feet like paddles. A plant like a pincushion. Why would anything grow that way?
description: "The right tools", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He asked the keeper whether the duck minded its silly feet. She asked him a question back. What would happen to a duck with feet like a chicken? He pictured it paddling hard and going nowhere.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every strange part, she said, is a tool for a problem. Webbed feet push against the water like oars. The cactus has a thick stem that stores water for the dry months, and its spines keep thirsty animals from biting in.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In the next room, a small desert fox with enormous ears was curled up asleep. Ravi guessed the ears were for hearing. They do help, the keeper said, but they also let heat escape, and that keeps the fox cool in the desert sun.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] An adaptation is a part or a habit that helps a living thing survive where it lives. The fox has a habit too. It sleeps through the hot day and hunts in the cooler night.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she asked one more question. What if you moved a polar bear to a forest? Its white fur hides it on snow. Among green trees, it would stand out.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When something looks odd, ask two questions: what problem does this place give it, and how does this part solve it? The answers turn the strangest creatures into the smartest.
description: "The right tools", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The piano.
description: The title of the story "The piano", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The movers could not lift Grandma's piano into the truck. Two of them strained until their faces went red, and the piano rose about an inch. Nina watched from the driveway, sure the piano was staying.
description: "The piano", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then they pulled a long metal ramp from the truck and laid it against the back. They rolled the piano up it, slowly, and it went in. Nina did not understand. The piano weighed the same as it had a minute ago. Where had the weight gone?
description: "The piano", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nowhere, the mover said. The ramp made a trade. Instead of lifting the piano straight up four feet, they pushed it along twelve feet of ramp. Less force, more distance. The work, the push times the distance, stayed about the same.
description: "The piano", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That ramp is a simple machine, an inclined plane. Nina counted the others that day. The dolly under the boxes rolled on wheels and axles. The crowbar that opened a crate was a lever. Next door, a flag went up its pole on a pulley.
description: "The piano", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every one made a job easier without an engine, and every one made the same trade. A long lever handle moves far so the other end can move a little and push hard.
description: "The piano", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] There are six simple machines: the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, the lever, the wheel and axle, and the pulley. None of them gives you something for nothing.
description: "The piano", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Machines do not make jobs smaller. They make them possible, by stretching a hard push into a long, easy one.
description: "The piano", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Four tests.
description: The title of the story "Four tests", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Leila's teacher tipped a box onto the table: a nail, a cork, a coin, a metal spoon, a wooden spoon and a sugar cube. Sort them, she said. Leila lined them up by size. Then by color. Neither felt like science.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher set out four tools beside them: a magnet, a bowl of water, a mug of hot water and a thermometer. Try each test on each object, she said, and write down what happens. Leila thought the answers would be boring.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The magnet grabbed the nail and ignored the cork. Iron is magnetic, and cork is not. In the bowl, the cork floated and the coin sank with a clink. The cork is less dense than water, and the coin is more.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she stood both spoons in the hot water. In less than a minute, the metal handle was too warm to hold. The wooden handle stayed cool. Metal conducts heat fast. Wood insulates, and keeps the heat from traveling.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Last, she stirred the sugar cube into a cup of water. It shrank, then vanished. It had not disappeared. It had dissolved, spreading through the water in pieces too small to see. Leave the cup on a sunny sill until the water dries up, and the sugar is left behind.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The thermometer measured the hot water. Mass, volume and temperature are properties you measure with tools. Floating, magnetism, conducting and dissolving are properties you test.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every kind of matter has properties. Measure what you can, test the rest, and a box of odd objects sorts itself.
description: "Four tests", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The strings.
description: The title of the story "The strings", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mr. Ortiz laid cards on the classroom floor: grass, grasshopper, mouse, snake, bird and hawk. Each student held a string running from a thing that gets eaten to the thing that eats it. Grass to mouse. Mouse to snake. Mouse to hawk. Grass to grasshopper to bird to hawk. Snake to hawk.
description: "The strings", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Soon the strings crossed everywhere. It looked less like a chain and more like a spider web, which, Mr. Ortiz said, was the whole idea.
description: "The strings", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he picked up the mouse card. Three strings dropped to the floor. The class expected the hawk to fall too. It ate mice, after all. But the hawk card did not move. Why not?
description: "The strings", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Because the hawk still had the snake and the bird. A food chain is one line. A food web is all the lines at once, and an animal that eats more than one thing has more than one string holding it up. A web bends where a chain would break.
description: "The strings", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The arrows in a food web run the same way as the strings, from the eaten to the eater. They show where the energy goes. And every string, followed back far enough, starts at a plant.
description: "The strings", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mr. Ortiz added one last card: mushrooms. Decomposers break down dead plants and animals and return them to the soil, which feeds the grass. The web closed into a loop.
description: "The strings", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] More links mean more ways to survive a loss. That is why a meadow full of different living things stays alive.
description: "The strings", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The night the lights went out.
description: The title of the story "The night the lights went out", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] At seven the lights went out on the whole street. The first thing anyone learned was which energy was which: the lamp had been light, the heater heat, the radio sound, the fridge motion, and all of it had been electrical until the line went down.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second thing was a circuit. The flashlight only lit when the switch closed the loop, and when the batteries went in the wrong way round, nothing. Electricity needs a complete path from the battery, through the bulb and back. Open the switch and the path is broken.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The youngest child wanted to use a metal spoon to fix a loose wire. The oldest said no. Metal is a conductor, which is why the wires inside a cord are copper, and rubber and plastic are insulators, which is why the cord is wrapped in them. Nobody touched the wire.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Outside, the storm that had cut the line was doing other work. Rain was carrying the garden soil down the path: erosion, said the oldest child, who had done it in a tray at school. At the bottom, by the gate, it was piling into a small bank: deposition.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Water had done the first part too, long before the storm. The rock by the gate was cracked where ice had frozen in it winter after winter and pushed it apart. Breaking rock down is weathering. Carrying the pieces away is erosion. Dropping them somewhere else is deposition. The path had all three.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The moths on the porch had gone quiet, and the owl in the pine did not care about the dark at all. Its large eyes gather what little light there is, and its soft-edged feathers make almost no sound. An adaptation is a body part or behavior that helps a living thing survive where it lives.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The last thing was the pump. The basement was taking on water, and the hand pump worked with a lever, a bar with a long handle that turns on a fixed point. It took a lot of pulling to lift a little water, but it lifted it. A lever trades distance for force.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When the lights came back at midnight nobody was scared of the dark anymore. They had seen energy in five forms and a loop that must be closed. They had met a conductor and an insulator, land broken and carried and dropped, animals fitted to the night, and a machine that makes a hard job possible.
description: "The night the lights went out", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The big thing first.
description: The title of the story "The big thing first", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam wrote a paragraph about dogs. They fetch. They guard the house. They guide people who cannot see. My cat sleeps all day. It was all true, and his teacher wrote one question in the margin: what is this paragraph about?
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam was annoyed. It was about dogs, obviously. But when he read it again, he saw that every sentence was a fact standing on its own. Nobody had told the reader what the facts added up to.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he wrote the big thing first. Dogs make good helpers. That is a topic sentence, and it makes a promise: the rest of the paragraph will show how.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the facts followed, and suddenly they were not loose facts. They were three ways of proving one idea. Fetching helps. Guarding helps. Guiding helps most of all.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then Sam asked the test question of every sentence: does this back up the first one? My cat sleeps all day. No. It was true, and funny, but it was about a cat, not dogs helping. It moved to a paragraph of its own.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher called the topic sentence the sign on the door. It tells you what is inside the room. Every sentence after it has to belong in that room.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Write the big thing first. Then make every sentence after it back the big thing up. A reader will know where they are going from the very first line, and so will you.
description: "The big thing first", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Longer recess.
description: The title of the story "Longer recess", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena wanted a longer recess, and so did everyone. When the principal visited, half the class shouted it at her. She smiled and said, tell me why, and the room went quiet. Wanting something, it turned out, was not a reason.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena went home and tried to write why. The first draft said recess should be longer because it should. She read it back and felt her face go hot. It was the same shout, written down.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second draft had a shape. Her opinion came first: I think recess should be longer. Then reason one, with a helper word: first, we think better after we have run around.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then reason two: also, friends who play together get along better in class. The little words first and also held the reader by the hand, one step at a time.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then a closing sentence that said the opinion again in new words: give us twenty more minutes outside, and you will get better students back. Her dad read it and said it sounded like a lawyer wrote it.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The principal read it twice, then read it to the teachers. Recess grew by ten minutes the very next week, and nobody had to shout.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] An opinion paragraph is an opinion, two reasons and a closing sentence. Say what you think at the start, prove it in the middle, and say it again at the end. That is how a wish becomes an argument.
description: "Longer recess", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The bird in the house.
description: The title of the story "The bird in the house", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] A sparrow flew in through the open door, and the whole afternoon turned upside down. That night Ava had to write about something that happened. She wrote: a bird got in and then it got out. Her teacher wrote back: I was not there. Let me see it.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ava did not know what that meant. It was true. A bird got in and got out. But reading it back, she could not see the bird either, and she had been standing right under it.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So she wrote it again in three parts. The beginning said who and where: our living room, a hot afternoon, the door propped open. Then a sparrow shot in like a thrown ball.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The middle said what happened. It circled the lamp twice, landed on the curtain rod, and everyone in the room froze with their hands up. The cat crouched under the couch, tail twitching.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The end said how it turned out. Dad slid the window open, and after one more circle the bird found the light and was gone. Nobody breathed until it was over the fence.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher circled one line: everyone froze with their hands up. Ava had not written that they were scared. She had shown it, and the reader felt it anyway.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A small story has a beginning, a middle and an end. Show what happened with words a reader can see: not a bird got in, but a sparrow like a thrown ball. Your reader was not there. Your words take them.
description: "The bird in the house", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Mike writes it down.
description: The title of the story "Mike writes it down", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike spent the summer hauling scrap with his uncle for money the house needed. The truck was old, the metal was heavy, and by July his hands had stopped hurting. He did not think of any of it as something to write about.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When school started, the first assignment was a paragraph with a topic sentence. A topic sentence tells the reader what the whole paragraph is about. Mike wrote the only big thing he knew: hard work is not the same as hard. Then the details: the truck, the weight, his hands.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher showed him how the details held the topic sentence up, the way posts hold up a fence. Take one away and the paragraph leans. Put in a detail that does not belong, like the sandwich he ate in June, and the reader stops trusting the fence. A good paragraph stays on its topic from the first sentence to the last.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The opinion paragraph was harder, because Mike had opinions and no practice saying them nicely. Recess should be longer. Reason one: kids think better after running. Reason two: kids get along better after playing. Then say the opinion again, a new way, at the end.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher wrote good in the margin, and underneath, one question: how do you know? Mike added a fact. After recess, his class had finished a math page faster than before it. An opinion with a reason is stronger. An opinion with a reason and a fact is harder to argue with.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The small story was about the bird that got into the house that August. Every story needs a problem, and a bird in the living room is a good one. Beginning: the door left open in the heat. Middle: the bird on the curtain rod and everyone frozen. End: his uncle opening the window, and the bird finding its way out into the yard.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Revising was the part Mike liked least and learned most from. He read the story out loud and heard where it dragged. He cut two sentences about the curtain, added the sound of the wings, and changed went to flew. The story got shorter and better at the same time.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike had not known a summer of scrap could be a story. It turned out everything could, if you gave it a beginning, a middle and an end, and then read it out loud and fixed what you heard. He kept every page in a folder with the truck drawn on the front.
description: "Mike writes it down", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three kitchens.
description: The title of the story "Three kitchens", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] When Diego's class was asked what the first Texans ate, he said buffalo, because that was the picture in every book. His teacher put a map of Texas on the wall and asked where. Diego waved his hand over the whole state.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she pointed at three places. The wet forests of the east. The dry, open plains of the north and west. The gray, marshy coast. Would a buffalo hunter do well in a marsh? Would a fisher do well on a dry plain? Diego was not so sure anymore.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In the wet east, rain fell often and the soil was rich. The Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash, and they lived in villages of tall, round houses made of grass. People who farm can stay put.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On the dry plains, the Comanche followed the buffalo on horseback. They rode into Texas in the 1700s, on horses whose ancestors had come over with the Spanish. The herds kept moving, so the people carried tipis they could pack.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Along the coast, the Karankawa fished the bays from dugout canoes and gathered shellfish. They moved with the seasons, camping wherever the food was best that season.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Many nations lived in Texas, and they traded, fought and made peace with one another for centuries. When Spain, Mexico and the United States arrived, each found peoples already at home.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Land decides a way of life. Look at where a people lived, and you can guess what they ate, what they built and how far they moved. The map was the first cookbook.
description: "Three kitchens", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The mission bell.
description: The title of the story "The mission bell", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The bell in the old mission near San Antonio had rung every morning for about a hundred years, since Spain built the mission, its walls and the little farm around it. Lucia's great-great-grandmother had heard it as a girl. The bell never changed.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Spain had claimed Texas in the 1500s. From the 1690s on, it built missions and forts to spread its faith and hold the land, and San Antonio grew up around them. Lucia had never known any flag on the pole but Spain's.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then, in 1821, Mexico won its independence from Spain. One morning the bell rang under a new flag on the same pole. Texas was part of Mexico now. Lucia wondered how a place could belong to one country at breakfast and another by lunch.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mexico had a problem. Texas was huge and had few settlers, and an empty land is hard to hold. So Mexico opened the door to American settlers. Stephen F. Austin brought the first three hundred families in the 1820s.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They came, and kept coming. Within about ten years, Americans outnumbered the Tejanos, the Texans of Mexican descent like Lucia's family. The newcomers disagreed with Mexico City about laws, language and slavery.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The bell rang over more and more faces that had never seen Spain or Mexico. One of the old missions had another name by then: the Alamo.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Two flags in a row, Spain and then Mexico, and the roots of a third growing under the same bell. The missions are still standing, and some still ring their bells.
description: "The mission bell", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The thirteen days.
description: The title of the story "The thirteen days", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike wanted to know why the most famous battle in Texas was one Texas lost. Georgette poured the tea, spread an old map on the table and put her finger on San Antonio.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In the fall of 1835, she said, Texans rose up against Mexico. Late that winter, Santa Anna's army surrounded the Alamo, an old mission in San Antonio. On March 2, 1836, while it was still under siege, Texans signed a declaration that Texas was free.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] About two hundred defenders held the Alamo for thirteen days. On March 6, the army broke through, and the defenders who fought were killed. A few women, children and one enslaved man named Joe survived to tell what happened.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Georgette slid her finger east to a bend where two waters met. About six weeks later, here at San Jacinto, Sam Houston's army attacked on the afternoon of April 21. The battle lasted eighteen minutes. Santa Anna was captured the next day, and Texas was free.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mike looked from one finger to the other. So why remember the loss?
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Because the Texans at San Jacinto did, Georgette said. They charged shouting, Remember the Alamo, and the name carried them. Many Texans believe those thirteen days also bought the rest of Texas time.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] For nine years Texas was its own country, the Republic of Texas, and Sam Houston was elected its first president. That is why its flag has one star. Georgette folded the map. Some defeats are not the end of a story. They are part of the price of the ending.
description: "The thirteen days", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The 28th star.
description: The title of the story "The 28th star", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Mia found an old flag in her grandfather's attic with twenty-eight stars on it, not fifty. He told her the twenty-eighth star was Texas. For nine years Texas had been a country of its own. Then, in 1845, it joined the United States as the twenty-eighth state.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Mexico had never accepted that Texas was free, and a fight over the border helped start a war between the United States and Mexico in 1846. When it ended, the border was the Rio Grande.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] But the story was not a straight line. In 1861 Texas left the Union to join the Confederacy in the war over slavery. Mia asked whether the star came off the flag. It did not. The United States never removed the stars of the states that left.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When that war ended, freedom did not reach Texas the day it was declared. Mia asked how freedom could be late. The news traveled slowly, and some people did not want it heard.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On June 19, 1865, Union soldiers arrived in Galveston with the order that every enslaved person in Texas was free. That day became Juneteenth, a holiday that began in Texas and now belongs to the whole country.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then, in 1901, at Spindletop near Beaumont, oil roared out of the ground, and Texas changed again. Six flags had flown over Texas by then: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederacy and the United States.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Statehood in 1845, the Confederacy in 1861, Juneteenth in 1865 and oil in 1901. History is a line with bends in it.
description: "The 28th star", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Six flags over one town.
description: The title of the story "Six flags over one town", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The town had been a town for a very long time. Before the roads, the Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash on the river flats to the east, and the Comanche rode the plains beyond. People had lived on this ground for thousands of years before anyone raised a flag over it.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then a mission bell rang, and Spain called the place its own for more than a hundred years, though the priests were few and the settlers fewer. For a few years a French explorer named La Salle kept a fort on the coast, and France claimed the land too. His fort did not last, but his flag is still counted.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In 1821 a new flag went up: Mexico, newly free of Spain. Mexico opened the door to families from the north, and Stephen F. Austin led the first of them to farms along the Brazos. More came than anyone planned, and they brought their own ideas about how they wanted to be governed.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The arguments turned into a war. In October 1835 the first shots were fired at Gonzales, over a small cannon. In March 1836 the Alamo fell. In April, at San Jacinto, the fight took eighteen minutes, and the town belonged to a new country, the Republic of Texas, with a single star on its flag.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The Republic had to do everything a country does, with very little money. It printed its own paper money, which soon lost most of its value. It moved its capital more than once and chose Austin in 1839. Sam Houston led it twice, and people argued about joining the United States the whole time.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nine years after San Jacinto the star joined twenty-seven others. Texas was the 28th state. Sixteen years after that, in 1861, Texas left the Union and joined the Confederacy, and the town sent its young men to the Civil War. After the war, on June 19, 1865, a Union general announced in Galveston that the enslaved people of Texas were free, and Juneteenth began.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The flags in the town square today tell the whole story in cloth: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic, the Confederacy and the United States. Six flags, but more than six peoples, because the Caddo and the Comanche were here before any cloth went up a pole.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The children who walk past them on the way to school are walking the same ground the Caddo farmed. One of them stopped to count the stars on the last flag. Fifty. The single star is still there too, on the Texas flag beside it.
description: "Six flags over one town", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Twenty-three boxes.
description: The title of the story "Twenty-three boxes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The art teacher asked Leo to count the crayons in the supply room. There were 23 boxes with 4 crayons in each. Leo started multiplying in his head, lost the number and started again. Twenty-three fours is a lot to hold at once.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He tried counting the crayons one at a time and got to thirty before the teacher came back. This was going to take all afternoon. The boxes smelled like wax, and he was tired of them already.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he broke the 23 into pieces he could handle: twenty boxes and three boxes. Twenty boxes of four is 80 crayons. Three boxes of four is 12. And 80 plus 12 is 92. Two easy multiplications and one addition, instead of one hard one.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher was impressed, so she gave him a harder one. The markers came in 14 bags of 23. Now both numbers were big. Leo broke both of them. Twenty and three. Ten and four.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He multiplied every piece by every piece. Twenty times ten is 200. Twenty times four is 80. Three times ten is 30. Three times four is 12. Then he added them: 200, 80, 30 and 12 make 322 markers.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He checked with a picture: a rectangle 23 wide and 14 tall, cut into four smaller rectangles, one for each piece. The four areas added up to the whole.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every big multiplication is a set of small ones in disguise. Break the numbers into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add the pieces together.
description: "Twenty-three boxes", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Sharing in rounds.
description: The title of the story "Sharing in rounds", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Grace had a sheet of 96 stickers and four friends waiting. She did not want to hand them out one at a time. That was 96 moves, and her friends were already bored.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So she tried a bigger step. Could everyone get twenty? Four twenties is 80. Yes. She peeled off twenty for each friend and had 16 left. Sixteen was a much smaller problem than 96.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Second round. Four more each used up all 16. Twenty and four: every friend had 24, and the sheet was empty. Share the big part first, see what is left, then share that.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her the written way, one digit at a time. How many fours fit in 9, the first digit? Two, with 1 left over. Bring down the 6 to make 16. How many fours fit in 16? Four, exactly. The digits made 24. The same answer, in a tidier tower.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next day her little brother added one more sticker to the sheet, 97 in all. Everyone got 24 again, and one sticker was left in her hand. That leftover is the remainder: 97 divided by 4 is 24, remainder 1.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] To check it, Grace multiplied back. Four times 24 is 96. Add the remainder, 1, and you get 97. The check came out exactly.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Long division shares a big number in steps. Share what you can, bring down what is left, and always check by multiplying back and adding the remainder.
description: "Sharing in rounds", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Twelve chairs.
description: The title of the story "Twelve chairs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Dev had to set out twelve chairs for the school play, in equal rows. He put them in one long row of twelve and stepped back. It looked like a bus. He tried five rows and had two chairs left over with nowhere to go.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Some numbers of rows worked, and some did not, and he could not tell which until he had dragged every chair. There had to be a way to know first.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He wrote down the ones that worked. One row of twelve. Two rows of six. Three rows of four. Four rows of three. Six rows of two. Twelve rows of one. The numbers that worked were 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Those are the factors of twelve, his teacher said: the numbers that go into it exactly, with nothing left over. Five was not a factor. That was why two chairs had nowhere to go.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] For the next show, the class wanted chairs in rows of four. Four, eight, twelve, sixteen, twenty: any of those numbers of chairs would fill the rows exactly. Those are the multiples of four, what four makes when you count by it.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then a latecomer brought a thirteenth chair. Dev tried every row he could think of. Only one long line worked. Thirteen has exactly two factors, itself and one, so it is prime.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A factor goes into a number exactly. A multiple is what a number makes. A prime has exactly two factors. And a prime number of chairs only ever makes one long line.
description: "Twelve chairs", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The quarter.
description: The title of the story "The quarter", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] June found a quarter on the sidewalk and asked her dad why it was called that. Because it is a quarter of a dollar, he said. But he also called it twenty-five cents, and the price tag at the store said 0.25. Three names, one small coin.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She lined up four quarters, and they made a dollar. So one quarter was one fourth of the whole. But twenty-five? And that dot in 0.25? None of it looked like a fourth.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her dad drew a dollar as a hundred pennies in a square, ten rows of ten. A quarter covered twenty-five of them. Twenty-five out of a hundred can be written as a fraction, 25/100, or as a decimal, 0.25. One fourth, twenty-five hundredths and 0.25 are the same money.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice. Read 25/100 as the story means it, never as a date.

text: [warm and friendly] A decimal is a fraction with 10 or 100 on the bottom, he said, written with a point instead of a line. The first place after the point is tenths. The second is hundredths.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So a dime is one tenth of a dollar, 0.1. Three dimes are 0.3, and so are thirty pennies, 0.30. The zero at the end changes nothing, because three tenths and thirty hundredths are the same amount.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he gave her a puzzle. Which is more, 0.7 or 0.65? June said 0.65, because 65 looks bigger than 7. Her dad lined up the points. Seven tenths against six tenths. Seven dimes beat six dimes and a nickel. The tenths decide first.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fractions and decimals are two names for one amount. Read decimals place by place, tenths first.
description: "The quarter", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Half and a quarter.
description: The title of the story "Half and a quarter", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Two boxes came back from the party. Half a pizza in one, a quarter of a pizza in the other. Mateo wanted to know how much pizza that was altogether. He wrote one half plus one fourth, then stopped. Halves and fourths were different sizes.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He tried adding the tops and the bottoms and got two sixths, which was less pizza than he had started with. That could not be right. The cheese was cold, and the math was getting worse.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he cut. One slice of the pizza wheel through the half, and it became two quarters. Now every piece was a quarter. Two quarters plus one quarter is three quarters. Same bottoms, so he added the tops and kept the bottom.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next weekend there were leftovers from two parties: seven quarter slices in all. Seven fourths. Mateo laid them out. Four quarters made one whole pizza, and three quarters were left over. Seven fourths is one and three fourths.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister ate three of the slices. Seven fourths take away three fourths is four fourths. Same bottoms, so he subtracted the tops. Four fourths was exactly one whole pizza.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the end, he looked at a pizza cut into eighths with four slices left. Four eighths. Both numbers could be divided by four, so four eighths was the same as one half. Simplify at the end, and the answer gets easier to read.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fractions add and subtract when their pieces are the same size. Same bottoms: work with the tops, keep the bottom.
description: "Half and a quarter", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Around and inside.
description: The title of the story "Around and inside", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Hannah's mom asked her to measure the new garden bed so they could buy fence wire and soil. Hannah walked around the edge with a tape measure: four feet, three feet, four feet, three feet. Fourteen feet. She wrote down fourteen and thought she was done.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the store, fourteen feet of wire was exactly right. Then her mom picked up the soil bags and asked how many square feet the bed was. Hannah said fourteen. Her mom tilted her head. Was it, though?
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The wire went around the edge. The soil filled the inside. Those were two different questions, and one number could not answer both.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At home, Hannah drew the bed on grid paper, one square for every square foot. Four rows of three squares. Twelve squares. The bed covered twelve square feet, not fourteen. That was the area. The fourteen feet around the edge was the perimeter.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They had bought soil for fourteen square feet, so two square feet of soil were left in the bag. Her little brother used them to plant a single sunflower by the back steps.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her mom gave her a harder one: a square sandbox, five feet on every side. Around the edge: five, five, five and five, twenty feet. Inside: five rows of five, twenty-five square feet. Hannah did not mix them up this time.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Perimeter is the walk around the edge, measured in feet. Area is the surface covered, measured in square feet. Before you measure, ask which one the question wants.
description: "Around and inside", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The door.
description: The title of the story "The door", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Kai's homework asked for an acute angle, a right angle and an obtuse angle from around the house. He looked at the clock, the table and the roof and could not find any. He even checked under the bed. Angles seemed to live only on worksheets.
description: "The door", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then his little sister opened his door a crack to spy on him. The door and the wall made a thin wedge. Kai pushed it a bit wider. A bigger wedge. He pushed it straight out. A square corner.
description: "The door", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The door had been drawing angles the whole time. Barely open, a small wedge: acute, less than a right angle, like the tip of a pizza slice. Kai drew it in his notebook.
description: "The door", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Straight out from the wall: a right angle, 90 degrees, the corner of a square. Pushed farther: obtuse, wider than a right angle but not yet flat, like a chair tipped back.
description: "The door", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he swung it all the way back until it lay flat against the wall beside it. A straight angle: 180 degrees, two right angles side by side.
description: "The door", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister pointed at the top and bottom edges of the door. They ran side by side and never met, like railroad tracks. Parallel. The edge of the door met the floor in a square corner. Perpendicular. Kai wrote both words down before he forgot them.
description: "The door", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Angles are everywhere two lines meet. A right angle is 90 degrees, acute is smaller and obtuse is wider. Open any door, and you can see all of it.
description: "The door", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Chloe and the mural.
description: The title of the story "Chloe and the mural", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe was nine and had been given a wall. The community center wanted a mural, her art teacher had said she could plan it, and planning turned out to be arithmetic. The wall was 23 feet wide and 4 feet high, and she wanted a row of 4 birds for every foot of it.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That was 23 times 4. She broke it into 20 times 4 and 3 times 4, eighty plus twelve, ninety-two birds. Breaking a number apart by place value turns a hard multiplication into two easy ones. She drew ninety-two birds on graph paper and lost count twice.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The paint came in cans that each covered 96 square feet. Area counts the squares that would cover a flat shape, and a rectangle takes length times height: 23 times 4, which she already knew was 92 square feet. One can would cover the wall once, with 4 square feet to spare. Two coats meant two cans.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The birds needed to be arranged in equal rows. Factors are numbers that multiply together to make another number. Twelve chairs can go one by twelve, two by six or three by four. Ninety-two birds could go one by ninety-two, two by forty-six or four by twenty-three.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Not three by anything, she found, because 92 is not a multiple of 3. She tried dividing and got 30 with 2 left over. A remainder, her teacher said, is what is left when things will not share out evenly. Chloe chose four rows of twenty-three.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The sky took a quarter of the wall and the grass a fourth. She wrote each as 0.25, a decimal, and added them: 0.50, the same as a half. Chloe had never cared about fractions and decimals until they told her where the horizon went. The birds would fly across the half in between.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On painting day, twelve volunteers came. Chloe split the ninety-two birds among them: 92 divided by 12 is 7 with 8 left over, so eight people painted eight birds and four painted seven. Nobody had to paint a fraction of a bird. Division, she decided, was fair sharing with a pencil.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The mural is still on the wall of the center. The birds are a little uneven, and she likes that now. Every time she walks past, she counts them, and every time there are ninety-two. She thinks of the numbers underneath the paint: the product, the area, the factors, the remainder and the decimals that put the sky in its place.
description: "Chloe and the mural", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The pizza of notes.
description: The title of the story "The pizza of notes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Bea counted the notes in one measure and got seven. The measure was only supposed to hold four beats, so she decided the music was broken. Her teacher asked her to add the notes up instead of counting them.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A whole note is the whole pizza: four beats. A half note is half the pizza: two beats. A quarter note is one slice: one beat. An eighth note is half a slice: half a beat. Each note lasts half as long as the one before it.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Bea's seven notes were one quarter note and six eighth notes. The quarter was one beat. The six eighths were half a beat each, and six halves make three. One beat plus three beats. Four beats. Not broken at all.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The number of notes did not matter at all. What mattered was how long each one lasted, and how they added up.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She drew the measure as a pizza and every note as a piece, and the pieces always filled the plate. When they did not fill it, she had miscounted, and the empty space on the plate showed her where.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Four quarter notes fill a measure of four beats. So do two half notes, or one whole note, or eight eighth notes. Notes are fractions of a measure, and they add up the same way fractions do.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Whole, half, quarter, eighth: four beats, two, one and a half. A measure is a plate that has to be full.
description: "The pizza of notes", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The ladder of letters.
description: The title of the story "The ladder of letters", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Luis could play any note if you told him its name, but he could not find the name on the page. Five lines, four spaces, and a dot somewhere on them. It looked like a fence with a bird on it.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher called the staff a ladder. Some ladders you climb with your feet. This one you climb with your eyes. Every rung and every gap between the rungs has a letter, and every note sits either on a line or in a space.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The lines of the treble staff, from the bottom up, are E, G, B, D and F. To remember them, she said: Every Good Boy Does Fine. Luis said it three times on the walk home.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The spaces, from the bottom up, are F, A, C and E. They spell a word you already know: face. Four letters, four spaces, one face.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] And the ladder went up in pitch. A dot higher on the staff was a higher note. Luis put his finger on the bottom line, E, and climbed, naming each rung and gap as he went: E, F, G, A, B, C, D, E, F.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By the end of the week, the bird on the fence had turned into a note he could name and play without stopping to count.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Five lines and four spaces; lines E, G, B, D, F; spaces F, A, C, E. Higher on the staff is higher in pitch. Learn two sayings, and you can name any note on the staff.
description: "The ladder of letters", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Four Italian words.
description: The title of the story "Four Italian words", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Nora played the piece exactly as written, every note right, and her teacher said it sounded like a grocery list. Nora asked what was missing. Her teacher pointed at four words she had skipped because they were not notes.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Forte means loud. Piano means soft. Those two are dynamics: how loud or soft to play. The piano got its name from them, her teacher said. Its full name, pianoforte, means soft-loud, because it could play both.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Allegro means fast. Adagio means slow. Those two are tempo: how fast the music goes. A composer writes the words right on the page so every player in the orchestra plays it the same way.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nora played it again with the words. The opening was piano and adagio, soft and slow, like someone tiptoeing into a room. The middle was forte and allegro, and the room filled with people and noise.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Same notes, same order. But now it sounded like a piece of music instead of a list. Her little brother, who never listened to her practice, came to the door to hear the ending.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher played two examples. A lullaby, piano and adagio, soft and slow. A march, forte and allegro, loud and fast. Nora could have guessed the words just from hearing them.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Forte is loud, piano is soft; tempo is speed, allegro fast and adagio slow. The notes say what to play. The Italian words say how, and how is most of the music.
description: "Four Italian words", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The school concert.
description: The title of the story "The school concert", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The concert began the way every rehearsal had, with the teacher tapping a pencil on the stand: tick, tick, tick, tick. The beat came first, before any note, and the twenty-two players found it the way you find a heartbeat, without looking. Every piece they would play that night rested on it.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The first piece was all quarter notes, one beat each, four to a measure. The time signature at the start said so: a 4 over a 4, four beats in every measure, and a quarter note gets one. Nobody rushed. Rushing is what happens when players stop listening to the beat.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second piece had a solo, and the soloist read it off the staff the way she had learned in September. Every Good Boy Does Fine named the lines from the bottom up, and FACE spelled the spaces. Reading music is reading a map of sound: higher on the staff means higher in pitch.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The half notes held for two beats, and the eighth notes came in pairs, two to a beat, quick as footsteps. The rests were the hardest part. A rest is a beat of silence that still counts, and the whole band had to keep counting through it and come back in together.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the end of the solo a whole note sat for four full beats while the room held still. Four beats is a long time to hold one sound, long enough to hear your own breathing. The soloist let it ring, then lowered her flute. Nobody clapped yet, because the page had one more piece on it.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The last piece was marked forte and allegro, loud and fast, and the drums took it at a run. In the middle the music swelled, a crescendo, each measure louder than the one before, until the trumpets were shining.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then, on the final page, a word nobody had noticed in rehearsal: piano. It means soft. The whole band dropped to a whisper, and the piece ended slow, adagio, on one long note that faded until nobody could tell when it stopped. Loud is easy. Soft, played together, takes a whole band listening.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The applause was forte. Nobody had told it to be. Afterward the teacher said the band had played the notes right all year, but tonight they had played the music: the loud and the soft, the fast and the slow, and the silence in between.
description: "The school concert", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The night librarian.
description: The title of the story "The night librarian", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ezra stayed up late finishing a game, and the next morning he could not remember what his teacher had said the day before. He had listened. It had gone in. It just was not there anymore.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His mom said the brain has a librarian who only works nights. All day long, new memories pile up on her cart: a spelling word, a math trick, a friend's joke. At night, while you sleep, she files them onto shelves where you can find them later.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Skip the night, and the cart stays full. Some things slide off before they are ever filed. That is why a tired morning feels like a cart with a wobbly wheel.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ezra asked how long her shift was. For a kid his age, nine to eleven hours of sleep a night. Growing bodies and busy brains need all of it, every night.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] And screens off an hour before bed, his mom said. The light from a screen tells the brain it is still daytime, and the librarian does not clock in.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That week Ezra went to bed on time and left his tablet in the kitchen. On Friday, he remembered every word on the spelling test, even the ones he had studied the night before, and it felt easy.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sleep is when the brain sorts and stores what you learned. Study, then sleep, and more of it stays. Nine to eleven hours, and the screen goes off first.
description: "The night librarian", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The serving size.
description: The title of the story "The serving size", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Isla compared two cereal boxes and picked the one with less sugar on the label: nine grams against fourteen. Easy choice. Her dad asked her to read the very first line before she decided. Serving size: half a cup on hers, one cup on the other.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every number on a label is per serving. Nine grams in half a cup was eighteen grams in a whole cup. Her cereal had won a race it should not have, because it had run only half the distance.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her dad showed her the ingredients list. Ingredients are listed from most to least, so the first word is what the food is mostly made of. Her box began with sugar. The other began with whole grain oats.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Isla felt a little tricked. The label had told the truth twice, in small print. She had just read the big number first, like almost everyone does.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her dad turned the box over. Protein, he said, from beans, eggs, fish or meat, builds and repairs muscle. Fruits and vegetables bring vitamins. A good breakfast has more than cereal in the bowl.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Isla chose the oats, sliced a banana on top and poured herself a glass of milk. She read the serving size on every box in the pantry that weekend, just to catch them.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Check the serving size first, because every number is per serving. Then the sugar, then the first three ingredients. The small print tells the real story.
description: "The serving size", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The top of the stairs.
description: The title of the story "The top of the stairs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Andre raced up four flights of stairs at the library and wanted to know what his heart had done about it. He pressed two fingers on the inside of his wrist, below his thumb, and felt his pulse thumping. His aunt, a nurse, showed him how to count.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Count the beats for fifteen seconds, she said, then multiply by four. At the top of the stairs, Andre counted 36 beats in fifteen seconds. Thirty-six times four: 144 beats a minute.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Why so fast? Working muscles need more oxygen, and blood carries it to them, so his heart pumped faster to send more blood.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then his aunt had him rest and count again one minute later: 28 beats, or 112 a minute. His heart was already settling. How quickly a heart slows back down after hard work is called recovery, and it is one of the best signs of fitness.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Andre decided to try an experiment. For a month he played hard for about an hour every day: soccer, biking, tag with his cousins. It all counted, even in pieces.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he raced the same stairs and counted again. Nearly as fast at the top. But one minute later, his pulse had dropped much further than before. Training makes the heart stronger, so it pumps more blood with every beat, and the body learns to calm it down faster after hard work.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Muscles at work need more blood, so the heart speeds up. An hour of active play a day trains it, and a fit heart settles fast.
description: "The top of the stairs", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Twenty, twenty, twenty.
description: The title of the story "Twenty, twenty, twenty", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Zara's eyes ached after homework, and she could not fall asleep after watching videos in bed. She figured that was just how screens were. Everybody she knew had tired eyes.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her school nurse gave her three rules that fit on one sticky note. The first was for her eyes. Every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. Staring at something close keeps the focusing muscles in your eyes working hard, and looking far away lets them relax.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The second rule was for sleep. Screens off an hour before bed, because the light from a screen tells the brain it is still daytime. Zara moved her phone charger to the kitchen.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third rule was not about her body at all. Anything she shared online, a photo, a message, where she was, went past a trusted adult first. And never her address or her school.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Zara asked why. What goes online stays online, the nurse said. A photo can be copied and passed around long after you delete it, by people you will never meet.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A week later, Zara's eyes felt better by the end of homework, and she fell asleep faster. She stuck the note on her desk where she could see it, and one on her little brother's tablet too.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Screens are useful and fun, and they have costs. A break every twenty minutes, off an hour before bed, and nothing shared without a trusted adult.
description: "Twenty, twenty, twenty", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The week the phone charged and I did not.
description: The title of the story "The week the phone charged and I did not", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The notebook started as a dare from a teacher: one week, write down when you sleep, what you eat, when you move and when you look at a screen. No rules, no grades, just the truth on paper. The notebook was small enough for a pocket. Monday was honest and a little embarrassing.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nine hours of sleep, but the last hour before sleep had been a screen, and the morning felt like wading. Children need about nine to twelve hours of sleep. The brain, the teacher had said, files the day at night, and Monday's files were still on the desk.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Tuesday was the cereal. Twelve grams of sugar per serving, and the serving was half of what went in the bowl, so the bowl held twenty-four. Sugar was the second ingredient on the list, and ingredients are listed from most to least, so there was a lot of it. Reading a label is reading the truth about food.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Wednesday was the stairs. Sitting still, the heart beat twelve times in ten seconds, seventy-two a minute. At the top of the stairs it was twenty-five in ten seconds. A minute later, eighteen. After two minutes, thirteen. The heart came back fast, and that, it turned out, was the whole point.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A heart that recovers quickly is a heart that is getting stronger. Kids need about an hour of moving every day, and it does not have to happen all at once. Recess counted. So did the walk to the bus and the stairs, twice.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thursday was the screens. The tablet had been on for two hours straight, and the eyes felt dry and tired. The teacher's rule: every twenty minutes, look at something twenty feet away for twenty seconds. The eyes need to change focus, the way legs need to change position.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thursday dinner was a plate the notebook could be proud of: half of it fruits and vegetables, green and orange, a quarter grain, a quarter protein, and water instead of soda. Nobody had planned it that way. The notebook had just made the plate easier to see.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By Friday the notebook had a rule in it that nobody had assigned: the phone charges overnight, and so do I. Screens off an hour before bed, eyes up every twenty minutes, half the plate green and orange, an hour of moving in whatever pieces the day allowed. Nothing in the week had been hard. It had only needed to be written down.
description: "The week the phone charged and I did not", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] A face, a flower, a fence.
description: The title of the story "A face, a flower, a fence", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Felix drew a face and folded the paper down the middle. The two halves matched. Then he drew a flower from above, and no fold worked. It matched all the way around its center instead. His teacher said he had found two of the three kinds of balance by accident.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A face is symmetrical: the same on both sides of a line. It feels calm, like the front of a cathedral. A flower seen from above is radial: everything spreads from a center, like a wheel.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The third kind took a tree. Felix drew a big, quiet tree on the left side of a page and a small, bright red bird on the right. Different things, but the page felt even. That is asymmetrical balance, and it feels alive.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he drew the garden fence. Picket, picket, picket: a shape repeated with a rule, which is pattern. He painted every fourth picket red, and the fence had a beat. Pattern with a beat is rhythm, the same word musicians use.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Last, he painted one picket bright yellow in the middle of the fence. Everyone who looked at the drawing looked there first. Change one thing in a pattern and the eye goes straight to it. That is emphasis, made out of almost nothing.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Balance is how a picture stands still. Rhythm is how it moves.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Balance can be symmetrical, radial or asymmetrical. Pattern is repetition with a rule, and rhythm is pattern with a beat. A face, a flower and a fence hold it all.
description: "A face, a flower, a fence", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The road into the distance.
description: The title of the story "The road into the distance", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Clara drew a road, and it lay flat on the page like a ribbon. She wanted it to go somewhere. Her teacher said a page has no depth, so depth has to be faked, and there were four fakes and one ruler.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Overlap: the near tree covers part of the far one, so the far one must be behind. It is the simplest trick, and the strongest. Clara tried it with two trees.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Size: the near tree is drawn bigger, and the far tree smaller. Placement: the far tree sits higher on the page. Detail: the near tree has every leaf, and the far one is a pale green smudge.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the ruler. Clara drew a horizon line where the sky met the ground. She picked one point on it, the vanishing point. The road's two edges ran toward that point until they met, and every fence post and rooftop leaned toward it too.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The road left the page. It went somewhere now, over a hill and out of sight, and Clara wanted to walk it.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher pointed at the gaps between the trees. The trees were positive space, the shapes of the things. The gaps were negative space, the shapes around them. Artists plan the empty parts as carefully as the full ones.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Overlap, size, placement and detail make a flat page look deep. Perspective lines everything up to a vanishing point on the horizon. Depth is a trick, and the trick has rules.
description: "The road into the distance", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The handprint.
description: The title of the story "The handprint", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] On the cave tour, Theo saw a red hand on the wall, outlined in paint that someone had blown around their fingers more than twenty-five thousand years ago. Before writing. Before farms. Theo asked why anyone would do that.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nobody knows for certain, the guide said, and that was the beginning of a long answer. People made art before they wrote a single word, and every culture since has made it, never for only one reason.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Some art records. Painted animals running across a cave ceiling may show the animals people knew and hunted.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.
