text: [warm and friendly] Some art honors: a carving of a queen, a statue of a leader, a painting for someone who died. Some art teaches: a church window full of stories for people who could not read.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Some art decorates: a pot with a pattern, because plain was not enough. And some art questions: a painting that made a whole city argue about what was fair.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo asked about masks. The guide said one mask might hide a face at a festival, another might hold an ancestor's spirit, and another might hang on a wall as a portrait. Same object, three meanings. So always ask who made a thing, when and for whom.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Art records, honors, teaches, decorates and questions. The hand on the wall might have been any of those. It might have simply meant, I was here. It is one of the oldest messages we have, and it still reads.
description: "The handprint", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Chloe draws the road home.
description: The title of the story "Chloe draws the road home", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe could not make the road home look like a road. It sat on the page like a ribbon, flat and the same width all the way up. She had drawn it five times, and five times it looked like something lying on the paper instead of going into it.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher drew a dot on the horizon and said everything runs to it. The road wide at the bottom, thin at the top. The near tree big and detailed, the far tree small and plain. Overlap, size, placement, detail. The page was suddenly deep enough to walk into.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That dot is called a vanishing point, her teacher said, and painters in Italy worked out its rules about six hundred years ago. Before that, many pictures stacked things up the page to show distance. After it, a flat wall could look like a window. It was one of the biggest ideas in the history of art, and it fit on a single dot.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next lesson was balance. Her own face was symmetrical, nearly the same on both sides. A flower spread from the middle: radial balance. The fence along the road was a pattern, a post, a post, a post. She had been drawing all three for years without knowing they had names.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Knowing the names made her choose them on purpose. She gave the farmhouse at the end of the road two matching windows, symmetry, and a round flower bed by the door, radial. The fence posts marched toward the vanishing point, each one a little smaller than the last.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Color came next. Her teacher showed her that far-off hills look paler and bluer than near ones, because there is more air between you and them. Artists call it atmospheric perspective. Chloe painted the near field a strong green and the far hills a soft blue-gray, and the distance deepened again.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The last lesson was the oldest pictures in the world: hands on cave walls. At a cave in France, people painted spotted horses and outlined their own hands beside them more than twenty thousand years ago, a story told with no words long before writing.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe put her own hand on the road drawing and traced it. Art tells a story, her teacher had said. Hers was about the way home, the near tree and the far hill and the point where the road disappeared, and the hand said who had walked it. She signed it small in the corner, the way the painters did.
description: "Chloe draws the road home", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two prices.
description: The title of the story "Two prices", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus wanted a cupcake for two dollars fifty and a cookie for one dollar thirty-five. He added the numbers the way they looked on the sign, digits pushed together, and got a total that made the girl at the table laugh. It was more than a pizza.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He tried again in his head and got a different number. The line behind him was growing and his coins were sweating in his hand. Numbers with a dot in them seemed to have their own rules.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The girl wrote the two prices one above the other and lined up the dots. Cents under cents, dollars under dollars. Then she added column by column, just like whole numbers, and the dot stayed where the dots were. Three dollars eighty-five.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus paid with a five-dollar bill, and now the change was his problem. He wrote 5 as 5.00, because a whole number has a hidden decimal point at its end, and zeros can fill the empty places without changing anything. Five dollars minus three eighty-five, cents under cents: one dollar fifteen.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He checked it the fast way before he walked off. Two fifty is about two and a half, one thirty-five is about one and a half, and together they make about four. Three eighty-five is close to four, so the answer made sense. An estimate cannot give the exact answer, but it catches a silly one.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Decimals are money, and money lines up. Put the decimal points under each other, add or subtract each column, and carry the point straight down. Every other rule you know for whole numbers still works.
description: "Two prices", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Half of a half.
description: The title of the story "Half of a half", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] There was half a pizza left in the box, and Priya was allowed half of it. She ate her share and felt cheated. It was one slice. Half of something should be big, she thought, and this was small.
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She tried to write what she had eaten. Half of a half. A half times a half? That gave her one over four, which was a quarter, and a quarter was smaller than either half she had started with. How could multiplying make something smaller?
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Because of meant multiply, and she was multiplying by a fraction. Half of a whole pizza is big. Half of half a pizza is a quarter, and the box agreed: two cuts, four pieces, one in her hand. Tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms, one over four.
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her mother was baking and wanted two thirds of a recipe that called for three quarters of a cup of flour. Priya tried the rule. Two times three is six, three times four is twelve: six twelfths. Simplified, that is one half. Half a cup, less than the recipe asked, which made sense, because she was making less.
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she tried a whole number. Three friends each ate a quarter of a pizza. A whole number is itself over one, so three over one times one over four is three over four. Three quarters of a pizza, gone.
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When you multiply by a fraction, you take a part of something, and a part is smaller. Tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms, then simplify if you can. And when a problem says of, it is telling you to multiply.
description: "Half of a half", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Cartons of 24.
description: The title of the story "Cartons of 24", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen had 288 eggs and cartons that held 24. His aunt wanted to know how many cartons to order. Owen started filling cartons by hand to count them and gave up around the fourth one. There had to be a faster way.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Dividing by a number like 4 was easy. Dividing by 24 felt impossible. Twenty-four was too big to see how many times it fit into anything, and there were far too many eggs to count one by one.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he guessed. Ten cartons would hold 240 eggs. That left 48. Two more cartons would hold exactly 48. Ten and two: twelve cartons. He checked it backward, twelve times twenty-four is 288, and the answer stood.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next week there were 300 eggs. Owen guessed with rounder numbers: 24 is close to 25, and four 25s make 100, so 300 would need about twelve cartons. Twelve cartons held 288, and 12 eggs were left over. A remainder.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The remainder changed the answer. Twelve eggs would not fit in twelve full cartons, so his aunt needed thirteen, and the last one was half full. Division gives a number, and the question decides what to do with what is left. His aunt said that was the most useful thing he had learned all week.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Dividing by a two-digit number is guessing well. Estimate how many times the divisor fits, take that much away, bring down what is left and estimate again. Then multiply your answer back and see if it lands.
description: "Cartons of 24", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Sugar cubes.
description: The title of the story "Sugar cubes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena's job was to count the sugar cubes in the box before the party. She lifted them out one at a time and lost count at nineteen. Then she put them back and lost count again. The cubes were sticky and the party was in an hour.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandmother asked how many were in one layer. Lena looked at the top: four across, three deep. Twelve. And how many layers? She looked at the side. Two. She still did not see how that helped.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Twelve cubes in a layer, two layers. Twelve twice is twenty-four. She had counted the whole box in two looks. The length times the width gave one layer, and the height told her how many layers to stack.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] At the party her grandmother brought out a bigger box. Five across, four deep, three layers. Lena did not lift a single cube. Five times four is twenty in a layer, and three layers of twenty is sixty.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandmother said scientists count the same way, with tiny cubes one centimeter on each side. A box that holds sixty of them has a volume of sixty cubic centimeters. The cube is the unit, and the answer counts how many would fit.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The volume of a box is length times width times height, and the reason is the sugar cubes. Picture one layer, then count the layers. Every box, tank and room is filled the same way, one layer at a time.
description: "Sugar cubes", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three east, two north.
description: The title of the story "Three east, two north", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The treasure map said the prize was at 3, 2 and nothing else. Jamal stood at the start of a park laid out in straight paths and had no idea what the two numbers wanted from him. Three what? Two what?
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He tried walking two paths and then three and found himself at a bench with nothing under it. He tried three and then two in every direction and found another bench. The map was either broken or he was.
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister took the map. Across first, then up, she said. Three blocks east along the bottom, then two blocks north. The corner she reached had a small stone with an X on it. Two numbers, one point, and the order was the whole secret.
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The map had a second clue: 0, 4. Jamal laughed. Zero across meant no walking east at all. He walked four blocks straight north from the start and found a flag on a lamppost. The start of the park, where both numbers are zero, is called the origin.
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister wrote the pairs the way mathematicians do, in parentheses with a comma: (3, 2) and (0, 4). The first number goes along the x-axis, across the bottom. The second goes up the y-axis. Every point on the plane has exactly one address.
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The coordinate plane works exactly like that park. The first number says how far across, the second says how far up, and swapping them lands you somewhere else. Two numbers, one point, always across first.
description: "Three east, two north", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The package.
description: The title of the story "The package", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Two friends solved 3 + 4 × 2 and got two answers. Sam added first and got fourteen. Eli multiplied first and got eleven. They argued until the teacher came over, and each was sure the other had broken something.
description: "The package", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam said you read left to right, like a sentence. That seemed fair. Eli said multiplying came first. That seemed like a rule someone had made up. Who decided?
description: "The package", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher drew a box around the 4 × 2. Think of it as a package, she said. It arrives already wrapped. Multiplication and division are packages, so their answer, eight, is ready before any adding starts. Then add the three. Eleven. If you want to add first, you need parentheses to say so.
description: "The package", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam got his fourteen back, with parentheses. (3 + 4) × 2 means add first, because the parentheses say so: seven, then fourteen. Both boys had been right about something. Sam had been right about the answer to a different question.
description: "The package", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher wrote one more: 12 ÷ 3 × 2. Division and multiplication are equal partners, she said, so go left to right. Twelve divided by three is four, and four times two is eight. Doing the multiplying first would give two, and two is wrong.
description: "The package", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Parentheses first, then multiply and divide from left to right, then add and subtract from left to right. It is a rule everyone agreed to so that a math sentence means one thing everywhere, and the package is how to remember it.
description: "The package", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The dimes.
description: The title of the story "The dimes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Maya multiplied five dollars by a tenth and got fifty cents. She was certain something had gone wrong. Multiplying was supposed to make things bigger, and fifty cents was much smaller than five dollars.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She did it again and got fifty cents again. She tried it on the calculator and it said 0.5. The machine was on the other side. She stared at the dot as if it might move.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she thought about dimes. A tenth of a dollar is a dime. Five dollars, a tenth each: five dimes. Fifty cents. The answer was smaller because a tenth of something is smaller than the thing. Multiply the digits as whole numbers, five times one is five, then give the answer as many decimal places as the question had.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher gave her a harder one: 0.5 times 0.4. Five times four is twenty, and the question had two decimal places, one in each number, so the answer needs two: 0.20. Half of four tenths is two tenths, the same thing.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then one that grew: 2.5 times 3. Twenty-five times three is seventy-five, one decimal place, 7.5. Maya checked it with money: three people each paying two dollars fifty spend seven dollars fifty. Times a number bigger than one, the answer grows. Times a number smaller than one, it shrinks.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Multiplying by a decimal less than one makes a number smaller, and that is correct, not broken. Multiply the digits, then count the decimal places in the question and put that many in the answer. The dimes never lie.
description: "The dimes", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Ten beans.
description: The title of the story "Ten beans", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa grew ten bean sprouts for the science fair and measured each one. Four centimeters, four, three, four, five, four, seven, three, four, five. She wrote the ten numbers in a row and stared at them. They told her nothing.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher asked which height was most common and which sprout was the odd one. Rosa started counting the fours on her fingers and lost track. Ten numbers was enough to get lost in.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So she drew a line, numbered it, and put one dot above each measurement. The dots stacked. The pile at four was tallest by far, five dots high. And one lonely dot sat above seven, the surprise sprout that had beaten everyone. She could see the whole experiment in one look.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher showed her what else the dots could say. The most common height, the mode, was four. The range, tallest minus shortest, was seven minus three: four centimeters. Lined up from shortest to tallest, the middle fell between the fifth and sixth sprouts, and both were four.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The seven made her curious. That cup sat closest to the window and got the most sun. A line plot cannot say why a dot is alone. It shows you where to look, and then you go and look.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A line plot stacks one dot per measurement, so the common answer piles up and the odd one stands alone. A line graph is different: it joins points to show how one thing changes over time. Pick the picture that matches the question.
description: "Ten beans", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The bake sale.
description: The title of the story "The bake sale", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The bake sale needed a table, a cash box and a price list, and the price list was where the decimals lived. Brownies were 1.25, lemonade 0.75. A brownie and a lemonade: line up the points, add the cents, add the dollars, 2.00. The first customer paid with a five, and the change was decimals in reverse: 5.00 minus 2.00, three dollars back.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Six lemonades for one family meant multiplying a decimal: six times 75 cents. Six times 75 is 450, and the price had two decimal places, so the answer did too: 4.50. Four dollars fifty, which the family's youngest checked by counting out eighteen quarters.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The brownies came from a recipe that made a tray, and half the tray had been eaten by breakfast. Half of what was left went to the sale: half of a half, a quarter of the tray. Multiplying by a fraction had made the brownies fewer, which is exactly what fractions do.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The cookies came in boxes of 24, and 288 cookies had been baked: how many boxes? Ten boxes used 240, two more used the 48, twelve boxes on the table. Checked backward, twelve times twenty-four was 288, and nobody had to count a single cookie twice.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The table sat on a grid painted on the gym floor, and the lemonade stand was three across and two up from the corner, the point (3, 2). The cash box was a box: four cookies long, three wide, two layers high, room for twenty-four cookies.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every hour someone made dots on a line plot for the brownies sold: eight, ten, eleven, nine. The tallest stack showed the busiest hour was the third, just after lunch, and next year the brownies would be ready for it. A line plot does not tell you why. It tells you where to look.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thirty-eight brownies sold at 1.25 each came to 47.50. At the end, the total came from a long sum with parentheses in it, and the parentheses went first: 38 times 1.25, then the lemonade, then the cookies. The sale had made 143 dollars and 50 cents.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Decimals, fractions, division, a grid, a box, a line plot and parentheses. Nobody at the table would have called it a math test, but every number on it was one. The class counted the money twice anyway, on two sheets of paper side by side, and both said the same thing. That was the best part.
description: "The bake sale", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] What it was really about.
description: The title of the story "What it was really about", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The reading test asked what the story was about, and Kai wrote two friends. He was proud of that answer. The story was about two friends who fought and made up. What else could it be about?
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher marked it half right. Half. He had named exactly who was in the story. He went back and read it a third time, looking for the half he had missed, and found only the same two friends.
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then she asked a different question. Not who is in it, but what does it say? The friends fought, said awful things, and were still friends by the last page. The story was saying that a real friendship can survive a fight. That was the theme, the thing the story said about life. The friends were only the topic.
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Kai tried again with the next story, about a girl who lied to win a race and then could not enjoy the medal. He wrote honesty. His teacher said honesty was still only a topic, one word. A theme is a whole sentence: winning by cheating takes the joy out of winning.
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Later Kai noticed that two very different books, one about a soldier and one about a dog, said the same thing: loyalty costs something. Different topics, one theme. The theme was the part that could travel from book to book.
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Every story has both. The topic is what it is about: two friends, a dog, a war. The theme is what it says about being alive, and you find it by looking at what changed by the end. Name the topic, then ask what the story wanted you to know.
description: "What it was really about", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two cameras.
description: The title of the story "Two cameras", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ana had to write about the afternoon the storm came, and she wrote it two ways by accident. In the first draft she wrote, I saw the storm coming. In the second she wrote, she saw the storm coming. Her teacher said both were fine and they were completely different.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] How could the same afternoon be different depending on one word? The storm was the storm. The window was the window. Ana read both drafts aloud and could feel the difference but could not name it.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher explained with cameras. When you write I, the camera is on your head. The reader sees only what you see and feels what you feel. That is first person. When you write she, the camera is on a tripod in the corner. The reader can see the whole room, including you. That is third person.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her teacher showed a third camera, a rare one. You see the storm coming. That is second person, and it puts the reader inside the story as the one doing things. Directions and some games use it, but most stories do not.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Third person has two kinds of tripod too. One can only see inside one character's head. The other can see inside everyone, knowing what each person thinks. Ana rewrote the storm from that all-knowing corner and found out her little brother had been scared the whole time.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] I and we mean first person. He, she and they mean third person. The point of view decides what the narrator can know and what the reader gets to see, so choose the camera before you choose the words.
description: "Two cameras", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Break a leg.
description: The title of the story "Break a leg", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Right before Theo went on stage for the school play, his friend Maya grabbed his arm and said, break a leg. He froze. He had known Maya since kindergarten and she had never wished him harm before.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He spent the first scene worrying about his legs. Had she cursed him? Was there a loose board? By the second scene he had said all his lines without falling, and Maya was grinning at him from the wings.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Afterward she explained. Break a leg means good luck in the theater. Nobody breaks anything. It is an idiom, a phrase whose meaning is not in its words at all. You cannot work it out. You learn it by meeting it, the way you learn a nickname.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo started collecting them. His grandmother said he had his head in the clouds when he forgot his lunch. His coach said the test would be a piece of cake. His dad told him to hold his horses when he rushed. None of it was about clouds, cake or horses.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Maya said other languages have their own. In Spanish, estar en las nubes, to be in the clouds, also means daydreaming. But many idioms do not travel. Translate break a leg word for word into another language and the actor might really worry.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Raining cats and dogs. Piece of cake. Hit the hay. Every language is full of idioms, and each one means something its words do not say. When a phrase makes no sense taken literally, ask what it means to the people who use it.
description: "Break a leg", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Point to the line.
description: The title of the story "Point to the line", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] In the book club, Priya said the boy in the story was scared. Marcus said he was not, he was just tired. They argued for five minutes and got nowhere, because each was sure and neither had anything but being sure.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The teacher asked one question. Where? Priya said, in the middle somewhere. Marcus said, you can just tell. The teacher waited. Being sure, it turned out, did not count.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Priya opened the book and hunted. Page twelve: his hands shook as he reached for the door. There it was. Not a feeling about the boy but a line the author had written, and it showed fear more directly than any other line in the chapter. Marcus read it and gave in.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then Marcus found his own line on page fifteen: he yawned twice at dinner. Tired had evidence too. The teacher smiled. A story can hold more than one truth. The boy was scared at the door and tired by dinner, and both claims now stood on something.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The last step was to explain. Priya wrote her claim and the line in quotation marks with its page number. Then she added one sentence saying how the line proved it: shaking hands are what fear does to a body. Claim, evidence, explanation.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A claim about a text needs a line from the text behind it. Point to the page. Pick the line that shows the claim most directly, not the one that sort of hints at it. Evidence is what turns being sure into being right.
description: "Point to the line", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two storms.
description: The title of the story "Two storms", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen read two things about the same storm. A poem said the sky broke open and the street became a river. The newspaper said two inches of rain fell in one hour. He decided one of them was lying.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Which one? He had been in the storm. The street had felt like a river. But two inches did not sound like much, and nobody had seen the sky break. He could not make the two texts agree.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His mother said they did not have to. The poem was telling how the storm felt. The newspaper was telling what the storm measured. Both were true, and side by side they were the whole storm: the feeling and the facts. What they shared was the event. How they differed was the job each one was doing.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen wanted proof anyway, so he found a third source: the rain gauge in his own backyard. It held just over two inches. The newspaper had measured right. And the photo on the newspaper's front page showed a car up to its doors in water, which the poem had said first.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His mother asked why each writer wrote. The reporter wanted readers to know what happened, so every sentence carried a number, a time or a place. The poet wanted readers to feel the storm, so every line reached for a picture. The purpose shaped the words.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] To compare two texts, ask what they share, how they differ, and what the difference shows. When they seem to disagree, a third source often settles it. Two texts on one subject are not a contest. They are two windows on the same room.
description: "Two storms", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The cousin.
description: The title of the story "The cousin", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] A letter to the school newspaper said classes should start later. Lena agreed before she finished the first line. Then she got to the reason. The writer's cousin went to a school that started later and liked it.
description: "The cousin", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena wanted the letter to be right. But she could hear her teacher's voice asking, and how many cousins is that? One. One cousin, who liked something. Was that enough to change the whole school's day?
description: "The cousin", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It was not. A claim is held up by reasons, and reasons are held up by evidence. One cousin's opinion is a story, not evidence. Sitting on the desk next to the letter was a study of two thousand students who slept more and did better when school started later. That was evidence. The writer had never opened it.
description: "The cousin", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena opened the study herself. It said who was studied, how many, and for how long, and it compared schools that started earlier with schools that started later. Good evidence tells you where it came from, so you can check it.
description: "The cousin", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She wrote her own letter back. She agreed with the claim, added the study as her evidence, and answered the strongest reason against it: buses would have to change their routes. An argument that answers the other side is harder to knock down.
description: "The cousin", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When you read an argument, find the claim, then the reasons, then ask what holds each reason up. Without evidence, an argument is only an opinion with good posture. With it, even a short letter can change a school.
description: "The cousin", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The play.
description: The title of the story "The play", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The class was putting on a play about two friends who fight over a bicycle and make up. The topic was two friends. The theme, which took a week of rehearsal to find, was that friendship survives a fight. The topic was two words; the theme was a sentence.
description: "The play", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The play had come from a short book, and the class read both. The book spent three pages inside the younger friend's head. The play had no room for that, so it showed her feelings in what she did: she walked past the bicycle twice without looking at it. Same story, two different jobs.
description: "The play", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The script was in first person for one scene, the narrator saying I, and the audience only knew what she knew. Then the camera moved to the corner: third person, she and he, and suddenly the audience could see the bicycle hidden behind the shed that neither friend could. That was the whole trick of the play.
description: "The play", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] One line said the older friend had cold feet. A first grader in the front row asked why nobody brought him socks. An idiom, said the narrator, not skipping a beat. It means he was nervous. The audience laughed, and the first grader learned a new phrase.
description: "The play", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] When a parent asked afterward how they knew the ending was happy, the cast pointed to the last line. The two friends ride off on the bicycle together, one pedaling and one on the handlebars. A claim about a story needs a line behind it, and that line was the evidence.
description: "The play", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The week before, someone had written to the principal asking to cancel the play because it took time from math. The class read the letter the way they had learned. The claim was clear. The reason was time. The evidence was missing: no numbers, no schedule, nothing anyone could check.
description: "The play", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So the class wrote back, and this time the evidence was there: rehearsals had happened at lunch, and not a minute of math had been lost. The principal read both letters and let the play go on. An argument with evidence beat one without. The class pinned both letters to the bulletin board, side by side.
description: "The play", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] After the last bow, the teacher said the play had used every skill of the year: theme, point of view, idioms, evidence, comparing two versions and weighing an argument. The first grader in the front row said it was a good play. That was also true.
description: "The play", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two glasses.
description: The title of the story "Two glasses", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo stirred a spoon of sand into one glass of water and a spoon of salt into the other. The sand swirled, then sank. The salt swirled, then was gone. Same spoon, same water, and one of them had disappeared.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Where did the salt go? He looked from the side and from the top. Nothing. He was ready to say it had stopped existing until he took a sip and pulled a face. It was in there, all right, in every drop.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The sand had made a mixture. Each part kept its own properties, and he could pour the water off and leave the sand behind. The salt had made a solution, a special mixture where one part dissolves so completely into the other that you cannot pick it out, though you can still taste it.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His sister showed him how to get the salt back. She poured some of the salty water into a shallow dish and set it on a sunny windowsill. Three days later the water was gone and a crust of white crystals was left. Evaporation had pulled the solution apart.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Theo kept adding salt to a fresh glass to see how much would vanish. Spoon after spoon disappeared, until one spoonful sat on the bottom and stayed. The water could hold no more. Warm water, his sister said, would have held a little more before it stopped.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A mixture keeps the properties of its parts and can be separated. A solution is a mixture where one part dissolves and spreads evenly through the other. Sand and salt look alike in the spoon and behave nothing alike in the glass.
description: "Two glasses", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Top, lamp, marble.
description: The title of the story "Top, lamp, marble", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ava could not keep the three things straight. A day, a month, a year. They were all just time, and the sky did not come with labels. Her dad cleared the kitchen table and turned off every light but one.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He set a spinning top near the lamp. Which side of the top is lit? The side facing the lamp. Now watch the top spin. Every side gets its turn in the light and its turn in the dark. Ava said, day and night. He nodded. One spin, one day.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he carried the spinning top in a slow circle around the lamp. One lap, one year. Then he rolled a marble in a small ring around the top. One ring, about one month, and the marble was the moon. Three motions, three clocks.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then her dad crouched to the height of the top and asked her to watch the marble. As it went around, Ava saw its lit side full, then half, then a thin sliver, then dark. The marble never changed shape. She was seeing different amounts of its sunny half. Those are the phases of the moon.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] There was one more trick. As the marble circled, her dad turned it slowly so the same painted dot always faced the top. The real moon does that too, spinning once for every trip around Earth, which is why we always see the same face.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The Earth spins for day and night, circles the sun for the year, and the moon circles the Earth for the month. Once you have seen it on a table, you never lose it in the sky.
description: "Top, lamp, marble", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The lake that would not stay.
description: The title of the story "The lake that would not stay", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Chloe had decided to paint the lake once a day for a year. Same spot, same hour, sunrise. She wanted to see if a place could hold still.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It could not. In July the shore crept out and the rocks showed. In October the lake climbed back and swallowed them. On cold mornings a white mist rose off the water like the lake was leaving.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It was leaving. That mist was the lake, evaporating, becoming air. It rose, cooled, and gathered into cloud. The cloud drifted over the hills and fell as rain into the streams that ran back into the lake. What Chloe thought was one still thing was a loop she was standing inside.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On the coldest mornings the grass by her easel was wet though it had not rained. Water vapor in the air had touched the cold grass and turned back into drops: condensation, the same step that builds a cloud. In February the rain came down as snow, and in March the snow melted and ran back to the lake.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Some rain never reached the lake by the streams. It soaked into the ground and moved slowly through the soil and rock underneath, feeding the springs that bubbled up by the shore. Trees drank it too, and breathed some of it back out through their leaves.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her three hundred and sixty five paintings were not one lake. They were the same water, caught at different points on its journey.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The water in your glass has been a cloud, a river, and a lake, and it will be again. Nothing is used up. It only moves.
description: "The lake that would not stay", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Eyes and wheels.
description: The title of the story "Eyes and wheels", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Diego's homework asked which of his traits were inherited and which were learned. He had brown eyes, like his dad. He could ride a bike, like his dad. Both came from his dad, he figured, so both were inherited.
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His dad laughed and asked how the bike riding had gone at first. Diego remembered. Twenty falls, two scraped knees, one bent pedal. His dad had not handed him the skill. He had handed him the bike.
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That was the difference. Brown eyes came from his parents before he was born, and no amount of practice could change them. That is inherited. Riding came from falling twenty times and getting up twenty-one. That is learned. The question that sorts them is simple: could this have been practiced?
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Diego tried the question on animals. A spider spins its first web without ever seeing one, so that behavior is inherited; scientists call it instinct. His neighbor's dog sits when told, but only because someone taught it with a hundred treats. That is learned.
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Some things mix both. Height is mostly inherited, but good food helps a body reach it. Diego inherited long legs from his mom, but how fast he runs also depends on how much he practices. The legs came first. The speed came from the track.
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Inherited traits come from parents. Learned traits come from practice and experience. Every living thing has both, and the way to tell them apart is to ask whether it could have been learned at all.
description: "Eyes and wheels", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The rope that did not move.
description: The title of the story "The rope that did not move", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Two teams pulled on the rope with everything they had, and the flag in the middle did not move an inch. Faces were red. Shoes were digging into the grass. Kai, watching from the side, thought nobody was pulling at all. How could that much effort add up to nothing?
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The coach asked him the same thing. Both teams were pulling hard, so why did the flag stay put? Kai said maybe the rope was stuck. The coach shook his head and pointed at the small girl beside Kai.
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She walked over and grabbed the end of one team's rope. The flag slid across the line and the other team stumbled forward. Two equal pulls had canceled out, balanced, and the flag had no reason to move. One more pull tipped the balance, and the motion changed.
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The coach added one more idea. Why did both teams dig their shoes into the grass? Friction, the force that grips where two surfaces rub. On a wet floor in socks, both teams would have slid, pulled along by the rope instead of holding against it.
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he rolled two carts across the field, one empty and one full of water jugs, and pushed each just as hard. The empty cart shot away. The full one crept. The same push moves a lighter thing more. Gravity was pulling on both the whole time, holding them to the ground.
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A force is a push or a pull that changes motion. Balanced forces cancel and nothing changes. Unbalanced forces make things start, stop, speed up or turn. The flag was never stuck. It was perfectly balanced, until it was not.
description: "The rope that did not move", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The shell on the mountain.
description: The title of the story "The shell on the mountain", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Two thousand feet up a mountain trail, Nadia found a seashell pressed into the rock. A seashell. She checked the map in case the sea was nearby. The nearest ocean was three hundred miles away.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Had somebody carried it up and dropped it? It was inside the rock, not on it. Had the sea once come up this high? That was a lot of water. Her uncle told her the shell had never moved. The rock had.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The rock was made of layers, like pages in a book, each one laid down as mud and sand on an old sea floor. The shell had settled into one of those layers when this place was under water. Then, over millions of years, the land rose, and the sea floor became a mountain with the shell still in it. Deeper layers were older; the shell's layer said the place had once been a shallow sea.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her uncle said fossils come in more than one kind. Some are the hard part itself, turned to stone. Some are only a print, like a leaf pressed into mud that hardened. Some are tracks, the footprints of an animal that walked across soft ground and left.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Coal was made in a similar way, he said, from swamp plants buried in layers and squeezed for millions of years. The energy in it first came from sunlight those plants caught long ago. That is why coal is called a fossil fuel.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fossils are traces kept in layered rock. The deeper the layer, the older it is, and every fossil says what its place was like when it formed. A shell on a mountain is not a mystery. It is a page from the mountain's own book.
description: "The shell on the mountain", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The trip to the lake.
description: The title of the story "The trip to the lake", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The lake trip started with lemonade. Sugar in water: it vanished, but the drink was sweet. Sand from the shore in the bucket: it sank and could be poured off. A solution and a mixture, before the tent was even up. A cup left in the sun dried to a sticky ring, the sugar staying behind when the water left.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That night the moon came up over the water, and the youngest wanted to know why it changed shape. A ball, a flashlight, a slow walk around the campfire: the moon circles the Earth, and we see its lit side from different angles. It was full that night, the oldest said, because the moon sat on the far side of Earth from the sun.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In the morning the tent was wet on the inside. Nobody had spilled anything. The night air had cooled, and the water in it had turned to drops: condensation. By noon the drops were gone again, up into the air, and the clouds building over the far hills were the same water on its way back. The lake was one stop on a loop that never ends.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] After lunch they took the canoe out. Paddling on one side only sent the canoe in a slow circle, and paddling on both sides together sent it straight. Every stroke pushed water back, and the water pushed the canoe forward. When everyone stopped, the canoe slowed and drifted still, the water dragging against the hull until the push was used up.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On the far shore the rocks lay in flat layers, like a stack of books on its side. In one of them the youngest found a tiny shell pressed into the stone. A fossil, which meant this ground had once been under water. The layers below it were older still.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That evening the cousins skipped stones. The trick was a flat stone thrown low and fast with a spin, so it bounced instead of sinking. Nobody was born knowing it. Every cousin learned it that afternoon, one sunk stone at a time.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] On the last day the cousins compared: two had brown eyes like their fathers, inherited; all of them could now skip a stone, learned. The drive home passed a field of sunflowers turned toward the sun, and the youngest, who had been paying attention, said that was inherited too. Nobody argued.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Back home, the youngest made a list of everything the lake had taught. A solution and a mixture. The moon. The loop of water. A push and a drag. A shell in stone. And the difference between what you are born with and what you practice. It was a longer list than the one for school, and nobody had assigned it.
description: "The trip to the lake", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The tour.
description: The title of the story "The tour", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] New families were coming to see the school, and Diego was asked to write a guide. He wrote everything he knew in one long paragraph: the gym, the library, the lunch line, the garden, the smell of the art room. His teacher read it and said she felt lost.
description: "The tour", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Lost? It was all there. He had not left anything out. But when he read it back, he could not find the library either. It was buried between the lunch line and the garden with nothing to mark the door.
description: "The tour", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So he wrote it like a tour. An introduction that said what the school was: the entrance. One paragraph for the gym, one for the library, one for the garden: the rooms, each with its own idea and its own details. A conclusion that invited them to visit: the exit. Now a reader could walk through it.
description: "The tour", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he added signs. A heading over each paragraph, like the names over real doors: The Gym, The Library, The Garden. A small map with the rooms labeled. A caption under his photo of the garden. Readers who skimmed could still find their way.
description: "The tour", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher crossed out one sentence: the library is the best room. Informational writing gives facts, she said, and best is an opinion. He changed it to something a reader could check: the library has four thousand books and a reading corner by the window.
description: "The tour", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] An informational piece is a building. Introduction with the topic, a paragraph for each part, a conclusion at the end. Each paragraph holds one idea and the details that belong to it. Write it like a tour and nobody gets lost.
description: "The tour", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Five paragraphs.
description: The title of the story "Five paragraphs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa had one paragraph about why the class should have a pet, and it was a good one. Her teacher asked for five. Rosa thought that meant saying the same thing five times, and her second paragraph was the first one in different words.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] By the third she had run out of ways to say it. The essay was getting longer and emptier at the same time, like a balloon. There had to be a reason for five.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] There was. Paragraph one: the opinion. Our class should have a pet. Paragraphs two, three and four: one reason each, with room to explain it. It teaches us to care. It calms the room. It is fun. Paragraph five: the opinion again, carried by the three reasons behind it. Five jobs, five paragraphs.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher said each reason needed something to stand on. It calms the room became: when the class next door got a fish tank, their teacher said the loudest part of the day got quieter. A reason with an example is harder to wave away.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa also thought about who would read it. The principal would decide, and the principal would worry about weekends. So Rosa added a sentence to her conclusion: families could sign up to take the pet home, one weekend each.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] An opinion essay is an introduction with the opinion, one paragraph per reason, and a conclusion that says it again with the reasons behind it. Linking words like first, also and finally carry the reader from one to the next. Five is not more of the same. It is five different jobs.
description: "Five paragraphs", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The moment.
description: The title of the story "The moment", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Sam wrote about the day he learned to ride a bike in three sentences. My dad took the training wheels off. I rode. It was fun. It was all true and it took eight seconds to read, which felt wrong for the biggest day of that summer.
description: "The moment", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher asked which part had mattered most. The moment his dad let go, Sam said. She asked how long that moment had taken. About two seconds. And how many words had he given it? Two.
description: "The moment", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He wrote it again and slowed down at the right place. First the scene: a Saturday, the driveway hot, the wheels in the grass. Then the build: the wobble, his dad running beside him, the hand on the seat. Then the moment, stretched out: the hand gone, the front wheel shaking, and the second where it stopped shaking. Then what changed: he was a rider now.
description: "The moment", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His teacher pointed at one word: fun. Fun tells, she said. Show it instead. Sam crossed it out and wrote what his body did: the wind in his ears, his mouth open, a laugh that came out before he could stop it. The reader could feel the fun without being told.
description: "The moment", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then he added the one thing his dad said, in quotation marks: You are doing it by yourself. Real words from a real person made the moment sound true. Sam kept the whole story on one page, and it took a full minute to read.
description: "The moment", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A personal narrative sets the scene, builds to the moment, and says what changed. The secret is pace. Move quickly through the ordinary parts and slow right down at the moment that mattered, so the reader lives there as long as you did.
description: "The moment", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Georgette and the class pet.
description: The title of the story "Georgette and the class pet", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Georgette was ten and had decided the class needed a pet. She could not just ask. Her teacher said a good case is built, not wished for, so Georgette started building. She began with a question she could not answer yet: what does a class pet really need?
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She wrote an informational piece first, three paragraphs on how hamsters live, with an introduction that walked the reader in and a conclusion that walked them out. Her teacher said it read like a tour of a house. That was the idea. Informational writing gives facts, not feelings.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The facts had to come from somewhere. Georgette used two sources, a library book and a page from an animal shelter, and wrote down which fact came from which. When they disagreed about how long hamsters live, she wrote down both: two to three years, said one, and up to four, said the other.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the opinion essay. Paragraph one: our class should have a pet. Paragraphs two, three and four: one reason each, it teaches care, it calms us, it is fun. Paragraph five: all of it again, with the reasons behind it.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her first draft had a hamster that was very, very, very cute. Revising, she cut two of the verys and added a reason instead. Editing, she found three missing capitals and a their that should have been there. Revising changes what you say. Editing fixes how it is written.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The class voted. The hamster arrived in October and was named after a poet Georgette liked, which nobody else in the room had heard of. She wrote a care schedule for the wall: who feeds it, who cleans the cage, which family takes it home each weekend. It hung by the door all year.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The personal narrative came last, and it was about the moment the hamster escaped and she found it in her coat pocket after an hour of everyone searching. Set the scene, build to the moment, say what changed. She slowed the moment down the way her teacher showed her: the empty cage, the whole class on hands and knees, then a small warm weight moving in her pocket.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] What changed was that Georgette learned she could make a room of people do something with five paragraphs. She kept every draft in a folder, the messy ones too, because the messy ones showed how the good ones were made. She never forgot it.
description: "Georgette and the class pet", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Three rows.
description: The title of the story "Three rows", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Maya had to learn thirteen colonies for a test, and thirteen felt like a lot of names to hold. She tried a song. She tried flashcards. By Thursday she could remember nine, and never the same nine.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandfather looked at her map and asked what the weather was like in each place. Maya said she was studying colonies, not weather. He asked again, and she looked at where they sat along the coast.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They fell into three rows. New England up top, cold and rocky, where people fished and built ships and lived in tight towns. The Middle colonies in between, with rich soil for wheat and busy ports. The South, warm and wide, with big farms along slow rivers. Settled between 1607 and 1732 by people wanting land, faith or a fresh start, and the land told each row how to live.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her grandfather added one more pattern. The colonists were far from the king, so they learned to govern themselves. Virginia had an elected assembly, the House of Burgesses, from 1619. New England towns held meetings where settlers argued and voted on local matters. That habit of deciding for themselves would matter later.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] And not everyone came by choice. In the South especially, the big farms depended on enslaved Africans, brought by force and denied every choice the colonists prized. The three rows were shaped by weather and soil, and also by who was made to do the work.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thirteen colonies in three regions, each with its own way of living, shaped by its own weather and soil. Learn the three rows first, and the thirteen names have somewhere to hang.
description: "Three rows", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Four steps to a war.
description: The title of the story "Four steps to a war", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Eli's family had a very old teapot that nobody used, and a story to go with it. In 1765 his ancestors had to pay a new tax on paper, stamps and later tea, and they had never been asked. No vote, no say, just a bill.
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] They grumbled and paid and grumbled more. Eli wondered why grumbling turned into a war. Plenty of people pay taxes they hate. What made these people different?
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It happened in steps. In 1765, taxes with no vote. In 1773, colonists dumped tea into Boston Harbor rather than pay, and the teapot went on a shelf for good. In 1775, shots at Lexington. And on July 4, 1776, a declaration that governments exist to serve the people, and a people may change one that does not.
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Eli found more steps in between. In 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston and five colonists died, and the colonists called it a massacre. In 1774, Britain closed Boston Harbor to punish the tea party, and delegates from twelve colonies met in Philadelphia as the First Continental Congress.
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The colonists had a slogan for all of it: no taxation without representation. They were not against every tax. They were against taxes voted by a Parliament across the ocean, where they had no members at all.
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Taxes without a vote, then protests, then shots, then a declaration. Each step made the next one possible, and none of them was the whole story alone. A war is rarely one event. It is a staircase, and the teapot sat on the first step.
description: "Four steps to a war", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The second plan.
description: The title of the story "The second plan", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The country's first plan of government, the Articles of Confederation, could not even pay its own bills. Nadia could not believe it. A whole country with no way to collect money, no way to settle fights between states, no one in charge.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] She asked why they did not just fix it. Her teacher said they tried, and every fix needed every state to agree, and one state always said no. The plan was so weak that even fixing it was impossible.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] So in 1787, fifty-five delegates met in a hot hall and wrote a second plan. It gave the country three branches: a Congress to make laws, a President to carry them out, and courts to judge them. Each branch could stop the others, so no one branch could take over. Then a Bill of Rights was added to protect what the government could never touch.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The big states and the small states nearly broke the meeting apart. Big states wanted votes by population. Small states wanted one vote each. The answer was a compromise: two houses of Congress, the House of Representatives by population and the Senate with two senators from every state.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The plan still had to be approved. Nine of the thirteen states had to say yes, and in 1788 the ninth one did. Some states agreed only after a promise that a list of rights would be added. In 1791 the first ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, kept that promise.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The Constitution was written after the Articles failed: three branches that check each other, and a Bill of Rights added soon after. The point was never that the government would be strong. The point was that no part of it could be too strong.
description: "The second plan", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Doubling the map.
description: The title of the story "Doubling the map", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] In 1803 the United States bought a piece of land from France for fifteen million dollars, and the country doubled in size overnight. Priya thought that sounded like a great deal. Her teacher asked what the country planned to do with all that empty space.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Nothing, at first. Nobody lived there but the peoples who had always lived there, and few Americans knew what was in it. A map twice as big is not twice as useful if the new half is blank.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then the blank half filled. Trails carried wagons west through the plains. In 1848 gold turned up in California, and tens of thousands rushed to it. A war with Mexico added the southwest, and railroads would later follow the trails. By 1850 the country reached the Pacific Ocean, and the map that had doubled was full to the far edge.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] First came the explorers. In 1804 Lewis and Clark set out up the Missouri River with a small crew, helped along the way by guides like Sacagawea, and reached the Pacific in 1805. Their maps and notes filled in some of the blank half.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The filling had a cost. The land was never empty to the nations who lived there. As settlers moved west, the government forced many Native peoples off their homelands, including the Cherokee on the Trail of Tears in 1838. The railroad that crossed the continent in 1869 carried more settlers still.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The Louisiana Purchase doubled the country in 1803; trails, gold and war carried it to the Pacific by 1850. A country grows twice: once on paper, and once when people go and live in the lines.
description: "Doubling the map", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The split.
description: The title of the story "The split", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] In a shoebox in the attic Marcus found a letter from 1862, written by a soldier to his sister. The soldier wrote that the country had split in two and he did not know if it would ever be one again. Marcus read it three times. A country can split?
description: "The split", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] It can. Between December 1860 and June 1861, eleven southern states left the Union over slavery, which they wanted to keep and expand. The rest of the country said no. Neither side would give in, and the argument became a war.
description: "The split", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The war lasted four years. In 1863 President Lincoln declared the enslaved people in the rebelling states free. In 1865 the South surrendered, more than six hundred thousand soldiers had died, and the 13th Amendment ended slavery everywhere in the country. The soldier's sister got her letter. The country got itself back, changed.
description: "The split", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Marcus looked up the soldier's years. The war had begun at Fort Sumter in April 1861. In July 1863 the Union won at Gettysburg, in Pennsylvania, and that November Lincoln gave a two-minute speech there about a nation that should not perish.
description: "The split", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Five days after the main Southern army surrendered in April 1865, Lincoln was shot at a theater in Washington, and he died the next morning. He did not live to see the 13th Amendment ratified that December, or the long work of rebuilding the South that came after.
description: "The split", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A split over slavery, war from 1861 to 1865, emancipation in 1863, and an amendment that ended slavery for good. The letter in the shoebox is how history reaches a boy in an attic: one family at a time.
description: "The split", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The ship in the family tree.
description: The title of the story "The ship in the family tree", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa's great-great-grandmother came to America at nineteen with one bag, and Rosa wanted to know what was in it. Clothes, her grandmother said. A photograph. And the recipe for the bread the family still baked every Sunday.
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa tried to picture the trip. A ship packed with strangers, and a harbor she had only seen in books. Then Ellis Island, where they checked your eyes and your papers and let you through or sent you home. Why would anyone take that risk for a bag and a recipe?
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] For work, mostly. Around 1900 the cities were full of factories that needed hands, and millions came for them. They lived in tenements, one room for six people, one window, and worked long days. They also brought their food, their music and their words, and the cities grew larger and louder and more mixed than any cities had ever been.
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Rosa looked it up. Ellis Island opened in 1892, and about twelve million people passed through it before it closed. On the other coast, many who crossed the Pacific came through Angel Island in San Francisco Bay, where some were held for weeks or months.
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The cities strained to hold everyone. Some neighbors helped. In Chicago in 1889, Jane Addams opened Hull House, where new arrivals could learn English, leave their children in a nursery and find help getting work. The newcomers built the cities that had not been ready for them.
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.
