text: [warm and friendly] Around 1900 immigrants arrived through Ellis Island, worked in factories, lived in tenements and reshaped the cities. Every family that came changed the country a little, and the bread on Rosa's table is the proof that the change is still going on.
description: "The ship in the family tree", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Fourteen hours.
description: The title of the story "Fourteen hours", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena's history project was a shirt. Before machines, a skilled seamstress needed about fourteen hours of hand sewing for one fine shirt, more than a full day of work. After machines, a factory could turn out a hundred in a day. She wrote the two numbers down and did not believe them.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Fourteen hours for one, and a hundred in a day. How could anything speed up that much? And if shirts changed that fast, what else did? She started a list and it would not stop growing.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Steam engines turned the machines, so a factory no longer had to sit beside a river. The telegraph carried news across the country in seconds instead of weeks. Railroads carried the shirts, and everything else, to towns that had never seen a factory. The light bulb stretched the working day past sunset. Each invention pushed the others faster.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Machines also changed who worked, and for how long. Many factories hired children, some younger than ten, for twelve-hour days, because they were paid little and their small hands fit between the machines. It took decades of protest before laws kept young children out of factories.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The speeding up kept going. In 1913 Henry Ford set car parts moving past his workers on a line. Building one Model T dropped from about twelve hours to about an hour and a half. Every worker did one job, over and over, and the car came to them.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Factories, steam, the telegraph, the railroad and the light bulb moved work and life faster than anyone had known. A shirt in a day was not the whole story. It was the first thing people noticed in a world that had started to run.
description: "Fourteen hours", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The road from the coast.
description: The title of the story "The road from the coast", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The first of them came off a ship in 1620 and built a house on the coast, in the New England row of what became thirteen colonies. The winters were long, and half of the first settlers did not live to see spring. Their grandchildren farmed rocky fields and fished the cold water, and voted in town meetings on everything from roads to the minister's pay.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Their great-grandchildren paid a tax on tea they had no vote about, and in 1773 one of them was on a dark harbor tipping crates into the water. In 1775 the fighting started at Lexington and Concord, a day's ride away, and two of the family's sons marched.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In 1776 the family signed nothing but heard the Declaration read aloud in a market square. In 1787 they argued about the Constitution at the dinner table: a stronger plan than the first one, three branches, each able to stop the others.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In 1803 a cousin went west into the Louisiana Purchase, fifteen million dollars for land that doubled the country, and did not come back. His letters, when they came, told of rivers wider than the town and of the nations who had lived there long before him. His grandson crossed the plains in a wagon in 1849, headed for California gold.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] In 1861 two brothers of the family fought on opposite sides. In 1865 the one who lived came home to a country that had ended slavery at the cost of more than six hundred thousand lives. His brother never came home; his name is carved on a stone in the town square with forty others.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next generation went to work in the mills. A daughter ran a loom in a factory town where the machines never stopped and a whistle told everyone when to eat. Her husband laid track for the railroad that, by 1869, crossed the whole continent.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Around 1900 the family changed again. A young man from Italy came through Ellis Island with one bag, found work in the city, and married the loom worker's granddaughter. He brought a recipe and a language, and the family took both. From then on, holiday dinners were louder and better.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The house on the coast is a museum now. Visitors can walk from its door down the old road inland, the same road the family took west, to war, to the mills and back again. It runs all the way to Texas, and every mile of it is someone's story.
description: "The road from the coast", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The scoreboard.
description: The title of the story "The scoreboard", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Ana kept score at the park with a flip board. HOME on one side, VISITORS on the other, and numbers she changed every time someone scored. Her brother said the board was a computer program with two variables.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A variable is a named box that holds a value and can change. The box called HOME held 3. When the home team scored, the box still said HOME and the value became 4. The name stayed; the number moved.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Ana saw why the name mattered. The program did not need to know the score ahead of time. It needed to know where to look. Add one to HOME, whatever HOME holds. The board could keep score for a game that had not been played yet.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her brother showed her a second trick. TOTAL could be HOME plus VISITORS, worked out fresh every time either one changed. At 4 to 2 the total was 6. At 5 to 2 it was 7, and nobody had to count again.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] He also said the names should tell you what the boxes hold. A box called X could be anything. A box called HOME could only be one thing. Math uses letters the same way: n plus 3 works for any n, the way the scoreboard works for any game.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] A variable is a named box that holds a value and can change. The name stays, the value moves, and a program that uses the name works for a score it has never seen.
description: "The scoreboard", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The thermostat that never sleeps.
description: The title of the story "The thermostat that never sleeps", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen asked who turned the heat on at night when everyone was asleep. His father pointed at the thermostat and said it had been making the same decision every few seconds since they moved in. Nobody had touched it in weeks.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The decision was one sentence. IF the room is colder than the setting, THEN turn the heat on. ELSE, turn it off. A condition, and two roads.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] That is all the thermostat knows, and it is enough. It checks, picks a road, checks again. Owen wrote the same sentence for his game: IF the player touches the star, THEN add a point, ELSE keep going. The thermostat had taught him the shape of every choice a computer makes.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] His father showed him a harder choice on the sprinkler timer. IF it is six in the morning AND the ground is dry, THEN water the lawn. Both parts must be true. At six on a rainy morning, the sprinklers stay off.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Owen added one to his game. IF the player touches the star AND the timer is still running, THEN add a point. Late stars no longer counted. Before that, a player could grab a star after the clock ran out and still score. One small word, AND, had made the rule fair.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] IF a condition is true THEN a step runs. ELSE is the other road. AND means both parts must be true. A program chooses the way a thermostat does: check, pick, check again.
description: "The thermostat that never sleeps", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Facing the wall.
description: The title of the story "Facing the wall", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] Lena's robot was supposed to reach the flag in the corner. It drove forward, turned, drove, and stopped with its nose against the wall. Lena rewrote the whole program from scratch. It hit the wall again.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Her teacher told her to stop rewriting and start reading. One step at a time, out loud, with her finger on the line and her eye on the robot. Forward two. Good. Turn right. Good. Forward four.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Forward four was the bug. The room was three squares wide. One number, one wrong step, and everything after it had been right and useless. She changed the four to a three and the robot found the flag. Debugging was not rewriting. It was reading.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The next day a friend's robot had a different problem. It reached the corner and then turned the wrong way. Every number was right, but two steps were in the wrong order: turn, then forward, instead of forward, then turn. A bug can be a wrong value or a wrong order.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] After each fix, Lena ran the whole program again, start to finish, not just the step she changed. A fix can break something that used to work. Testing again is the only way to know. Her teacher called it checking your work, the same as in math.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Debugging is reading the steps one at a time and checking each. The bug is usually one small wrong thing, and rewriting everything hides it instead of finding it.
description: "Facing the wall", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] The game that kept score.
description: The title of the story "The game that kept score", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and friendly] The class built a game in a week. On Monday it had a ball and a paddle and no memory: every point was forgotten the moment it was scored. The ball bounced, the paddle moved, and nothing that happened mattered to anything that happened next.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Tuesday brought variables: a box named score, a box named lives, and the game began to remember. Score went from 0 to 5 to 8, and lives went down from 3 to 2 when the ball got past. The names stayed the same all game long; only the numbers inside them changed.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Wednesday was for deciding. IF the ball touches the paddle THEN bounce, ELSE lose a life. IF lives is 0 THEN show the end. The game did not decide anything by itself; it asked yes-or-no questions the class had written and took whichever road the answer pointed down.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The questions had to be asked again and again, many times every second, or the ball would slip past the paddle between two checks. So the whole program sat inside a loop: move the ball, check the paddle, check the lives, draw the screen, and start again. A loop is a set of steps a program repeats.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Thursday, the game was wrong. It ended after two lost balls, not three. Nobody deleted anything. They read the steps one at a time, and found the line that checked lives before taking one away instead of after. One line moved, and the game was fixed.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Then they tested it the way players would try to break it. One student held the paddle at the very edge. Another pressed two keys at once. A third just let the ball go by, to see whether the end screen appeared. Every test that passed was one less surprise on Friday.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] Friday was for playing, and for one last box. A variable named best kept the highest score anyone had reached, and IF a new score beat it, THEN best took the new number. By lunch the best score was 41, and a quiet student who had written the loop held it.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm and friendly] The game was simple, but it held the whole of programming: boxes that remember, questions that decide, a loop that keeps asking, and a careful reading when something goes wrong. Everything bigger is built from the same four parts. The class kept the game on the classroom computer, and the best score has changed hands eleven times since.
description: "The game that kept score", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, friendly voice.

text: [warm] Two blues to one yellow.
description: The title of the story "Two blues to one yellow", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Chloe found the green in a market far from home: a deep, wet, leaf green that she mixed by accident on a scrap of card. Two blobs of blue, one blob of yellow. She wanted a whole jar of it.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So she poured in more blue and more yellow, a bit of each, and stirred. The jar turned a green she did not want. Too yellow. She added blue. Too blue. The scrap of card sat there, still perfect, still tiny.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The card had the answer. Two to one. The mix did not care how much paint there was. It cared about the proportion: for every two parts of blue, one part of yellow. Four blues and two yellows is the same green. Twenty and ten is the same green. Two and two is a different green.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Chloe measured the jar in spoonfuls, two blue for every one yellow, and got her leaf green by the pint.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At the paint shop she used the same idea on prices. Three small jars cost 12 dollars, so one jar cost 4. A big jar held as much as four small ones and cost 13 dollars. Four small jars would have cost 16, so working out the price of one, a unit rate, showed the big jar was the better buy.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She also noticed that two to one meant the green was two thirds blue. Two parts out of every three were blue, and one part out of three was yellow. A ratio compares the parts to each other; a fraction compares a part to the whole.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A ratio is a recipe that ignores size. It is why a photo can be printed as a poster and still be the same picture.
description: "Two blues to one yellow", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] How many halves.
description: The title of the story "How many halves", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal had three pizzas and a rule that everyone at the party got half a pizza. How many kids could he feed? He wrote three divided by one half and stopped, because everything he knew said dividing made numbers smaller, and the answer had to be at least three.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He tried to work it the long way and got one and a half, which meant one and a half kids, which was ridiculous. The pizzas were cooling. The kids were counting.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So he stopped calculating and looked at the pizzas. Each one held two halves. Three pizzas held six halves. Six kids. Dividing by a half was not making the pizzas smaller; it was counting how many halves fit inside them. And the shortcut said the same thing: flip the half into two over one and multiply. Three times two, six.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At the end of the party three quarters of a pizza was left, and his mother wanted to know how many eighth-size slices it made. Three quarters divided by one eighth. Flip the eighth and multiply: three quarters times eight is six. Six slices. He checked it backward: six eighths is three quarters.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal liked the checking best. Division asks how many of one thing fit inside another, and multiplication puts them back together. If the answer multiplies back to where you started, it is right.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] To divide by a fraction, flip it and multiply. Dividing by something smaller than one gives a bigger answer, because you are counting small pieces inside a big thing. Three pizzas, six halves, six happy kids.
description: "How many halves", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The elevator that counted backward.
description: The title of the story "The elevator that counted backward", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena parked on level minus three. She knew because the sign said so, in big white paint, and because the elevator button for it sat below the button marked 0.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her meeting was on the second floor. She pressed 2. The elevator rose, and rose, and rose, and she started to wonder if it had broken. It stopped exactly where it should.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Zero is the ground. Below it the numbers keep going, with a minus sign to say which way. From minus three to two is not two floors. It is three floors up to zero, then two more: five floors in all. The distance between two numbers is how far apart they sit, no matter which side of zero they are on.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Outside, the bank sign showed the temperature: minus five in the morning, three by lunch. A rise of eight degrees, five up to zero and three more. It was the same counting as the elevator, turned sideways into weather.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her niece asked which was bigger, minus three or minus five. Minus three, because it sits higher, closer to zero. Their distances from zero, three and five, have a name of their own: absolute value. Distance is never negative, whichever side of zero you start from.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the way down that evening she pressed minus three again, and counted the floors past zero on her fingers.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A thermometer, a bank balance, a diver under the sea: the world needs numbers on both sides of nothing.
description: "The elevator that counted backward", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Half a rectangle.
description: The title of the story "Half a rectangle", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The new garden bed was a triangle, and Priya needed its area to order soil. She knew rectangles: base times height. But a triangle had a slanted side and no rule she could remember, and the soil truck was coming Tuesday.
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She pegged a rectangle of string around the bed just to see it better. Base six feet, height four. The rectangle was twenty-four square feet. That was too much, but by how much?
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She looked at the two leftover corners of the rectangle, the parts outside the triangle. Together they made up exactly the same shape as the triangle itself. The triangle was half of the rectangle around it. Twenty-four divided by two: twelve square feet. Six bags of soil, not twelve.
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her brother wanted to measure the slanted side instead. It was five feet. Six times five, halved, is fifteen, three square feet too many. The height has to be the straight-up distance from the base to the top corner, the way a plumb line would hang.
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next bed was a slanted four-sided shape, a parallelogram. Priya cut a paper copy, sliced the triangle off one end and slid it to the other. It became a rectangle with the same base and height, and the same area. Base times height, no halving, because nothing had been cut away.
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A parallelogram is base times height. A triangle is half of that, because every triangle is half of a rectangle drawn around it. Use only the straight-up height, never the slanted side, and the halving does the rest.
description: "Half a rectangle", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The mystery box.
description: The title of the story "The mystery box", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] On the science table sat a balance with a sealed box and five weights on one pan and twelve weights on the other, perfectly level. Owen's job was to find out how heavy the box was without opening it. He stared at it as if the answer might be written on the lid.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He tried guessing. Ten? Then the box plus five would be fifteen, and the scale would tip. Six? Then eleven, and it would tip the other way. Guessing could take all afternoon.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he did something simpler. He took five weights off the left pan and five off the right at the same time. The beam did not move. Now the box sat alone on one side and seven weights on the other. The box weighed seven. He had undone the adding by subtracting, and the balance had stayed true because he did it to both sides.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next setup had three identical boxes on one side and twelve weights on the other. Owen split each side into three equal groups: one box against four weights. He had undone multiplying by dividing both sides by three. Three x equals twelve, so x equals four.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he checked both answers by putting them back. Seven plus five is twelve. Three times four is twelve. Both scales would stay level, so both answers were right. Checking takes ten seconds and catches most mistakes.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An equation is a balance. Do the same thing to both sides and it stays level. Undo adding by subtracting, undo multiplying by dividing, and check by putting the answer back in. The box is x, and x was seven all along.
description: "The mystery box", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The friend who moved the mean.
description: The title of the story "The friend who moved the mean", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Six friends compared allowances at lunch: two, three, three, four, five and nine dollars. Nadia said the average was about four dollars and thirty-three cents. Marcus said most people got three. Lena said the middle was three and a half. All three were right, which made no sense.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They argued about which number was the real one. The nine-dollar friend, Sam, said the average was more than four dollars and that proved everyone was doing fine. The two-dollar friend did not feel fine.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] There were four honest numbers, and each told something different. The mean added it all and shared it out: twenty-six dollars among six, about 4.33, pulled upward by Sam. The median was the middle after sorting, three and a half, and Sam could not move it. The mode was the most common, three. The range was highest minus lowest, seven, and it measured the gap between Sam and everyone else.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Lena asked what would happen without Sam. The other five allowances added to seventeen dollars, and seventeen shared by five is 3.40. The mean dropped by almost a dollar. The median only slipped from 3.50 to 3. One big number had moved the mean a long way and the median hardly at all.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So which average should they give a teacher who asked what a typical kid got? The median, they decided, because it was where most of them actually were. The mean was not wrong. It answered a different question: how much each would have if everyone shared.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Mean: add and share. Median: the middle. Mode: the most common. Range: highest minus lowest. One big number can drag the mean far from where most people are, which is why the median often tells the truer story.
description: "The friend who moved the mean", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] East and north.
description: The title of the story "East and north", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Ava's new city counted its streets from the center. Three blocks east and two blocks north was her school, at 3, 2. She understood that. Then her friend gave an address of minus three, minus two, and Ava did not know a street could be negative.
description: "East and north", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She walked three blocks east and two north and found the school. Then she tried to walk minus three blocks and stood on the corner, stuck. You cannot take a negative step. Or could you?
description: "East and north", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her friend showed her. Negative across just meant west instead of east. Negative up meant south instead of north. Minus three, minus two was three blocks west and two blocks south, the same distance from the center as the school, on the opposite corner of the city. The center split the city into four quarters, and the signs told you which one you were in.
description: "East and north", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Another friend lived at 3, minus 2: three blocks east, two south, a mirror image of the school across the main east-west street. Change one sign and you flip across one axis. Change both and you land on the opposite corner.
description: "East and north", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The library sat at minus 3, 2, three blocks west on the same street as the school. Walking from the school took six blocks: three to the center line and three more, the two distances from zero added together.
description: "East and north", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Positive across is right, negative is left; positive up, negative down. The four quadrants count counterclockwise from the top right, and a point's signs tell you which quadrant it lives in before you take a single step.
description: "East and north", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The paint job.
description: The title of the story "The paint job", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The fence needed painting, and the paint was a mix: two parts blue to one part yellow made the green the neighbor wanted. A ratio. Double the batch, four to two, and it is the same green. The older friend wrote it as a table, 2 and 1, 4 and 2, 6 and 3, so nobody had to think about it on a ladder.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The paint came in half-gallon cans, and the fence needed three gallons: how many cans? Three divided by a half is six. Dividing by a small piece counts the pieces. They bought six cans and checked it the other way: six halves make three wholes.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The money got complicated. They had been paid twenty dollars up front and had spent twenty-three on paint. They were at minus three, three dollars in the hole, and the younger one drew a number line on the sidewalk in chalk to see it: three steps left of zero.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then the neighbor said to forget the extra three. Taking away a debt is subtracting a negative: minus three, take away minus three, and they were back to zero. When she added a ten-dollar tip, they were ten dollars up. The number line had never been so interesting.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fence had a triangular gate, and the paint can said how many square feet it covered. So they measured the gate: base six feet, height four feet, half of twenty-four, twelve square feet. The younger one wanted to measure the slanted edge instead, and the older one said the height has to stand straight up from the base.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fence itself was a long rectangle, forty feet by five, two hundred square feet on one side. With the gate, two hundred and twelve. A gallon of this paint covered about 150 square feet of rough boards, so two coats, about 424 square feet, took just under three gallons: exactly what they had bought.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At the end the neighbor asked how many hours they had worked, and they only knew the total pay and the rate: forty-two dollars at seven an hour. x times seven equals forty-two, so x equals six. One-step equations, said the older one, who had done them that week, and the younger one said that was just the fence backwards.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They wrote the numbers on the last can before they washed the brushes: a ratio, a division, a negative, an area and an equation. It had been one fence and five kinds of math, and none of it had felt like homework.
description: "The paint job", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The reason that fell.
description: The title of the story "The reason that fell", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus had three minutes at the podium and one thing he wanted: school should start an hour later. That was his claim. He had three index cards, one reason on each, and his hands were sweating onto the top one.
description: "The reason that fell", paragraph 1 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Card one: teenagers' bodies are wired to fall asleep late, so early starts cut into their sleep. Card two: his cousin in Ohio starts later and likes it. Card three: students who sleep more get better grades. He read all three and sat down feeling good. Then a girl in the back raised her hand and asked what his cousin liking it had to do with the rest of them. The room laughed. Marcus did not have an answer.
description: "The reason that fell", paragraph 2 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the walk home he worked out what had gone wrong. A claim is the thing you are trying to prove. A reason is only worth keeping if it actually holds the claim up, the way a leg holds up a table. Card one held: sleep science supports a later start for everyone. Card three held: better sleep, better grades, for everyone. Card two was about one person's taste. Pull on it and the claim did not move at all. He crossed it out.
description: "The reason that fell", paragraph 3 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next week he came back with evidence under each card that was left. For card one he cited the American Academy of Pediatrics, a national group of doctors for children, which in 2014 recommended that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30. The girl in the back nodded. A reason with evidence under it is a leg with a foot.
description: "The reason that fell", paragraph 4 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Every argument you will ever hear works the same way: find the claim first, then push on each reason and see whether the claim moves. The strong ones hold. The weak ones, like a cousin in Ohio, fall away, and the argument is better without them.
description: "The reason that fell", paragraph 5 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two rains.
description: The title of the story "Two rains", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Ava read two stories on the same rainy afternoon. In the first, the rain drummed happily on the roof and the family played cards. In the second, the rain would not stop and a man stared out at an empty street. Same rain. Ava felt cozy after one and trapped after the other.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher asked what the difference was. Ava said the rain. But it was the same rain, falling on the same kind of day. The difference was somewhere in the words, and she could not put her finger on it.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She pointed to them. Drummed happily: the first writer liked the rain, and that attitude was tone. Would not stop, empty street: those words made her feel shut in, and that feeling was mood. The writer chose the words. The words made the tone and the mood. And Ava could prove it by pointing.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher tested it with one word. A thrifty man and a stingy man may spend exactly the same money, but thrifty sounds wise and stingy sounds mean. Words carry feelings along with their meanings, and choosing between them is how a writer sets the tone.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Ava wrote a sunny afternoon that felt frightening. The playground was empty. The swings moved though there was no wind. Nothing in it was dark, and the mood was dark anyway. The details had done it.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Tone is the writer's attitude. Mood is the feeling you get. Both come out of the words on the page, so when someone asks how you know, point to the words. Two rains, two feelings, and the weather had nothing to do with it.
description: "Two rains", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The root port.
description: The title of the story "The root port", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus had five words to learn by Friday: transport, import, export, portable and porter. Five unrelated words, he thought, five separate things to memorize. He groaned and started with the first.
description: "The root port", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] By Wednesday he could spell them and not one of them meant anything to him. He kept mixing up import and export. They looked almost the same, and that was the problem, or so he thought.
description: "The root port", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then his tutor circled four letters in every word. Port. It meant carry. Transport: carry across. Import: carry in. Export: carry out. Portable: able to be carried. Porter: someone who carries. Five words, one meaning, and the front piece told him which way the carrying went. The list learned itself.
description: "The root port", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The pieces around the root had meanings too. Trans means across, im means in, ex means out, and able means able to be. His tutor called them prefixes and suffixes: the front and back of a word, with the root in the middle carrying the meaning.
description: "The root port", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] By Friday Marcus was hunting roots on his own. Spect means look: inspect, spectator, spectacles. Tele means far and phone means sound, so a telephone carries sound from far away. Many of these pieces came into English from Latin and Greek, and they are still doing their old jobs.
description: "The root port", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A root you know unlocks every word built on it. When a long word looks new, look for the part you already know. Port, aqua, bio, geo, tele: a few dozen roots open thousands of doors.
description: "The root port", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The same job.
description: The title of the story "The same job", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The article had three paragraphs. One about how bees pollinate. One about bees dying. One about what farmers could do. Lena had to say what the whole thing was about, and she wrote down the first paragraph's fact. Bees pollinate flowers.
description: "The same job", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Marked wrong. She tried the second fact. Bees are dying. Also wrong. She had read the article, she could repeat every detail in it, and she could not say what it was about. That felt unfair.
description: "The same job", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher asked what all three paragraphs were doing together. Not what each said, but what job they shared. Lena read them again as a team. Bees do essential work, bees are in trouble, and here is what to do about it. All three were pulling the same rope: we need bees, and we can help them. That was the central idea.
description: "The same job", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added one more difference. The topic was bees, one word. The central idea was a sentence about bees: we need them, and we can help them. A topic names the subject. A central idea says something about it.
description: "The same job", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Lena wrote a summary: the central idea first, then one key detail from each paragraph to hold it up, in her own words and without her opinion. Four sentences told the whole article.
description: "The same job", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The central idea is what every paragraph is helping to say. A detail from one paragraph is never the central idea, however true it is. Ask what job the paragraphs share, and the answer is the idea holding the whole thing up.
description: "The same job", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The hill.
description: The title of the story "The hill", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Owen liked the story about the boy and the flood, but when his teacher asked where the climax was, he had no idea. It all seemed important. The town, the storm, the river, the boat, the morning after. How could one part be the top?
description: "The hill", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She told him to draw the story as a hill. He started at the bottom with what he knew at the beginning: the boy, the town, the storm coming. That was the exposition, the setup. Then he climbed.
description: "The hill", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The river rose. The bridge went. The boy had to get his grandmother across in the dark. Each step up the hill was the conflict getting worse. At the very top, the boat in the black water, the moment when everything could go either way. That was the climax. Then the slope down: the far bank, the morning, the resolution.
description: "The hill", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher asked what the boy was fighting. The river, first: a person against nature. But he was also fighting his own fear of the dark water: a person against himself. Most good stories have more than one conflict, and the climax is where they meet.
description: "The hill", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Owen drew the hill for his favorite movie that night. It worked there too: the setup, the rising trouble, the one moment where it could go either way, and the calm after.
description: "The hill", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A plot rises from exposition through conflict to a climax and settles in the resolution. Draw any story as a hill and the climax finds itself: it is the one point where the whole thing hangs in the balance.
description: "The hill", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The song without music.
description: The title of the story "The song without music", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Priya's teacher asked the class to clap along to a nursery rhyme, and everyone found the beat in a second. Then she asked them to clap along to a paragraph from the science textbook. Nobody could. The class laughed. Priya wanted to know why.
description: "The song without music", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Both were words. Both were English. But one of them had a pulse you could feel with your hands and the other lay flat on the page like a road with no bumps. Where did the pulse come from?
description: "The song without music", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] From how the poem was built. The beat they clapped was rhythm, the pattern of stressed sounds. Cat and hat at the line endings were rhyme, matching sounds where the lines stop. The groups of lines with space between them were stanzas, a poem's paragraphs. Some poems keep the rhythm and the rhyme. Free verse keeps neither and finds its shape another way.
description: "The song without music", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher showed two more tools. Alliteration repeats the first sounds of nearby words: silver snakes sliding. Onomatopoeia is a word that sounds like what it names: buzz, crash, sizzle. Poets use sound on purpose, because a poem is meant to be heard.
description: "The song without music", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she read a free verse poem aloud, and Priya noticed the line breaks. The poet stopped each line where she wanted a breath or a surprise. Even without rhyme or a steady beat, the shape on the page told the reader how to read it.
description: "The song without music", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Stanzas are a poem's paragraphs, rhyme matches endings, rhythm is the beat, and free verse keeps neither. A poem is a song with the music taken out, and clapping is how you put it back.
description: "The song without music", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The editorial.
description: The title of the story "The editorial", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The claim was simple: the school should start an hour later. The first draft had five reasons and three of them were the writer's cousin liking it. A reason has to hold the claim up, said the editor, and the cousin held nothing. Two reasons stayed: teenagers sleep late by biology, and rested students learn more.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each reason needed something under it. For the first, a doctors' group that had studied teenagers' sleep. For the second, a school district that had moved its start later and measured more sleep and better grades. Evidence a reader could check, not a feeling a reader had to trust. The editor circled every claim without a source until the page looked spotted.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The tone was the next fight. The first draft sounded angry, and angry writers get skipped. The second draft was warm and a little funny, and the mood a reader was left with was that the writer could be trusted.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Along the way a word had to be looked up: somnolent, from the root somn, sleep, the same root as insomnia. The writer liked it so much that it went into the headline, then came out again, because a headline that sends readers to a dictionary loses them.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then came the part the editor called fairness: the other side. Some parents worried that a later start meant later practices and later dinners. The editorial said so plainly and answered it: many schools that moved their bells moved their practices to match.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The last read-through asked one question of every paragraph: is it doing the same job? One paragraph about the cafeteria was not, and it went. What was left was one central idea, held up by reasons that held, in a voice a reader would sit with.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The layout editor wanted a pull quote, one line big enough to read from across the room. The writer chose the sentence with the evidence in it, not the one with the feeling. A reader skimming the page would still get the strongest part. Evidence travels farther than anger.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It ran on the front page. The principal read it, wrote a letter back, and put the question on the next school board agenda. Nothing changed that year, but the argument was in the room, and it was a good one. The writer kept the red-marked first draft, because it showed how far the argument had come.
description: "The editorial", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Letters and words.
description: The title of the story "Letters and words", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa's science homework said water was made of hydrogen and oxygen, and she found that hard to believe. Hydrogen was a gas that burned. Oxygen was a gas she breathed. Water was a drink. How could two gases add up to a drink?
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She read the formula, H2O, and it looked like a code. Two Hs and an O. She knew the letters but not the word, and she could not see how letters became something you could swim in.
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her brother said to think of it as spelling. H is a letter, one kind of atom, an element. O is another letter, another element. H2O is a word spelled from them: two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom, and the word is a compound with properties of its own. Letters burn and breathe. The word puts out fires.
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He showed her another word. Sodium is a soft metal that fizzes, and can burst into flame, in water. Chlorine is a poisonous yellow-green gas. Joined, they spell NaCl: table salt, which she sprinkled on her dinner. The compound had none of the danger of its letters.
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The alphabet has 26 letters. Chemistry has 118 elements, laid out in the periodic table, and every substance on Earth is spelled from them. Some words are short, like O2, the oxygen she breathed. Some run to thousands of letters, like the proteins in her own body.
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An element is one kind of atom. A compound is two or more kinds joined, and it can be nothing like its parts. Read a formula the way you read a word: the letters say which elements, the small numbers say how many of each.
description: "Letters and words", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Three ways.
description: The title of the story "Three ways", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] At the campsite, Diego burned his hand on a pan handle that had never touched the flame. Then he watched the soup stir itself, and then he felt the fire warm his face from six feet away with nothing in between. Heat seemed to go wherever it wanted.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He asked his aunt how the handle got hot when only the pan was in the fire. She asked him to think about the three things he had just noticed, and whether they were really the same trick.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They were three tricks. The handle was conduction: heat passing by touch through the metal, atom to atom, up to his hand. The soup was convection: hot broth rose, cooled at the top, sank at the sides, and carried heat around in a loop. His face was radiation: heat crossing the empty air as rays, the way sunlight crosses space.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His aunt handed him an oven mitt and a wooden spoon. Some materials let heat pass quickly, like metal. Others slow it down, like wood, cloth and plastic. Those are insulators, which is why good pans have wooden or plastic handles.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That night the metal cup on the table felt colder than the wooden bowl beside it, though both had sat in the same cool air for hours. They were the same temperature. The metal just pulled heat out of his fingers faster. Cold, his aunt said, is only heat leaving.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Heat always moves from warmer to cooler, and it has three roads. Conduction by touch, convection by a moving liquid or gas, radiation by rays that need nothing to travel through. One campfire shows all three in a minute.
description: "Three ways", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two rugs.
description: The title of the story "Two rugs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai's teacher said mountains were made by the ground moving, and Kai laughed. The ground did not move. He had stood on it his whole life and it had never gone anywhere.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That night he pushed two rugs together on the living room floor and they buckled into a ridge. He pulled them apart and the bare floor showed in the gap. He slid them past each other and they caught, then jerked. He sat back on his heels and stopped laughing.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The Earth's outer shell is not one piece. It is plates, like rugs, riding on hot rock that flows very slowly, and moving a few centimeters a year. Push two together and they buckle: mountains. Pull them apart and new floor rises into the gap: a rift, or the middle of an ocean. Slide them past each other and they catch and jerk: an earthquake.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher showed him the proof people first noticed. The coast of South America fits into the coast of Africa like two puzzle pieces. And fossils of the same small ancient reptile, Mesosaurus, are found on both, though it could never have swum the ocean between them.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The pushing has not stopped. India is still pressing into Asia, and the Himalayas, the tallest mountains on Earth, are still rising a few millimeters a year. In California two plates slide past each other along the San Andreas Fault, and every earthquake there is one of those jerks.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The Earth's shell is plates that move. Pushing together makes mountains, pulling apart makes new floor, sliding past makes earthquakes. The ground does move. It just moves slower than a boy on a rug can feel.
description: "Two rugs", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The pond that moved.
description: The title of the story "The pond that moved", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Frederick stood in a lab that smelled of pond water, thinking about a kitchen table from years before.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That day his dad had set a small digital microscope on the kitchen table and a jar of green water from the ditch. Look, he said. Frederick looked. The water was moving. Not sloshing. Moving. Tiny clear boxes drifted past, some with a green tint, some with a dark spot in the middle, one spinning slowly like it was searching.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He asked what they were. His dad did not know. So Frederick spent the years since finding out.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They were cells, the smallest things that are alive. Each one had a thin skin, its membrane, that let some things in and kept others out; the plant cells also had a stiff wall outside it. Most had a nucleus holding the instructions, and the green ones had tiny factories that turned sunlight into food. A leaf, a fish and Frederick himself were built from the same kind of box, arranged differently.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Some of the pond cells were whole living things, one cell each, swimming and eating on their own. Frederick was made of tens of trillions of cells working together, each with its own job.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In college he learned the three rules that tie it together. Every living thing is made of cells. The cell is the smallest unit of life. And every cell comes from another cell that divided. The boxes in the ditch water had come from boxes before them, all the way back.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Everything alive is made of things too small to see, each one busy. Frederick still keeps the jar.
description: "The pond that moved", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Follow the energy.
description: The title of the story "Follow the energy", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Maya watched a hawk circle a meadow and wondered what a hawk was made of. Birds, she supposed. And birds were made of grasshoppers. And grasshoppers were made of grass. So was a hawk made of grass? That felt wrong and right at the same time.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She followed it back one more step. What was grass made of? Dirt? Water? She dug up a blade and it did not look like dirt at all. Something else had built it.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Sunlight had. Grass catches light and makes food from it, which makes grass a producer. The grasshopper eats the grass, the bird eats the grasshopper, the hawk eats the bird, and every one of them is a consumer, passing the sun's energy up the line. When the bird dies, fungi and bacteria break it down and return it to the soil: the decomposers. Then the grass grows again.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added a catch. Energy passes up the chain, but only about a tenth of it at each link; the rest is used for living or lost as heat. That is why a meadow has millions of grass blades, thousands of grasshoppers, dozens of birds and one hawk.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] And the chain is really a web. The grasshopper is also eaten by a lizard, the hawk also hunts mice, and the mice eat seeds from the same grass. Take one strand away, and the others feel it.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Producers make food, consumers eat, and decomposers break things down and return what they held to the soil. Energy flows from the sun through everything alive, one link at a time, and most of it is spent along the way. A hawk really is made of sunlight, with several stops along the way.
description: "Follow the energy", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Feathers and rocks.
description: The title of the story "Feathers and rocks", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo had two boxes exactly the same size. One was packed with feathers and one with rocks. His cousin bet him that size was what made things sink, and that two boxes the same size would do the same thing in the water.
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Theo was not sure. The boxes were the same size, that was true. But one of them made his arms ache and the other felt empty. Could the water tell the difference?
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He dropped them in. The feather box floated. The rock box sank straight down. Same space, different mass. The rock box was denser: more stuff packed into the same volume. Water has its own density, and anything denser than water goes under, whatever its size.
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At home he weighed a wooden block and a stone of the same size, fifty cubic centimeters each. The wood was 30 grams: 0.6 grams in every cubic centimeter. The stone was 130 grams: 2.6 grams in every one. Water is 1. The wood floated and the stone sank, just as the numbers said.
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he poured honey, water and oil into one glass. They settled into layers, the densest at the bottom: honey, then water, then oil on top. Liquids have densities too, and they sort themselves.
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Density is mass divided by volume. Denser than water sinks; less dense floats, and size has nothing to do with it. A steel ship floats because its whole hull, air and all, is less dense than the water it pushes aside.
description: "Feathers and rocks", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The rooms in the cork.
description: The title of the story "The rooms in the cork", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena put a shaving of cork under the microscope, expecting to see cork. Brown, soft, boring. What she saw instead was a wall of tiny boxes in rows, like the rooms of a building seen from above. She checked the slide twice to be sure it was cork.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher asked how much bigger the boxes looked than they really were. Lena read the two lenses: ten and forty. She added them and said fifty. The teacher shook her head.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The lenses multiply. Ten times forty is four hundred, so each tiny room looked four hundred times its real size. The focus knob made the walls sharp. And in 1665, a man named Hooke had looked at cork through the same kind of lens and seen the same rooms. He called them cells, after the small rooms in a monastery.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] About ten years after Hooke, a Dutch cloth merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own tiny lenses and looked at pond water. He saw creatures swimming that no one had ever seen, and he wrote them down as tiny animals. They were living cells, each one a whole creature.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Lena learned the careful way to look, too. Start with the lowest power to find the thing, then turn to a stronger lens. Cut the slice so thin that light can pass through it, and lay a cover slip on top. Most blurry pictures come from a slice that is too thick.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Lenses magnify, magnifications multiply, and focus makes the picture sharp. Every living thing is built of cells, and a piece of cork was the first place anyone saw them.
description: "The rooms in the cork", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The kitchen laboratory.
description: The title of the story "The kitchen laboratory", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] It rained all Saturday, so the kitchen became a laboratory. First, the salt: a compound, two elements joined, sodium and chlorine, neither of which you would want on a table alone. Sodium fizzes in water and chlorine is a poisonous gas, and together they season the soup.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then the soup: the metal spoon got hot by conduction, the broth swirled by convection, and the face over the pot warmed by radiation. Three ways heat moves, one pot. Heat always moves from the warmer thing to the cooler one. The wooden spoon in the drawer stayed cool, because wood is an insulator.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The graham crackers came out for plate tectonics. Two crackers on a layer of frosting, pushed together: they buckled, the way mountains rise. Pulled apart: the frosting showed, a rift. Slid past each other: they caught and jerked, an earthquake in miniature.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The onion skin went under the microscope after that, a slice so thin the light came through. There were the cells in rows, the same kind of boxes Hooke saw in cork in 1665. Each one had a wall around it, and with a drop of iodine each showed a small dark spot, the nucleus.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] By evening the density tower was standing in a glass: honey, dish soap, water, oil, four layers that would not mix, the densest at the bottom. Density decides where each liquid sits, not how much of it there is. A grape dropped in stopped partway down, sinking through the layers above it and resting on one below.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The last experiment was dinner, which was a food chain on a plate: the chicken had eaten the grain, and the grain had grown from sunlight. Only a small part of the sunlight the grain caught ever reached the chicken, and only a small part of that reached the plate. That is why a meadow can feed many grasshoppers but only a few hawks.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The dishes went in the sink, and the water swirled down the drain on its way to the treatment plant, the river and eventually the sky. Even washing up was part of the water cycle. The same water might fall again next week.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The rain stopped at eight. Nobody had noticed. Seven experiments, one kitchen, and every one of them had been happening in that kitchen all along, waiting for someone to look. The youngest wrote them all on the fridge: compound, heat, plates, cells, density, energy, water.
description: "The kitchen laboratory", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Show the numbers.
description: The title of the story "Show the numbers", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Diego's school had two water fountains for six hundred students, and he wanted more. He wrote to the principal: we need more fountains because students get thirsty. The principal wrote back: everyone gets thirsty. Nothing changed.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Diego was angry. His reason was true. Students did get thirsty. But true was not the same as convincing, and he did not know what was missing. He read the letter three times looking for it.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His science teacher asked one question. How do you know? Diego went to the nurse. She had logged forty headaches last month, most in the afternoon, most from students who had not had water since lunch. He wrote it again: claim, reason, and now evidence, the nurse's forty.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He also answered the principal's worry before she could raise it. Fountains cost money, he wrote, but forty afternoon trips to the nurse cost class time every month. Naming the other side and answering it is called a counterclaim and a rebuttal. The principal ordered two fountains.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher added one more rule. Evidence counts most when a reader can trust where it came from. The nurse's log was better than a guess, and far better than a friend saying so. A number is only as good as the person who counted it.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An argument is a claim, reasons, and evidence for each reason. A reason without evidence is only a feeling, however true it happens to be. Show the numbers, and a feeling becomes a case.
description: "Show the numbers", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two towns.
description: The title of the story "Two towns", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa's assignment was to compare two towns on the same river. She wrote that both had a market and both sat on the water. Then she ran out of things to say. They were the same, and the same is boring to write about.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her father asked how she got from one to the other. The first town had a bridge. The second had a ferry that ran twice a day. Rosa wrote that down as a difference and still could not see why anyone would care.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she thought about what the difference did. The bridge town had a market every day, because farmers could cross whenever they liked. The ferry town had a market twice a week, when the ferry ran. The alike part set up the question. The different part answered it. And what it showed was that a river crossing shapes a whole town's week.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher showed her two ways to lay it out. Block by block: everything about the first town, then everything about the second. Or point by point: markets in both towns, then crossings in both towns. Point by point kept the differences side by side, where a reader could see them.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa drew a Venn diagram first: two overlapping circles, the shared things in the middle, each town's own things on its side. Then she wrote with signal words, both and similarly for the middle, while and however for the sides.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Compare by saying how things are alike, how they differ, and what the difference shows. The first two are lists. The third is the point, and it is the only part a reader remembers.
description: "Two towns", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Let them talk.
description: The title of the story "Let them talk", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai wrote a whole page describing his two characters. She was strict and always on time. He was easygoing and always late. His teacher read it and said she did not believe either of them yet.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Not believe them? He had explained exactly what they were like. But explaining, it turned out, was the problem. The reader was being told, and readers do not trust being told.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He cut the page and let them talk. "You're late," she said. "The bus was early," he said. Two lines, and a reader knew them both: her sharpness, his shrug. The dialogue also moved the story, because now they had somewhere to be and a problem getting there. Quotation marks around the words, a comma before the tag, and the characters did the rest.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher showed him one more rule of the page: every time a new person speaks, start a new paragraph. That way a reader always knows who is talking, even when the tags drop away.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Kai tried an action instead of a tag. She checked her watch. "You're late." The watch did the work of said, and it showed how impatient she was. He kept a few saids too; readers barely notice them, which is exactly why they work.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Dialogue moves the story and shows character faster than description ever can. Put quotation marks around the spoken words, a comma before the tag, and let people reveal themselves by what they say.
description: "Let them talk", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Mike argues for the later start.
description: The title of the story "Mike argues for the later start", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Mike wanted school to start later, mostly because he was up late most nights doing the dishes. His first draft argued from feeling. His teacher, a woman who did not care for feeling in an argument, sent it back with one word: evidence.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So Mike found it: the nurse's log of morning headaches, a study of a school that had moved its bell, numbers that could be checked. He wrote the claim, then each reason, then the evidence under each one, the way you would build a table: top, legs, feet.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher asked what the other side would say. Mike wrote it down himself: buses, sports, parents' work schedules. Then he answered the strongest one in its own paragraph. Answering the other side is called a rebuttal, and an argument that has already met its objections is hard to knock over.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The compare-and-contrast came next, two towns on a river, one with a bridge and one with a ferry. Mike laid it out point by point, the markets side by side, then the crossings side by side, and the last paragraph had to say what the comparison showed. The bridge town grew faster, because farmers could cross whenever they liked.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Mike liked that the essay ended with a finding instead of a feeling. His teacher liked that he had drawn a Venn diagram first, and that the middle of it was not empty. Both towns had a market; only one had a market every day; the difference was the bridge.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The narrative with dialogue was the one he did not want to write. It was about the night his mother said they might have to move and he said they would not. He wrote the talk first and the description second. "We might have to move," she said. "We won't," he said. Two lines, and a reader knew both of them.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He started a new paragraph for each speaker and cut every word that explained what the lines already showed. His mother did not sigh in the draft. She did not have to. The reader heard it.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He turned it in with his hands shaking. It was the best thing in the class. His teacher wrote one word at the bottom this time too: true. Mike kept all three pieces in a folder, an argument, a comparison and a story, and the story was the one he read again.
description: "Mike argues for the later start", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The orange globe.
description: The title of the story "The orange globe", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Maya's homework asked for the latitude and longitude of her town, and both numbers meant nothing to her. Lines on a globe. Why did a round world need lines at all, and why two kinds?
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her grandmother handed her an orange and a marker. Draw a belt around the middle, she said. Maya did. That was the equator. Now draw more belts above it and below it. Those were latitude, and they told you how far north or south you stood.
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then lines from the top to the bottom, like the segments of a peel. Those were longitude, counted east or west from one line everyone had agreed on. Where a belt crossed a segment, you had one spot on the orange, and one spot on the Earth. Seven continents and five oceans sat somewhere on that grid, and so did Maya's town.
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her grandmother cut the orange along the belt: two halves, north and south, the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. Then she cut along the agreed line and the one opposite it: east and west. Every place on Earth sits in one northern or southern half and one eastern or western half.
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.
