text: [warm and natural] Maya found her own town at last. Latitude runs from 0 at the equator to 90 at each pole, and longitude from 0 to 180 east or west. Austin sits at about 30 degrees north and 98 degrees west, in the Northern and Western Hemispheres.
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Latitude measures north or south of the equator; longitude measures east or west of the prime meridian. Two numbers name any place on the planet. The world has seven continents and five oceans, and every one of them has an address.
description: "The orange globe", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] What we would have to teach.
description: The title of the story "What we would have to teach", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] A new student was coming from another country, and Theo's class was asked to list what she would need to know. Theo thought it would be a short list. The classroom rules. Where the bathroom was. Done.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then the list started growing. The words for things. What to eat and how to eat it. Which holidays the school kept. What was polite and what was rude. How close to stand, when to shake hands, what everyone already knew without being told. By the end it filled the board and spilled onto the next one.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That whole board was culture: the way of life a group shares. Language, religion, customs, food, arts and government, and the thousand small habits underneath them. Theo had never seen his own culture because he had never had to explain it. The list was the first time it had stood still long enough to look at.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Cultures also borrow from each other. Pizza came from Italy and is now eaten nearly everywhere. Words travel too: kindergarten came into English from German. When a custom, a food or an idea spreads from one group to another, geographers call it cultural diffusion.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The new student taught the class some things as well: a greeting from her country, a game from her old school, a dish she brought to lunch. By spring some of those had become part of the classroom too. Culture is never finished; it keeps picking things up.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Culture is the way of life a group shares, and it travels: with people who move, with food, with music, with words. Everyone has one, and the quickest way to see yours is to imagine teaching it to someone who was not born into it.
description: "What we would have to teach", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The remote.
description: The title of the story "The remote", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] In Nadia's house the remote was power. Whoever held it decided what everyone watched. On Monday her older brother kept it all night. On Tuesday her parents took it back. On Wednesday there was a vote. Nadia thought it was just a family. Her civics teacher said it was a whole unit.
description: "The remote", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] How could a remote be a government? Nadia laughed. Then the teacher asked one question about every government they had studied, and it was the same question. Who decides?
description: "The remote", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] One person holds the remote for life because of who their parents were: a monarchy. One person grabs it and will not let go: a dictatorship. A small circle passes it among themselves: an oligarchy. Religious leaders decide what is watched: a theocracy. Everyone votes on the channel: a democracy. Five governments, one remote.
description: "The remote", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Some countries mix them. The United Kingdom has a king, but elected lawmakers make the laws; the king has little real power. That is a constitutional monarchy, a crown held inside the rules.
description: "The remote", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Democracies differ too. When everyone votes on every question, as the family did on Wednesday, it is a direct democracy. When people elect representatives to vote for them, as Americans do in Congress, it is a representative democracy.
description: "The remote", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Governments differ by who decides: the people, a monarch, one dictator, a small group or religious leaders. The rest of the differences follow from that one answer, and the question works on any country and any couch.
description: "The remote", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Who decides.
description: The title of the story "Who decides", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa's grandmother wove the same cloth her mother had woven, because that was what her village had always made. Rosa's uncle lived in a country where the government told factories what to build each year. Rosa lived where shops sold whatever people would buy. Three families, three worlds. Which one was right?
description: "Who decides", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa could not decide, and her teacher said that was the point. None of them was simply right. Each one was an answer to one question, and it was the same question every time.
description: "Who decides", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Who decides what gets made? In a traditional economy, custom and the elders decide. In a command economy, the government decides. In a market economy, buyers and sellers decide by what they buy and sell. Most real countries mix them, and the size of an economy is measured by GDP per person: everything made in a year, shared out across everyone living there.
description: "Who decides", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The question exists because of scarcity: there is never enough of everything for everyone. Rosa had money for a book or a movie, not both. Whatever she gave up to get the other was its opportunity cost. Every economy is a way of making choices like that for a whole country.
description: "Who decides", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher did one with numbers. A country whose economy makes 50 billion dollars in a year and has 10 million people has a GDP per person of 5,000 dollars. It is an average, so it cannot show whether the money is shared evenly or held by a few.
description: "Who decides", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Economies differ by who decides: custom, the government, the market, or a mix. GDP per person is GDP divided by the population, and it tells you how much economy each person has to live on. The loom, the office and the mall are three answers to one question.
description: "Who decides", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Push and pull.
description: The title of the story "Push and pull", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] When Jamal was seven his family moved from a small town to a huge city, and for years he blamed his parents for it. He had liked the town. Nobody had asked him. Then in sixth grade he had to write about why people move, and he asked his mother.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] There was no work in the town, she said. The factory had closed. And there was a job in the city. Jamal had assumed it was one decision, but it was two forces, and both of them had been stronger than his liking the town.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Geographers call them push and pull. Push factors drive people out of a place: no work, war, drought, floods. Pull factors draw them somewhere else: jobs, safety, family, land. And where people end up gets crowded: population density is people divided by area, and water, food and work decide it. The city was dense because it pulled.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal worked out an example. A town of 1,000 people on 4 square miles has 250 people per square mile. A city block can hold more people than that on a single street. Density is not about how big a place is. It is about how many share it.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Some moves are chosen and some are not. Families who move for a job choose it. Refugees are pushed out by war or danger with little choice at all. Moving within a country is internal migration; moving to another country is international migration.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] People move away from what pushes and toward what pulls. Population density is how many people share each square mile, and it follows water, food and work. Every family that ever moved was pushed by something and pulled by something else.
description: "Push and pull", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The neighborhood on the map.
description: The title of the story "The neighborhood on the map", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The test asked Marcus to name the regions of Africa, and he could not see any. A region was not a country. It had no flag, no border he could find on the map. How could he name something that was not there?
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher asked him to think about his own neighborhood. It had no border either. Nobody had drawn a line around it. But everyone in it knew where it started and stopped. What made it a neighborhood?
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The neighbors shared something. The same street, the same school, the same corner store. A region is a neighborhood on a bigger map, and its neighbors share something too: a landform, a climate, a language or a history. The countries along one coast are a region. The countries across one desert are another. The shared thing draws the line.
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave him examples from Africa. The Sahel is a dry belt of grassland just south of the Sahara, crossing many countries that share its rains and its droughts. North Africa shares the Arabic language and much of its history. What the places have in common draws the line of a region.
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Some regions are drawn around a center instead. A city and all the towns whose people drive into it for work make one region, even with no shared landform at all. And some regions live mostly in people's minds, like the places folks simply call the South.
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A region is a place that shares a landform, a climate, a language or a history, and every continent is made of them. Find what the places share, and the region draws itself.
description: "The neighborhood on the map", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The tag.
description: The title of the story "The tag", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena's new shirt said Made in Vietnam on the tag, so she assumed the whole shirt came from Vietnam. Her geography teacher asked where the cotton was grown. Lena checked the tag again. It did not say.
description: "The tag", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She followed the shirt backward and it kept going. The cotton was grown in one country. Spun into thread in another. Woven into cloth in a third. Sewn in a fourth. Shipped across an ocean and trucked to her store. The tag named one place. The shirt had been to five.
description: "The tag", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That road is a supply chain: the steps and places between a raw material and you. Each place along it does what it does best and cheapest, which is called specializing, and then trades for the rest. No one country makes a whole shirt. They make it together, one stop at a time.
description: "The tag", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added the reason it works. A country with warm weather and flat fields grows cotton well. A country with many workers and cheap power sews quickly. Each does what it does best and trades for the rest, and together they make a shirt for less than any one of them could alone.
description: "The tag", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The chain has a weak side too. When one stop closes, by a storm, a strike or a blocked canal, every stop after it waits. In 2021 a single stuck ship blocked the Suez Canal for six days, and goods around the world arrived late.
description: "The tag", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A supply chain is the steps and places between a raw material and you. Places specialize and trade, so almost nothing you own comes from just one place. The tag is the last stop, not the whole trip.
description: "The tag", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The market at the crossroads.
description: The title of the story "The market at the crossroads", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The market sat where two roads crossed, and you could find it on a map by two numbers, so many degrees north of the equator, so many east of Greenwich. Anyone with those two numbers could find the stalls from the other side of the world. The market had stood there for three hundred years.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On market day the town was a lesson in culture: the food, the words, the way people greeted each other, everything a newcomer would have to be taught. A spice seller from the east taught the bakers a new bread, and within a year it was the town's bread. That is cultural diffusion, one loaf at a time.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The town had been governed three ways in living memory: once by a lord who decided everything, once by a small council, and now by everyone who voted. The old men at the tea stall argued about which had been best, and the argument itself was the proof of the third.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Its economy had changed too, from farms that made what their grandparents made, to a plan handed down from far away, to a market where buyers and sellers decided. Custom, command, market: three answers to who decides what gets made.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The people at the stalls had come from four directions, pushed by drought and pulled by work. The town had grown from a few hundred people to many thousands on the same few square miles. The schoolteacher had the children work out its density on the blackboard. A thousand people on four square miles is two hundred and fifty to the mile, and the market town was far past that.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The goods had come from farther still: cotton grown in one country, spun in another, sewn in a third, sold at the crossroads. When a storm closed the port that year, the cloth stalls stood empty for a month, and everyone learned how long the chain was.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A region, the schoolteacher said, is a neighborhood on a bigger map. The traders from the mountains shared one language, the traders from the coast another, and the market was where the neighborhoods met. Maps colored them as two regions, and the market sat on the line.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At dusk the stalls folded and the four roads carried everyone home. The market would be there again next week, at the same two numbers on the map, and a little different, the way every crossroads is.
description: "The market at the crossroads", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The bird feeder that learned.
description: The title of the story "The bird feeder that learned", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Maya's grandfather was tired of squirrels emptying the bird feeder, so Maya pointed an old phone at it and set it to record every visitor. By Sunday she had two hundred short clips, and a program that was supposed to sort them into birds and squirrels.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The program came with no rules in it. It could not be told that squirrels have bushy tails, because nobody had written a place to type that. What it wanted instead was examples. Maya sat at the kitchen table and labeled clip after clip, bird, squirrel, bird, bird, until her grandfather brought her cocoa and took a turn.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] When the labeling was done, the program did something Maya could not see. It went through the two hundred clips and kept whatever the birds shared and whatever the squirrels shared, and dropped the rest: the time of day, the light, the particular sunflower seed. What was left, the program called a model.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On Monday the model met its first new clip and made a guess. Squirrel, it said, 94 out of 100, and the feeder's little door swung shut before the squirrel reached the seed. Maya cheered. Her grandfather asked how the program knew, and she found she could not quite say. It had never told her its rule.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It had never told her, because it had no rule to tell. It had a pattern, pulled from her two hundred labels, and the pattern was only as good as the clips. When a blue jay with a puffed-up tail landed, the door swung shut on a bird. The model had learned that a big tail means squirrel, and nobody had shown it a jay.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So Maya labeled twenty jays, and the model learned again. That, her grandfather said, is what the machine really is: not a thinker, but a keeper of patterns, and you are the one who decides which examples it sees.
description: "The bird feeder that learned", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The bridge that was never built.
description: The title of the story "The bridge that was never built", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo's report on the old iron bridge was due Friday, and the chatbot answered his first question in four seconds. The bridge, it said, was finished in 1887 by an engineer named Samuel Wray, and it had survived the flood of 1913 with only one cracked pier.
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It sounded wonderful. It sounded like a plaque. Theo typed the paragraph straight into his report, and he might have handed it in that way if his sister had not asked, over dinner, who Samuel Wray was. Theo did not know. He had not asked the machine how it knew, and it had not said.
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next day the librarian pulled a drawer of old newspapers. The bridge was real, and it was finished in 1889, not 1887. There was no engineer named Wray in any issue; the builder was a company from Pittsburgh, and the flood of 1913 had not cracked a pier. It had washed away the road on the far bank.
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Theo felt tricked, until the librarian explained what the chatbot had done. It had read millions of pages about bridges and learned what a paragraph about a bridge usually looks like: a date, a name, a flood. Then it had built one for his bridge, one likely word at a time, with no way to check any of it.
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Sounding sure was part of the pattern, she said, because nearly every page it learned from had been written with confidence. The number it had for Samuel Wray was not a fact. It was the shape of a fact.
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Theo rewrote the report from the newspapers and put the chatbot's version beside it in a box, with a title: how it looked, and how it was. His teacher gave the box its own grade. The most useful question, she wrote in the margin, is the one he asked too late: how do you know?
description: "The bridge that was never built", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The voice it never heard.
description: The title of the story "The voice it never heard", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The kitchen speaker understood Priya perfectly. It played her songs, set her timers and told her the weather in a cheerful voice. When her grandmother asked it for the same things, it played the wrong song, set no timer, and once answered a question about rain with the price of rice.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her grandmother laughed it off, but Priya did not. She spoke to the speaker in her grandmother's accent, slowly, and it failed for her too. So it was not the words. It was the voice: the shape of the vowels, the rhythm, the way the sentence rose at the end.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Priya's science teacher explained where a speaker learns to listen. It is trained on recordings, thousands of hours of people talking, each with the words written out. It keeps the patterns those voices share. If nearly all of the voices came from one place, the patterns fit that place and stumble everywhere else.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Nothing in the speaker was against her grandmother. She had simply been missing, along with everyone who sounded like her, from the pile of recordings someone had collected years before. It had been collected in a city where hardly anyone spoke the way she did. The unfairness was in the pile, not in the machine.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So Priya did the one thing that changes a model. She found the setting that let the speaker learn a new voice, sat her grandmother in front of it, and had her read a page of sentences. Then another. By the third page the timer worked. By the fifth, the speaker knew the difference between rain and rice.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A machine that is right for most people can still be wrong for the people it heard least. The fix is never a faster machine. It is asking who is missing, and adding them.
description: "The voice it never heard", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The postcard rule.
description: The title of the story "The postcard rule", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Dev's science-fair poster needed a picture of the solar system and a paragraph to go under it, and the AI tool on his mother's laptop offered both in under a minute. The picture was gorgeous. The paragraph was smooth. Dev was already reaching for the glue stick.
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then the tool asked, helpfully, for his full name, his school and his home address, so it could write him a cover letter to the judges. Dev had typed the first two before his mother looked over his shoulder and said the postcard rule. Anything you type into that box, she said, leaves this laptop and may be kept. Would you write it on a postcard?
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He deleted the school and the address, and kept the first name only. The cover letter could wait; the judges did not need a letter from a machine anyway. What went into the box was part of his digital footprint now, and a footprint is a trail you cannot rake away.
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The picture was the next problem. It looked like a painting, because it was made from millions of paintings and photos that people had made, and those people had names. Dev could not find them, so he wrote on the poster where the picture came from and what tool had made it, the way a book lists its sources.
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The paragraph he threw away. Not because it was wrong, but because it was not his, and the judges would ask him questions the paragraph could not answer for him. He asked the tool to quiz him on the planets instead, closed the laptop, and wrote the paragraph from his own head, twice, until it was better than the smooth one.
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Nothing private goes in, the work inside gets its credit, and the thinking stays yours. Dev won a ribbon. The judges said his answers were the best part.
description: "The postcard rule", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Frederick and the jar of pond water.
description: The title of the story "Frederick and the jar of pond water", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The jar of pond water had been on Frederick's bench for a week, and the professor wanted a count of each tiny creature in a drop of it. So the professor handed him a program that had learned to tell the creatures apart from pictures, and eight thousand labeled pictures to teach it with.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Frederick fed the folder into the program and watched a bar creep across the screen. Nobody had written a rule that says a paramecium is slipper-shaped or that a rotifer has a crown of beating hairs. It had only the pictures and their labels, and it kept whatever the paramecia shared and whatever the rotifers shared. By evening it had a model.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The first drop went under the microscope camera, and the model counted it in nine seconds: three hundred and ten paramecia, forty amoebas, two rotifers. At twenty, Frederick knew not to trust a fast number. He checked the count by eye, because his professor had taught him that a number you have not checked is a hope, not a result. The paramecia were right, and so were the amoebas. But there were eleven rotifers, not two.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The model had called nine rotifers paramecia, with the same calm number it gave everything else. Frederick opened the folder and started counting labels. Seven thousand paramecia, six hundred amoebas, and fewer than a hundred rotifers, most of them blurred. The model had barely met a rotifer in its life.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Nothing in the program was against rotifers. They had simply been rare in the pile, because whoever collected the pictures collected what was easy to find. The model was right on average and wrong for the creature it had seen least, and it could not tell, because it had no way to know what it had missed.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So Frederick spent two days making rotifers less rare. He photographed every one he could find, sharp, from every angle, with the crown of hairs open and closed, until there were nine hundred good pictures. He taught the model again. The next drop came back with ten rotifers, and by eye there were ten.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The professor asked what Frederick had learned, and he said: the machine is fast and the microscope is true. He would let the model make the first count of every drop and check a share by eye, because a model only knows the pile it was fed, and the pond does not care about the pile.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the last page of his notebook he wrote the rule he would keep: use the fast guess, check it against something real, and always ask who was missing from the examples. Then he went back to the jar, where something with a crown of hairs turned slowly in the light.
description: "Frederick and the jar of pond water", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The night before the test.
description: The title of the story "The night before the test", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Amir had a plan for the science test and the plan was to stay up. His sister Leila, who was fourteen and insufferable about brains, told him he had it backwards, and then, worse, explained why.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Your hippocampus files the day while you sleep, she said, tapping the side of her head as if it were a cabinet. Study until one in the morning and you hand it a stack of papers and then lock the office. Amir said that was not how offices worked. Leila said it was exactly how his worked.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She drew him the map from her class. The brainstem, breathing and heartbeat. The cerebellum, balance, the part that lets you ride a bike without thinking. The amygdala, the alarm. The hippocampus, the filing clerk. And the front of the cortex, the part that plans and stops, which she said was still under construction in both of them and would be until their mid-twenties.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That was the part that interested Amir, because it explained his cousin's birthday party, where he had done something on a dare that he would never have done alone at a desk. The alarm and the reward parts are done, Leila said. The brakes are being built. So you decide the big things ahead of time, when nobody is cheering.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He tested her claim the only way that seemed fair, by studying until nine, sleeping nine hours, and taking the test. His friend Devin studied until one and came in gray. Amir scored an 88 and Devin a 74. That proved nothing by itself, Leila said, since two people are not an experiment, but the studies with hundreds of people found the same thing.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Amir wrote the map of the brain on the inside of his notebook, with the front part drawn in dotted lines and a note beside it. Under construction. Decide early. Sleep.
description: "The night before the test", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The closed book.
description: The title of the story "The closed book", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Priya had reread the chapter four times and could have told you what the pictures looked like on every page, which is why the quiz was such a surprise.
description: "The closed book", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher, Miss Okafor, had seen it before. Rereading feels like learning because the page looks familiar, she said, and familiar is not the same as known. She handed her the chapter and a blank card. Read a page, close the book, write what you can, then check. That is called testing yourself. text: [warm and natural] His mother noticed and took him to see the school nurse, who kept a growth chart on her wall. She explained that puberty usually begins between about 9 and 14 for boys, and that growth spurts can come years apart for two healthy friends.

text: [warm and natural] She showed him how the pituitary gland, a small gland in the brain, sends the signal that starts puberty. Hormones such as testosterone then drive the changes: height, muscle, a deeper voice and more sweat. None of it runs on a schedule set by the calendar.

text: [warm and natural] The nurse also kept a drawer of supplies for girls whose periods began during the school day, and deodorant for anyone who needed it. Puberty, she said, is something every student in the building is going through or will go through.

text: [warm and natural] At Malik's next checkup, his doctor measured him and plotted a dot on the same kind of chart. He was growing steadily along his own curve. If anything ever looked unusual, the doctor said, they would check, but nothing did.

text: [warm and natural] By the spring of seventh grade, Malik's voice cracked in the middle of a class presentation. The class laughed, and so did he. He was finally on his way, right on his own schedule.

text: [warm] Savanah and the smallest heartbeat.
description: The title of the story "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Savanah's first job at a company that built ultrasound machines was in customer service, answering calls from clinics. She wanted to understand what the callers needed, so on Thursdays she went along with the company's trainer to a clinic with a new machine. There Doctor Reyes, a cardiologist, studied the smallest hearts of all, the ones still growing before birth.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That Thursday, Elena came in twenty weeks pregnant, with her ten-year-old daughter, Paz, holding her hand. An earlier scan had raised a small question about the baby's heart, and the doctor wanted a closer look with a fetal echocardiogram. When Doctor Reyes asked, Elena said both visitors could stay.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Doctor Reyes dimmed the lights and moved the probe slowly. On the screen, a gray shape the size of a grape flickered. Paz gasped, and Elena squeezed her hand. That is the heart, the doctor said, and it is beating about 145 times a minute, right in the range a baby's heart should be.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Doctor Reyes showed them the four chambers, two on top and two on the bottom, and the valves opening and closing like tiny doors. The heart had started beating around week 6, she explained, when the baby was smaller than a pea, and it had been building itself ever since. She saved two views, one for her report and one for the family.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She studied every view and then smiled. The question from the earlier scan had only been the angle of the picture. The heart was healthy. Elena let out a long breath, and Paz asked whether she could have a printout.

text: [warm and natural] While the printer worked, Paz asked how a baby could have a heart before it was even born. Doctor Reyes told her that every person begins as one cell, a fertilized egg, that divides again and again, and that by week 12 all the major organs have formed. After that, the baby mostly grows.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Elena talked about her prenatal care, the folic acid she started early, the vitamins her doctor prescribed, the checkups she never missed, the coffee she cut back on and the alcohol she stopped completely. She also walked every evening. The baby had about twenty weeks to go, Doctor Reyes added, and the lungs would be among the last organs to finish.
description: "Savanah and the smallest heartbeat", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the way out, Paz asked Savanah how a machine could see a heart. With sound, she said. The probe sends out sound too high for anyone to hear, the echoes come back, and the machine turns them into a picture many times a second. Paz folded the printout carefully and put it in her backpack, between her math book and her library book. Savanah said Thursdays like this made her want to learn how the machines were built.

text: [warm] The tick on the trail.
description: The title of the story "The tick on the trail", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Mateo was twelve when his scout troop spent a June weekend hiking in the Texas Hill Country. He packed sunscreen, a water bottle, insect repellent and his toothbrush, which his mother checked twice.
description: "The tick on the trail", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the first night, his tentmate Owen started wheezing. Mateo knew the steps from health class. He helped Owen sit up, handed him his inhaler and ran for the scoutmaster, ready to call 911 if Owen's breathing did not improve. After two puffs and a few slow minutes, it did.

text: [warm and natural] The next afternoon, after a trail through tall grass, the scoutmaster called a tick check. Mateo found one on the back of his knee. With fine-tipped tweezers, she grasped it close to the skin, pulled straight up with steady pressure and cleaned the spot. She told him to watch for a spreading red rash or a fever over the next few weeks, the early signs of Lyme disease.
description: "The tick on the trail", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At dusk the mosquitoes rose over the creek. The scoutmaster explained that mosquitoes can carry West Nile virus. Most people who catch it never notice, but some get very sick, so the whole troop put on repellent and long sleeves before the campfire.
description: "The tick on the trail", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Back home, Owen found a website claiming that garlic pills keep ticks away. Mateo asked the questions from health class: who wrote it, what evidence did it give, and was it selling something? It was selling the garlic pills. The CDC page recommended repellent and tick checks instead.
description: "The tick on the trail", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On Monday, Mateo had his yearly check-up and a dental cleaning. The dentist found no cavities and said the twice-a-day brushing was working. The nurse reminded his mother that a vaccine was due before seventh grade, and Mateo, who now knew how vaccines train the immune system, did not complain.

text: [warm and natural] Ana was eleven when her grandfather moved in, and she took charge of the grocery list. His doctor had sent one instruction: less sodium. She had never read a food label in her life.

text: [warm and natural] In the soup aisle, she compared two cans of chicken noodle. The regular can listed 890 milligrams of sodium per serving, and the can held two servings. The lower-sodium can listed 480. If her grandfather ate the whole regular can, that was 1,780 milligrams.

text: [warm and natural] Her grandfather wanted milk with dinner, and Ana learned why it mattered for her, too. text: [warm and natural] The canned green beans came in a no-salt-added version, and the fresh ones were cheaper that week anyway. Her grandfather said fresh food was what he had grown up on, and he could taste the difference.

text: [warm and natural] After dinner they started walking around the block, twenty minutes the first night and thirty by the end of the week. Ana already got her sixty minutes a day between recess and soccer practice, so the walks were for him, and for the stories he told on the way.

text: [warm and natural] A week later, Leo and Kai were riding bikes when Kai skidded on gravel and cut his arm. Leo pressed a clean shirt firmly on the cut and kept pressing while Kai's mother drove over. The bleeding slowed in a few minutes.

text: [warm and natural] That weekend, both boys wrote personal safety plans: who to call, where to go and what to do. Leo also changed his passwords to long sentences only he would think of and set his accounts to private. The photo was gone from the group chat by Monday.
description: "The group chat", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The summer she turned seventeen, Savanah worked as a junior counselor at a day camp outside Austin, in charge of twelve campers who were eleven and twelve years old. text: [warm and natural] In the second week, the heat index passed 105 degrees. During kickball, a camper named Rosa went pale, sweaty and dizzy. text: [warm and natural] Rosa recovered within the hour. text: [warm and natural] In the last week, a camper found a vape in the parking lot and brought it to Savanah, half proud and half scared. She thanked him, gave it to the director, and answered the cabin's questions honestly: nicotine is highly addictive, and most teens never start.

text: [warm and natural] The field trip was to the university museum, and Amara's history teacher had made a deal with the art teacher. One hour, two rooms, and every student would come back able to say how a picture answers an event.
description: "The wall that answered a war", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The first room held a full-size print of Guernica. Picasso painted it in 1937, the docent said, after German planes bombed the town of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. text: [warm and natural] Amara asked why there was no red. Because red would let you look away, the docent said. Gray keeps you inside it. That was the first time Amara understood that a color could be a decision about the viewer.

text: [warm and natural] The second room held panels from Jacob Lawrence's Migration Series, painted between 1940 and 1941. text: [warm and natural] On the way out they passed the museum building itself, columns and a dome, and the art teacher stopped them. Buildings answer questions too, she said. text: [warm and natural] On the bus Amara wrote the sentence the teachers had asked for. A picture answers an event by choosing what you are allowed to look away from. She was not sure it was right, but it was hers, and it had the vocabulary.

text: [warm] Twelve bars and a repeat sign.
description: The title of the story "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Mateo could play the trumpet by ear before he could read a note, and the first page of band music looked to him like a fence with birds on it. The band director gave him one rule for the first week: every mark on the page is an instruction, and none of them is decoration.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The birds were note values, and they were fractions. A whole note held four beats in 4/4 time; a half note two; a quarter one; the eighth notes, joined at the top by a beam, half a beat each. The empty spaces had marks too, rests, silences measured as carefully as the sounds. Mateo, who liked math, could count a bar before he could play it.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice. Read 4/4 as the story means it, never as a date.

text: [warm and natural] Then the words. Piano under the first line, soft. A long hairpin opening to the right, crescendo, growing louder, until forte at the top of the hill. Allegro in the corner meant quick, and ritardando in the last bar meant slow down, as if the music were arriving. Dots over the notes meant staccato, short and separated; a curved line over a group meant legato, smooth.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] At the end of the eighth bar stood two dots before a double bar line. Mateo played on, alone, into silence, while the band went back to the beginning. A repeat sign, the director said, without looking up. The cheapest instruction in music. Two dots, and you play it twice.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] By the third rehearsal Mateo could see the form. The tune of the first eight bars came back after a different middle section, so the piece was ternary, ABA, and he felt the return coming. He learned that rondo would have gone out and come home more than once, ABACA, and that theme and variations would have changed the tune each time it came.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fence with birds turned into a page he could read the way he read a map. Every mark was an instruction. He played the repeat both times, soft where it said soft, and short where it said short.
description: "Twelve bars and a repeat sign", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The judge with five questions.
description: The title of the story "The judge with five questions", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The district solo contest needed a student shadow judge, someone to sit beside the real judge and fill in a sheet that would not count. Lena, who had played cello for four years, said yes before she knew what the sheet asked.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It asked five things. Intonation: were the notes in tune? Rhythm: was the beat steady and the timing right? Tone: was the sound full and clear? Balance: could every part be heard, the soloist against the piano? Expression: did the player follow the dynamics and the tempo the composer wrote? Five criteria, the judge said, and nowhere on the sheet does it ask whether you liked it.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The first player was loud and fast and got a burst of applause from his friends in the back, and Lena, honest, marked him down. The rhythm rushed. The forte was there but the piano was not; he had played a whisper as a shout. The judge, without looking, marked the same.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fourth player brought a button accordion and a piece of conjunto from the Texas border, and Lena had never judged anything like it. The judge told her to do what she had done for the cello: compare it to the best example of its kind she knew. Lena did not know one, so the judge played her thirty seconds on her phone, and then Lena could hear that the player's tone was clear and his rhythm exact.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Between players Lena watched the room as much as the stage. The good listeners were quiet and still, phones dark, applause only at the end. She realized the sheet was teaching her to hear the way the etiquette was teaching the room to listen, and that both were the same lesson.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The winner was a flute player nobody had cheered for, in tune to the last note, soft where the page said soft. Lena's sheet, which did not count, matched the judge's on four of five.
description: "The judge with five questions", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The mural that changed its mind.
description: The title of the story "The mural that changed its mind", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] When the town of Alder Creek built its new library, the council set aside one long wall for a mural and asked the middle school's art class to advise on which of two proposals should be painted there.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The first proposal was pretty. A sunrise over the creek, cottonwoods, a heron, the library itself drawn small and neat in the corner. The second was harder to look at: the flood of 1921 that took the old library, brown water to the second-story windows, and above it, in gold, the town rebuilding. The class did what the course had taught them and refused to vote until they had done the four steps.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Describe took an afternoon. Analyze took another. The sunrise proposal had unity and not much else, every element the same soft weight. The flood proposal had emphasis, a single gold band against brown, and movement, the water pushing left and the builders pushing right. The sunrise meant peace, one student said. The flood meant we survived, said another, and that is the bigger meaning for a library.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then a girl named Ines asked the question that settled it. Which proposal answers an event? The sunrise answered nothing; it could hang in any town. The flood answered 1921, and a mural on a library wall, she argued, ought to remember why the library was there at all. Evaluate: the class recommended the flood, with reasons, in a two-page letter the council read aloud.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The painter, a woman who had grown up in Alder Creek, changed one thing on the class's advice: a small figure in the gold band, a child carrying a single book up the steps of the new building, a symbol, she said, that anyone could read.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The unveiling came with a concert on the library steps. The school band played a rondo. The class, who had learned the form that spring, heard the tune go out and come home three times and elbowed each other at each return. A conjunto trio from the border played after, accordion and bajo sexto, and the whole town learned that a style has a place.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A retired music teacher judged nothing that night, but he told the class afterward what he had listened for: intonation, rhythm, tone, balance, expression. The band's balance was off, he said, the trumpets too loud for the flutes, and he said it kindly, and the band director agreed.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The mural has stood on the library wall for a year now. Visitors stop at the gold band and the child with the book. Nobody stops at a sunrise, the painter likes to say, because a sunrise never had to decide anything.
description: "The mural that changed its mind", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The price of one.
description: The title of the story "The price of one", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The school store sold three pens for sixty cents, and Marcus wanted five. He tried to work it out in line and got a different answer every time. Sixty for three, so five would be, what, a dollar twenty? Ninety? The cashier waited.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He had the price of three and needed the price of five, and five was not three times anything easy. That was the snag. He was trying to jump straight from three to five.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So he stopped at one. Sixty cents for three pens means twenty cents for one pen. Now five pens was easy: five times twenty, a dollar. He handed it over. And to check, he cross-multiplied: three over sixty equals five over a hundred, since three times a hundred is sixty times five.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His math teacher called twenty cents the unit rate, the price of one, and said it was the constant that ties the two numbers together. Price equals twenty cents times the number of pens. Double the pens, double the price; zero pens, zero cents. That straight-line pattern is what makes a relationship proportional.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus found unit rates everywhere after that. A car that drives 150 miles in 3 hours goes 50 miles in one. A recipe for 4 people that uses 2 cups of rice needs half a cup per person, so 6 people need 3 cups.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In any proportion, find what one unit is worth, then multiply by however many you need. Cross-multiply to check. The price of one is the key that opens the price of anything.
description: "The price of one", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Half off what?
description: The title of the story "Half off what?", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa ran a small clothes shop, and every spring she put the winter coats on sale. One year she tried something: she raised every price by fifty percent on Monday, and on Tuesday put up a sign that said half off.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A coat that had been eighty dollars was now sixty. The customers were delighted. Rosa was confused. Half off should have undone the raise and put the coat back at eighty. Instead it was twenty dollars below where it had started.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Because a percent is not a number. It is a fraction of whatever is in front of it. Fifty percent of eighty is forty, so the price went to one hundred twenty. But fifty percent of one hundred twenty is sixty, not forty. The second half came off a bigger pile.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] To get back to eighty from one hundred twenty, she would only have needed to take off forty dollars, which is a third, about thirty-three percent. The same forty dollars is fifty percent of eighty and a third of one hundred twenty, because the whole it is measured against has changed.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her accountant showed her the rule for percent change: the change divided by the starting amount. From 80 to 120 is a change of 40 on a start of 80, a fifty percent rise. From 120 to 60 is a change of 60 on a start of 120, a fifty percent fall. Same percent, different starting points, different dollars.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Percent means out of a hundred, and the hundred is always the current amount, not the original one. That is why a fall and a rise of the same percent never bring you back to where you started.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa took the sign down and put the old prices back. A fifty percent rise and a fifty percent cut had cost her twenty dollars on every coat she sold that day.
description: "Half off what?", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The debt.
description: The title of the story "The debt", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Nadia had five dollars in her jar and owed her sister three. So how much did she really have? Five, said her hands. Two, said her conscience. Owing money was like having less than nothing in that spot, and she did not know how to write that.
description: "The debt", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She tried writing five and three side by side and staring at them. The owing part would not sit still. It was a minus, somehow, and minuses were supposed to make things smaller.
description: "The debt", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then her sister forgave the debt. Nadia gained no cash, but she was three dollars better off, because a minus three had been taken away. Before, she was at two: five in the jar plus a minus three. Two minus negative three is five. On a number line, taking away a negative moves you right, and adding a negative moves you left. When a plus and a minus meet, the bigger one wins and keeps its sign.
description: "The debt", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her brother had a harder case. He owed three dollars to each of four friends. Four times negative three is negative twelve: twelve dollars in the hole. A positive times a negative is negative. When the friends forgave every debt, he was twelve dollars better off.
description: "The debt", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Their mother added the last rule at dinner. A negative times a negative is positive, the way taking away four debts of three dollars is the same as gaining twelve. The signs had rules, and the rules matched the money.
description: "The debt", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Adding a negative moves left; subtracting a negative moves right. When a negative and a positive meet, the difference takes the sign of the larger. Money owed is the number line with feelings, and forgiveness is subtracting a negative.
description: "The debt", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Shoes then socks.
description: The title of the story "Shoes then socks", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Two x plus three equals eleven. Diego wanted to divide by two first, because the two came first, and got a mess with fractions in it. He tried subtracting three from just one side and the equation stopped being true. He put his pencil down.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The problem had two steps hiding in it, and he did not know which to undo first. Undoing in the wrong order was like taking off socks before shoes.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That was the trick. Whatever was done to x last is undone first. Someone had multiplied x by two, then added three. The plus three came last, so it went first: subtract three from both sides, and two x equals eight. Then undo the multiplying: divide both sides by two, and x is four. Two fours plus three is eleven. Shoes off, then socks.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave him a real one. A bike rental costs three dollars plus two dollars an hour, and Diego had eleven dollars. How many hours? Two h plus three equals eleven, the same equation in a new coat. Four hours.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she changed a few words: at most eleven dollars. Two h plus three is less than or equal to eleven, an inequality, and it undoes the same way. Subtract three, divide by two: h is at most four. Any number of hours from zero to four would do.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Undo the steps in reverse order: the last thing done to x is the first thing you undo, and you do it to both sides. Then put the answer back in and check. Any equation with two steps is just shoes and socks.
description: "Shoes then socks", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The string and the can.
description: The title of the story "The string and the can", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena needed the distance around a soup can for a label, and a ruler would not bend. She wrapped a string around it, marked where it met, and laid the string flat. Then she wondered how many cans across the string was.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She lined up cans. Three cans across, and a little bit more. She tried a mug. Three mugs across, and a little bit more. A plate. Three plates, and the same little bit. The little bit would not go away.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It never does. The distance around any circle is about three and a bit times the distance across it, and the bit is always the same: 3.14, called pi. So circumference is 3.14 times the diameter. And the space inside, the area, is 3.14 times the radius times the radius. The radius is half the diameter. Lena cut her label to length.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her soup can was 7.5 centimeters across, so the label needed 3.14 times 7.5, about 23.6 centimeters, plus a little overlap for the glue. The string had said the same thing, a bit less exactly.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her brother asked about pizza. A 12-inch pizza has a radius of 6, and 3.14 times 36 is about 113 square inches. A 16-inch pizza has a radius of 8: 3.14 times 64, about 201 square inches. Four more inches across gave nearly twice as much pizza. Pi itself never ends, 3.14159 and on forever, but 3.14 is close enough for labels and pizza.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Circumference is 3.14 times the diameter. Area is 3.14 times the radius squared. Every circle carries the same hidden number, and a string around a can is where most people meet it.
description: "The string and the can", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] A hundred flips.
description: The title of the story "A hundred flips", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Owen flipped a coin a hundred times to prove it was fair. Fifty-three heads. He frowned. Fair should be fifty. He flipped another hundred. Forty-eight. The coin seemed unable to make up its mind.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Along the way it had thrown six heads in a row once and five tails in a row twice. Owen was sure the coin was broken, or the universe was.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Neither. The probability of heads is one half: one wanted outcome over two possible outcomes. That does not mean fifty every time. It means that over many flips, heads comes up about half the time, with streaks along the way. Fifty-three and forty-eight are what half looks like in real life.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave the two numbers names. One half is the theoretical probability, what should happen. Fifty-three out of a hundred is the experimental probability, what did happen. Flip a thousand times and the experimental number usually crawls closer to one half, though it rarely lands on it exactly.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Owen asked whether heads was due after five tails. It was not. The coin has no memory; the next flip is still one half. But two heads in a row is one half of one half, one quarter, because both flips have to go right.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Probability is wanted outcomes over all outcomes, from zero for impossible to one for certain. A half is what you expect on average, not a promise for any hundred flips, and the streaks are not the coin being broken. They are chance doing what chance does.
description: "A hundred flips", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The bedroom on the page.
description: The title of the story "The bedroom on the page", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa wanted to rearrange her bedroom without moving anything twice, so she decided to draw it first. The room was twelve feet wide. The page was six inches wide. She drew the first wall and ran out of paper before the door.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She tried again smaller, but then the window was too big for the wall and the bed did not fit through the door on paper either. Everything she drew was a different size from everything else.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fix was one number. One inch on the page for every two feet in the room. Twelve feet became six inches. The eight-foot wall became four inches. The three-foot window became an inch and a half. Every length shrank by the same factor, so the shapes stayed true and only the size changed.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher wrote the scale a second way. One inch to two feet is one inch to twenty-four inches, a ratio of 1 to 24. Every real length is 24 times the drawn one, so a bed drawn three inches long is really six feet.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Area surprised her. The floor was twelve feet by eight, 96 square feet, and the drawing was six inches by four, 24 square inches. Lengths shrank by 24, but areas shrank by 24 times 24, which is 576. A square on the page covered far more floor than its size suggested.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A scale drawing multiplies every length by the same factor. The shape stays; only the size changes. Choose the factor once, and a room, a map or a blueprint fits any page.
description: "The bedroom on the page", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The road trip.
description: The title of the story "The road trip", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The map said 420 miles, and the car used a gallon every 30 miles, so the trip needed 14 gallons. That is a proportion: one gallon for every 30 miles, scaled up to the whole road. The youngest wanted to know how that worked, so the oldest drew it as a table: 30 miles, 1 gallon; 60, 2; 420, 14.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Gas was 20 percent more expensive than at home, which turned a 50-dollar fill-up into 60. Twenty percent of fifty is ten, and ten more is sixty. At the next town the price was 10 percent lower than that, and the youngest guessed it was back to 50. It was 54, because ten percent of sixty is six.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The trip budget was 200 dollars, and by lunch it was minus 12, which is what happens when you spend more than you have. Their mother added 30 from her own purse: minus 12 plus 30 is 18. The number line in the youngest's head went left past zero and came back.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Lunch was pizza, and the pizza was a circle. A 14-inch pizza is 7 inches from the middle to the edge, and the area is pi times seven squared, about 154 square inches. The youngest wanted it in slices; eight slices made each one about 19 square inches.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The oldest wanted the crust. The crust runs around the edge, so it is the circumference: pi times 14, about 44 inches of crust. The middle child, who only ate crust, asked whether a 16-inch pizza would be better, and it would: about 50 inches of crust and about 201 square inches of pizza.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] After lunch they drove on a map with a scale: one inch for every 20 miles. The next town was three and a half inches away, 70 miles. The youngest measured it with a crayon, and the crayon agreed.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The last stretch was an equation. They had driven for x hours at 60 miles an hour plus a 30-mile detour, and the total was 210 miles. 60x plus 30 equals 210. Take the 30 away, divide by 60, three hours. The oldest checked it: three hours at 60 is 180, and 30 more is 210.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In the back seat they played a game: guess whether the next car would be red. There were four red cars in the first twenty, so they guessed one in five. By the end of the trip it was closer to one in six. Nobody was sure who had started the math, but nobody wanted to stop.
description: "The road trip", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Three pages.
description: The title of the story "Three pages", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Nadia read three pages of the Sunday paper in a row. A weather report. An advertisement for a mattress. A comic strip. Her teacher asked what each writer wanted from her, and Nadia said, to be read. That was true and useless.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She looked again for what else they might want. The pages felt different in her hands, but she could not say how, and the words on each were just words.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she noticed the shape. The weather report was facts and dates, laid out to be checked: it wanted to inform. The advertisement was full of should, must and best: it wanted to persuade. The comic had a setup and a punch line: it wanted to entertain. Three pages, three purposes, and each shape told her which.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added a warning. Many pages mix purposes. A cereal box lists its vitamins, which informs, in order to make you buy it, which persuades. The main purpose is the one the rest of the page serves, and on the cereal box that is selling.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She also learned to ask who wrote it. The mattress ad came from the company selling the mattress. A review of the same mattress by a magazine that tests beds might still persuade, but it had less reason to tilt the facts.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Inform, persuade or entertain. The shape of the writing tells you which, and the purpose tells you how to read it: check the facts, doubt the pitch, enjoy the story. Ask what the writer wants before you decide what to believe.
description: "Three pages", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] One story against ten thousand.
description: The title of the story "One story against ten thousand", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus's friend swore a vitamin had cured his colds. Every winter, not one cold. Marcus was ready to spend his allowance on a bottle, because his friend was honest and the story was true.
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he found a study of ten thousand people that found the vitamin did not prevent colds. Now he had two true things that disagreed. His friend was not lying. Neither was the study. How could both be true?
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They could, because they were different kinds of evidence. His friend was one story: one person, one winter, no way to check what else changed. The study was many cases from a checkable source, counted and compared. One honest story is a start. Ten thousand counted cases are evidence. He kept his allowance.
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher pointed out what the study had that the story did not: a comparison group. Half the people took the vitamin and half took a look-alike pill with nothing in it, and neither group knew which. Only then could the study tell whether the vitamin, and not something else, made the difference.
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His friend's winter might have gone well for other reasons: fewer sick classmates, more sleep, luck. When two things happen together, one did not necessarily cause the other. Marcus wrote that on a sticky note for his wallet.
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Many cases from a checkable source beat one story or a feeling, however sincere. Weak evidence does not make a claim false, but it does not make it true either. Ask how many, and who counted.
description: "One story against ten thousand", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Slim, thin, skinny.
description: The title of the story "Slim, thin, skinny", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa called her friend skinny and her friend went quiet for the rest of the walk home. Rosa had meant it kindly. Skinny meant thin, and thin meant slim, and slim was a compliment. Where had it gone wrong?
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She lined the words up. Slim. Thin. Skinny. On a scale they meant the same thing. She would have sworn they were interchangeable.
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They were not, because words carry more than their meaning. Slim comes with approval. Thin is plain. Skinny carries a little worry, or a little scorn. That extra weight is connotation, the feeling a word carries beyond what it says. Swap a word for a plainer one, and notice what disappears. That is the connotation.
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher gave the plain meaning a name too, denotation: what a dictionary says. Curious and nosy share a denotation, wanting to know things, but curious sounds like a compliment and nosy like a complaint. House and home name the same building, and only one of them has a family in it.
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa started hearing connotation everywhere. An ad called a small apartment cozy. A coach called a stubborn player determined. Choosing the warm word or the cold one was how writers, and friends, took a side without saying so.
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Connotation is the feeling a word carries beyond its meaning. Writers choose it on purpose, and readers feel it whether they notice or not. Rosa apologized the next day, with a better word.
description: "Slim, thin, skinny", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] What she wanted and what she feared.
description: The title of the story "What she wanted and what she feared", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] In the novel, the girl lied to her brother about the letter from the bank. Kai stopped reading. She had been honest for two hundred pages. Why now? The author never said, and Kai wanted to close the book.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher asked him to look not at what the girl said but at what she did under pressure. She hid the letter. She took a second job. She stopped sleeping.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Kai wrote two columns. What she wanted: her brother's respect. What she feared: losing the house. The lie sat right where those two met. She could not tell him without losing the first, and she could not let him find out without the second coming true. Nobody had told Kai her motive. Her actions had.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave him a name for what the author had done: indirect characterization. The author never wrote she is afraid. She showed it through the girl's actions, her thoughts, what she said and how others reacted to her. Direct characterization just tells you; indirect makes you work it out.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.
