text: [warm and natural] Near the end the girl told her brother the truth, and he helped her keep the house. She had changed, and a character who changes over a story is called dynamic. The motive had not vanished; she had found a way to satisfy both columns.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Motive is what a character wants or fears, and it is shown by what they do, especially under pressure. Predict a character by their motive, not by their last line of dialogue, and the book stops surprising you for the wrong reasons.
description: "What she wanted and what she feared", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The clock that glared.
description: The title of the story "The clock that glared", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The clock glared at me, the story said, and Owen wrote in the margin: clocks cannot glare. He was right, and he was missing the point, and his teacher circled the note with a smile.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Later in the same chapter, a girl's smile was sunshine. Not like sunshine. Was. Owen underlined that too. The book seemed to be lying on purpose.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It was, and that was the craft. The glaring clock was personification: a thing given a human act, so the reader feels the pressure of midnight. The smile that was sunshine was a metaphor: one thing said to be another, no like or as. A face as bright as the sun would have been a simile, the gentler cousin with the little word in it.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher added one more, hyperbole: exaggeration on purpose. I have told you a million times. This backpack weighs a ton. Nobody counts the times or weighs the bag. The size of the exaggeration shows the size of the feeling.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she asked him to write the late night himself without any of them. The clock said 11:58. It was late. He was tired. It was true and dead on the page. He put the glare back.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Similes compare with like or as, metaphors say one thing is another, personification gives human acts to things, and hyperbole exaggerates on purpose. None of them is meant literally, and all of them make a reader feel what a plain sentence only reports.
description: "The clock that glared", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two rooms.
description: The title of the story "Two rooms", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena read an article about two rival cities and an article about a drought, and she understood the first and got lost in the second. Same magazine, same page size. Why did one feel like a map and the other like fog?
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She went back to the second one and looked for what the first had. The city article kept saying however and similarly. The drought article never did. Did that matter?
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It did. However and similarly were signal words for compare and contrast: two rooms side by side, the reader walking between them. The drought article said the trouble was, and then, one answer: a problem and its solution, one long hallway. The moment she knew each article's shape, she knew where to stand in it.
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added the others. First, next and finally mark time order, like a recipe. Because, so and as a result mark cause and effect: the drought began because the rains failed, and as a result the wells ran low. Some articles use more than one shape, so Lena learned to watch for signal words all the way through.
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She drew each shape in her notebook: a timeline, two rooms side by side, a knot and scissors, a row of falling dominoes. When she read, she pictured the shape and filled it in, and the fog lifted.
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A text has a structure, and its signal words tell you which one: time order, comparison, problem and solution, cause and effect. Find the signal words in the first paragraph, and the rest of the piece has a floor plan.
description: "Two rooms", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The mystery of the missing bicycle.
description: The title of the story "The mystery of the missing bicycle", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The novel was a mystery about a stolen bicycle, and the class read it the way detectives read a room. The first question was why the author had written it: not to inform, not to persuade, but to entertain, and knowing that told them to expect a trick. Mysteries hide the truth in plain sight, and the fun is finding it before the last page.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The second question was evidence. When a character said everyone knew the neighbor was a thief, the class wrote one story in the margin. When the police log said the bicycle was seen at the station at nine, they wrote evidence. One was a feeling said loudly; the other could be checked.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The words themselves were doing work. The neighbor was described as thin in one chapter and skinny in another, and the class caught the change: same size, different feeling. The author had turned the reader against him with a single word.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then there was the motive. The girl who took the bicycle wanted to reach her grandmother's house before dark, and she feared being late more than being caught. The author had shown both without ever saying them: she checked the sky, she skipped supper, she lied to her brother.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The author had tricks with language too. The rain spat at the girl as she rode; the streetlights watched her pass. Personification, said a boy in the back, and the whole class felt the town turn against her. It was a figure of speech, not a fact, and a good reader enjoys the one without mistaking it for the other.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The structure helped the detectives most. The chapters about the neighbor used however and on the other hand; the chapters about the girl went first, next, then. One side was a comparison; the other was a timeline, and the timeline led to the station at nine.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The bicycle turned up in the last chapter where the strongest evidence had pointed all along. The girl brought it back herself, soaked, and told the truth. The police had never had to look far; the station clock and the log had told them where she went.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Half the class had suspected the neighbor anyway, on the strength of one story and one skinny. That, the teacher said, was the lesson, and it was not about bicycles. Evidence can be checked. A feeling said loudly cannot, however many people repeat it.
description: "The mystery of the missing bicycle", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The city inside.
description: The title of the story "The city inside", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal bit into an apple and thought nothing of it. His science teacher asked him to think of everything. What had to happen for one bite to become part of his body?
description: "The city inside", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He said, you swallow it. She waited. He said, then it goes to your stomach. She was still waiting, and Jamal realized he did not actually know what happened next.
description: "The city inside", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Think of a city. The stomach and intestines are the kitchen, breaking the bite into pieces the body can use. The heart and blood vessels are the roads and trucks, carrying those pieces to every building. The lungs are the air supply. The brain and nerves are the phone lines running it all. Every system is a team of organs with one main job, and one bite needs all of them.
description: "The city inside", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The kitchen does more than chop. The stomach churns the bite with acid, and the small intestine, a tube longer than Jamal is tall, pulls the sugars and other nutrients into the blood. Then the nutrients and the oxygen carried by red blood cells from the lungs ride the roads together to every muscle.
description: "The city inside", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The city also keeps itself steady. When Jamal ran at recess and got hot, his skin sweated to cool him and his heart sped up to deliver more oxygen. The body is always adjusting to stay balanced, and scientists call that homeostasis.
description: "The city inside", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each body system is a team of organs with one job, and the systems depend on each other. One bite of an apple is a delivery to a whole city, and the city works only because no system works alone.
description: "The city inside", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The flower in the basement.
description: The title of the story "The flower in the basement", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Silas won the flower at the county fair, a prize-winning orange lily, and he wanted to keep it safe. So he put it in the basement, where it was cool and nothing could knock it over.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He gave it the best soil in town. He watered it every morning. Within a week the leaves turned pale, then yellow, and drooped like they were tired.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] More water did nothing. Better soil did nothing. The flower was fed and watered and dying, and Silas could not see why.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then his neighbor asked a strange question: "What is it eating?" Not drinking. Eating. Plants do not eat soil. They eat light. Inside every green leaf are chloroplasts, tiny solar panels that take carbon dioxide from the air, water from the roots, and the energy of sunlight, and build sugar out of them. No light, no sugar. No sugar, no lily. Without light, a plant also stops making the green chlorophyll that catches it, which is why the leaves had faded.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Silas carried it up to the window. In a few days the leaves began to green again, and within a week the whole plant had turned itself to face the glass.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The leaves gave something back, too. Building sugar splits water and lets oxygen out into the air, the same oxygen Silas breathed. And at night, with no light, the lily used some of the sugar it had made, the way he used his breakfast.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Every forest you have ever seen is made mostly of air and light, woven together by leaves.
description: "The flower in the basement", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The slope of the air.
description: The title of the story "The slope of the air", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] From the hilltop Priya watched a line of clouds come across the valley, and felt the wind pick up before they arrived. Her uncle said the wind was blowing toward the storm. That seemed backward. Should the storm not push the wind ahead of it?
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She could not see air, so she could not see what was pushing what. All she had was the feeling on her face and a line of clouds getting closer.
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her uncle told her to think of air as water on a slope. Cool air is heavy and piles up: high pressure. Warm air is light and rises: low pressure. The heavy air slides toward the light, and that sliding is wind. The storm was a place where warm air was rising, so the wind ran toward it. And the line of clouds was a front, where two air masses met and one shoved the other up.
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The sun sets it all going. It heats the ground unevenly, land faster than water, dark fields faster than pale sand, so some air warms and rises while other air stays cool. On a summer afternoon near a lake, the breeze blows in off the cool water toward the warm land.
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Fronts come in kinds. A cold front, cold air pushing under warm air like a shovel, brings tall clouds and short, hard storms, with cooler air behind them. A warm front, warm air sliding up over cold air, brings long, gentle rain. Priya's line of tall clouds was a cold front.
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Warm air rises and cool air sinks; wind blows from high pressure to low. A front is where two air masses meet, and that is where the weather happens. Feel the wind on a hill and you can read the sky.
description: "The slope of the air", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The moths.
description: The title of the story "The moths", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo read that the moths near an old factory town had turned dark over a hundred years, and he pictured moths going darker the way skin tans. His teacher said no moth had ever changed color in its life. Theo said then how did they turn dark?
description: "The moths", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She showed him a photo of a tree trunk gone black with soot, and a pale moth sitting on it like a light on a hill. Birds eat moths. Which one would a bird see first?
description: "The moths", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The pale one. On sooty trees, pale moths were easy to see and got eaten. Dark moths hid and lived, and they had dark children, because color is inherited. Year after year, more dark moths, fewer pale. Nobody changed. The group changed, because the ones who fit the place had the most children.
description: "The moths", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then the air was cleaned up. After laws cut the soot in the second half of the twentieth century, the trunks grew pale with lichen again, the pale moths came back, and the dark ones became rare. The same rule ran in reverse.
description: "The moths", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The same thing happens in hospitals. When a medicine kills most of a germ, the few germs that happen to survive it multiply, and soon the medicine works less well. Nobody taught the germs anything. The medicine chose which ones would have children.
description: "The moths", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Natural selection needs three things: variation, survival and inheritance. Helpful differences get passed on more, and over generations the group shifts to fit its place. No moth turned dark. The forest chose which moths would have children.
description: "The moths", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The kittens that did not match.
description: The title of the story "The kittens that did not match", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Two black barn cats had four kittens. Three were black. One was gray, soft as smoke, and nobody could say where it came from.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The farmer checked the barn for strays. There were none. Both parents were black, plain as night. How do two black cats make a gray kitten?
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each kitten gets two copies of a coat gene, one from each parent. The black copy is dominant: one black copy and the kitten shows black. The gray copy is recessive: it shows only when a kitten gets two gray copies. Both parents were carrying a hidden gray copy behind their black one. Three kittens got at least one black copy. One kitten drew gray from both, and the hidden trait finally showed.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The farmer's daughter drew it as a square. Each parent had one black copy and one gray copy. Four boxes: black-black, black-gray, gray-black and gray-gray. Only one box in four was gray-gray, so each kitten had a one-in-four chance of gray. Four kittens, one gray: the square came true this time, though it does not always.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Those copies live in DNA, a long code curled up inside the cells, and a gene is one stretch of it. The kitten carries the same code in its paws, its whiskers and its tail.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The farmer kept the gray kitten. It never had to wonder where it came from. It had always been there, in both parents, waiting.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A trait can skip a generation without leaving. Recessive does not mean weak. It means quiet.
description: "The kittens that did not match", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The pyramid.
description: The title of the story "The pyramid", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Maya wondered why the field had thousands of blades of grass, hundreds of grasshoppers, a few dozen birds and one hawk. If hawks were the strongest, why were there not more of them?
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She counted energy instead of animals. Say the grass held a thousand units of energy from the sun. How much reached the grasshoppers that ate it? She assumed most of it. That turned out to be the mistake.
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Only about a tenth. A grasshopper spends most of what it eats on moving, breathing and staying warm, and only a tenth becomes grasshopper. A thousand units of grass make a hundred units of grasshopper, ten of bird, one of hawk. The energy leaks away at every step, so each level has to be much bigger than the one above it.
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Maya asked where the lost energy went. Most of it left as heat, from every animal breathing, moving and keeping warm. Heat does not come back to the grass. That is why the field needs new sunlight every day.
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The matter is different. When the hawk dies, decomposers break its body down, and the carbon and nitrogen in it return to the soil to build new grass. Matter goes around in a circle. Energy flows through in a line, from the sun to heat.
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Only about a tenth of the energy passes to the next level of a food chain. That is why there is much more grass than there are hawks, and why the pyramid of life is always wide at the bottom.
description: "The pyramid", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The crumpled bag.
description: The title of the story "The crumpled bag", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai lived on a street with a storm drain and a creek at the bottom of the hill, and he had never once wondered where the creek came from. Then his teacher handed him a crumpled paper bag and a cup of water.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He poured a little water on the top of the bag. It ran along the creases, joined other trickles, and gathered in one low corner. He poured on the other side. Different creases, same corner. He could not make the water go anywhere else.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The creases were ridges. The folds between them were creeks. Every drop that fell on the bag ran downhill to the same river, and all the land that drained to that corner was its watershed. His street, his storm drain, the creek: one bag, one corner.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher showed a real map. In Austin, Texas, creeks such as Shoal Creek and Barton Creek run into the Colorado River, which widens into Lady Bird Lake downtown and flows on to the Gulf of Mexico. Every creek on the map had its own little watershed inside the big one.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That is why oil dripped in a driveway or fertilizer washed off a lawn matters. Rain carries it down the creases too, into the storm drain and the creek, and what happens on the hill shows up in the river.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A watershed is all the land that drains to one river, and upstream becomes downstream. What you pour on the top of the bag ends up in the corner, which is why a town cares what happens on the hill above it.
description: "The crumpled bag", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The garden that taught everything.
description: The title of the story "The garden that taught everything", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The school garden started as a rectangle of dirt in March. The first lesson was the body. The students who dug it went home tired and hungry, and the teacher drew a city on the board: roads for blood, a kitchen for the stomach, phone lines for the nerves. The heart sped up while they dug and slowed when they rested, keeping the city steady.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The second lesson was the leaves that came up in April: photosynthesis, light and water and carbon dioxide from the air turned into sugar, and oxygen given away. A pot of beans left in the shed came up pale and spindly, reaching for a light that was not there, and the class kept it as proof.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In May the weather turned. High pressure brought cool, sinking air and still mornings; then a low came through with a cold front, and a hard wind flattened half the beans. The class had watched the barometer drop the night before.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The beans with the thickest stems stayed standing and set seed; the thin-stemmed ones snapped. If stem thickness runs in bean families, that is natural selection in one bed, said the teacher: the wind had chosen which plants would leave seeds.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The tomatoes came up red and yellow from the same packet. Red is dominant in tomatoes and yellow recessive, so the class drew Punnett squares. Two red plants, each carrying a hidden yellow copy, would give about one yellow plant in four. They counted three yellow in fourteen, close enough to make them grin.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] By June the garden was feeding grasshoppers, which were feeding a pair of birds, which were feeding a hawk that came once a week. Only about a tenth of the energy passed up each step, and everyone could see why there was one hawk and a thousand grasshoppers.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The last lesson was the hose. The water came from the river the whole town drank, which came from the creeks in the hills, which is where the rain went. A watershed, ending in a school bean. When a parent spilled fertilizer by the storm drain, the class knew exactly where it was headed.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In August they pulled the plants and turned the soil, and the teacher asked what they had grown. Beans, said one student. A body, a leaf, a storm, a family tree, a food chain and a river, said another. Both were right. The bean seeds went into envelopes for next year.
description: "The garden that taught everything", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The summary that gave nothing away.
description: The title of the story "The summary that gave nothing away", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Diego's summary of the article was one sentence long and it was mostly his opinion. The article says cities should plant more trees, which is obviously right. His teacher crossed out the last four words and wrote: not yet.
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Not yet? Diego thought summarizing was about what he thought of the thing. Otherwise what was the point of reading it?
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The point came in two parts. First, the summary: the article says cities should plant more trees, for shade and cleaner air, and it gives three cities as examples. Nothing about what Diego thought. A reader could not guess his opinion, and that was the test. Then the response, where he finally got to say obviously right, and why.
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave him the rules for the first job. Name the author and the title. Give the main idea and the key details in your own words. Keep it much shorter than the original, and leave yourself out.
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The response had choices. Diego could agree and add a reason of his own, or disagree and say why. He could also connect the article to something he had seen, like the treeless parking lot by his school that baked every afternoon. He did all three in one paragraph.
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Summarize fairly first, then respond. Keep your opinion out of the summary so a reader can trust it, and then spend the response on what you think and what you would push back on. Two jobs, two paragraphs.
description: "The summary that gave nothing away", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The objection said out loud.
description: The title of the story "The objection said out loud", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Priya was arguing for a later school start, and she knew exactly what the coach would say: it would cut practice time. She planned to leave that out and hope nobody thought of it. Her teacher read the draft and asked where the coach was.
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Priya said she had left him out on purpose. If she brought up the objection, would she not be arguing against herself?
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The opposite. She wrote it in: some say a later start would cut practice time. True, up front. Then she answered it: practice could shift later, and rested players play better than tired ones. When the coach stood up at the meeting to object, half the room said, she already covered that. Her argument looked stronger for having met him first.
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher warned her about one trap. It is easy to answer a weak objection that nobody really holds. That is called a straw man, and audiences can smell it. Priya had chosen the objection the coach would actually make, which is why answering it worked.
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She also learned the sentences that carry it. While it is true that practice would move, rested players play better. Some say the buses cannot change; in fact, other districts have changed theirs. Each sentence gives the other side its due, then turns.
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Name the best objection and answer it. A fair counterclaim makes your argument stronger, not weaker, because it shows you have looked at the other side and still stand where you stand.
description: "The objection said out loud", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Starting where the reader is.
description: The title of the story "Starting where the reader is", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Sam had to explain how a board game worked to someone who had never played, and his first draft began with the scoring. His grandmother read it and asked what a piece was. Sam had been playing since he was six and had forgotten anyone could not know.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He started again, from the top, and got lost in a different way: every sentence had three new words in it. His grandmother read it kindly and asked what a turn was.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The third draft started where she was. A board, a die, a piece. Then one rule, roll the die and move that many spaces, and then the next rule. Each new word got its meaning the moment it appeared, and each rule got an example she could picture. By the end she was beating him.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher showed him what held the third draft together: transitions. First, then, after that, finally. Each one told his grandmother where she was in the explanation, the way signs tell you where you are in a building.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He added one small drawing, the board with an arrow showing which way to move, and a heading over the part about winning. A picture and a heading did in one glance what a paragraph had struggled to do.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An explanatory essay starts where the reader is and adds one idea at a time. Define a new word when it appears, and give an example for every rule. If your grandmother can follow it, anyone can.
description: "Starting where the reader is", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Chloe and the counterclaim.
description: The title of the story "Chloe and the counterclaim", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Chloe was twelve when the school cut the art budget, and she wrote to the board. Her first job was a fair summary of their reasons, with none of her opinion in it: reading scores were down, and the money had to come from somewhere.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Only then came her response. Summarize fairly first; then say what you think. She quoted their own words where she could, so no one could say she had bent them. The board member who read it said it was the first letter that had understood them.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her argument named the best objection before anyone else could: some say art is a luxury when reading scores are down. True, she wrote, and then the answer: the students who took art had raised their reading scores that year, and here were the numbers. She checked them twice with the school secretary before she mailed a single page.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She was careful with those numbers. Scores rising in the same year did not prove art had caused it, she added, but they did show art had not cost the students their reading. A board member underlined that sentence.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A fair counterclaim wins trust, and trust was what she needed. She did not answer a straw man, the weakest objection nobody held; she answered the one the board actually believed. She practiced reading it aloud to her grandmother, who asked the hardest question she heard all spring: what would you cut instead? She answered that too: the new scoreboard could wait a year.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The explanatory essay was for the board members who had never taken art. It started where they were, one idea at a time: what a color wheel is, then what value means, then what a child learns by mixing green. Each new word got its meaning the moment it appeared.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She used transitions like signposts, first, then, finally, and one small drawing of the color wheel, which did in a glance what a paragraph could not. She read the essay aloud once more and cut every sentence that explained what the drawing already showed.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The budget came back in the spring, smaller than before but back. Chloe kept the letter. Her handwriting had gotten neater in the middle of it, where she had stopped arguing with the board and started explaining to it. The next fall, two other students wrote letters of their own about the library hours, and they asked Chloe to read their drafts first.
description: "Chloe and the counterclaim", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Four regions.
description: The title of the story "Four regions", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai's family drove across Texas in one long day, and Kai noticed the land keep changing outside the window. Flat and wet and green. Then rolling hills. Then high and dry and endless. Then mountains. He asked if they had left the state. They had not.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His mother said the peoples who lived here first would have felt those changes more than he did, because the land decided what they ate. Kai did not see how land could decide anything.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It decided everything. Along the wet Gulf Coast, the Karankawa fished and gathered in the bays. In the piney woods of East Texas, still part of the Gulf Coastal Plains, the Caddo farmed corn, beans and squash in villages. On the rolling North Central Plains, the Wichita farmed along the rivers and hunted buffalo. On the high, dry Great Plains, the Comanche followed the buffalo on horseback. In the Mountains and Basins of the far west, the Jumano farmed beside the rare rivers.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The land even decided their houses. The Caddo built tall, round houses of grass over wooden frames. The Comanche carried tipis they could take down and move with the herds. The Karankawa paddled dugout canoes through the shallow bays, and the Jumano along the western rivers lived in adobe villages.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Kai started reading the land from the car. Where it rained, people farmed. Where it was dry and open, people followed the animals. Where the bays were shallow and full of fish, people fished.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Texas has four natural regions: the Gulf Coastal Plains, the North Central Plains, the Great Plains, and the Mountains and Basins. Each shaped how its first peoples lived, and you can still see the borders from a car window.
description: "Four regions", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Three centuries and a door.
description: The title of the story "Three centuries and a door", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Maya's history book said Spain owned Texas for three hundred years, and she pictured three hundred years of Spanish towns. Then she looked at the map from 1800. San Antonio. A few missions. And a great deal of nothing.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Three centuries and almost no one? How could a country claim a place that size and hardly live in it? Maya thought the map must be missing something.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It was not. Spain claimed Texas from the 1500s and settled little of it beyond San Antonio, founded in 1718, and a string of missions from the 1690s. The land was far from Mexico City and hard to hold. In 1821 Mexico won its independence, inherited the empty claim, and opened the door to American settlers to fill it. They came faster than anyone in Mexico City expected.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher explained why the missions were built at all. In 1685 a French explorer, La Salle, landed on the Texas coast and built a fort. Spain, alarmed, sent priests and soldiers to build missions in the east to hold its claim. Fear of France did more to settle early Texas than any plan.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Mexico's door had a name: the empresario system. Stephen F. Austin brought the first three hundred families, and many more followed. By the early 1830s settlers from the United States far outnumbered the Mexican Texans, called Tejanos, and quarrels over laws, slavery and self-rule began to grow.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Spain claimed Texas for three centuries and settled little of it. Mexico won independence in 1821 and invited settlers, who soon outnumbered everyone else. A claim on a map is not the same as a people on the land, and that gap is the next chapter.
description: "Three centuries and a door", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] From a cannon to eighteen minutes.
description: The title of the story "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo could not understand how a war could be won in eighteen minutes. His grandfather said the Texas Revolution had been, at San Jacinto, and Theo said that sounded like a story someone made up later.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His grandfather said, then start earlier. In October 1835, at Gonzales, the Mexican army came to take back a small cannon, and the settlers would not give it up. That was the first battle. Eighteen minutes was the last one.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In between were six months. In March 1836 the Alamo fell after a siege, and at Goliad hundreds of prisoners were executed. Sam Houston retreated east, gathering men and anger. On April 21 at San Jacinto his army surprised the Mexican camp during its afternoon rest, and the fighting was over in eighteen minutes. Santa Anna was captured, and Texas was a republic.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His grandfather added a date Theo had never heard. On March 2, 1836, while the Alamo was still under siege, delegates at Washington-on-the-Brazos signed the Texas Declaration of Independence. The war was already on; that paper said what it was for.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] After San Jacinto, the Republic of Texas lasted almost ten years. Sam Houston was elected its first president, and in 1839 the capital moved to a new town on the Colorado River named for Stephen F. Austin.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The revolution ran from Gonzales in October 1835 to San Jacinto in April 1836, with the Alamo and Goliad between. Eighteen minutes ended it only because six months had built it. That is how most quick endings work.
description: "From a cannon to eighteen minutes", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] A state, a war, and June nineteenth.
description: The title of the story "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Ava's great-great-great-grandmother was born in the Republic of Texas and died in the United States without ever moving house. Ava asked how that was possible. Her aunt said the country moved, not the grandmother.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In 1845 Texas joined the Union as the twenty-eighth state. Within a year the United States was at war with Mexico over where Texas ended. Ava thought that was the whole story. Her aunt said it was the first third.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Mexico said the border was the Nueces River; the United States said the Rio Grande, farther south. The war ended in 1848 with the Rio Grande as the line, and Mexico gave up a huge area that became much of the American Southwest.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In 1861 Texas left the Union to join the Confederacy in a war over slavery. The war ended in 1865, but freedom reached Texas late: on June 19, 1865, soldiers in Galveston read the order that every enslaved person in the state was free. Juneteenth started there. Ava's grandmother had lived through all of it in one town.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The order was read by a Union general, Gordon Granger, about two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation. For a long time Juneteenth was celebrated mostly in Texas. In 2021 it became a national holiday.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Texas joined the Union in 1845, war with Mexico followed in 1846, Texas left for the Confederacy in 1861, and freedom arrived in Galveston on June 19, 1865. One lifetime can hold a whole map of changes.
description: "A state, a war, and June nineteenth", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Three fortunes.
description: The title of the story "Three fortunes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal's town had a cattle brand on the welcome sign, a cotton gin turned into a museum, and an oil pump nodding beside the highway. He asked which one Texas was really about. His uncle said, all three, in order.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] How could one state be about three different things? Jamal thought a place picked one thing and stuck to it, the way his town had picked its football team and never let go.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Texas did not. From 1867, for about twenty years, cattle walked from Texas to the railroads in Kansas, and the drives made the first fortunes. Cotton came next, filled the fields and became the state's biggest crop. And in 1901 at Spindletop, oil blew more than a hundred feet into the air and changed everything again. Each fortune came from the same ground, and each one paid for the next.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The drives ended almost as fast as they began. Railroads reached Texas itself, so cattle no longer had to walk to Kansas, and barbed wire fenced the open range into ranches. The cowboys who had ridden the trails became ranch hands, and some of the ranches grew bigger than whole counties.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Oil changed more than the owners. Towns grew up around the wells almost overnight, refineries rose along the Gulf Coast, and money from oil on state land helped pay for Texas schools and universities.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Cattle, cotton and oil, one after another, from the same land. When you ask what a place is about, the honest answer is usually a sequence, not a single thing.
description: "Three fortunes", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] From farms to skylines.
description: The title of the story "From farms to skylines", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa counted the six flags on the plaza: Spain, France, Mexico, the Republic of Texas, the Confederacy, the United States. Six countries, one state. She thought the story was finished. Her teacher said the twentieth century added a seventh flag that was not a flag at all.
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa did not know what that meant. All the flags were up there already. What could the twentieth century have added?
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A skyline. In one century Texas went from farms and ranches to the second-largest state by land and by people. NASA came to Houston and put Mission Control in Texas, and the first words spoken from the surface of the moon were addressed to Houston. Highways, airports and glass towers rose where cotton had been. The seventh flag was the modern state itself.
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Most Texans now live in cities. Houston, San Antonio, Dallas, Austin and Fort Worth are all among the largest cities in the country, and more than thirty million people call the state home.
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The work changed too. Oil still matters, but so do computer chips in Austin, the world's largest medical center in Houston, and ports and farms that send goods around the world. A state that once lived on one fortune at a time now lives on many at once.
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In the twentieth century Texas became the second-largest state by land and people, and the space program made Houston famous around the world. The six flags are the past. The skyline is the seventh.
description: "From farms to skylines", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The land under the highway.
description: The title of the story "The land under the highway", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The highway runs from the coast to the plains, and every mile of it is a chapter. The first miles cross the wet coastal plain where the Karankawa fished the shallow bays, with the Caddo farming corn in the piney woods to the east. In the far west the Jumano farmed the rare rivers, and on the plains the Comanche followed the buffalo.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then a mission with a bell, built when Spain sent priests to hold its claim after a French explorer landed on the coast. Nearby is San Antonio, founded in 1718, a town Mexico inherited in 1821 and opened to settlers from the north.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The settlers came faster than anyone in Mexico City expected. Stephen F. Austin's first three hundred families were the start, and by the early 1830s they far outnumbered the Tejanos. Quarrels over laws, slavery and who would govern grew with every wagon.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The road passes Gonzales, where the first shots were fired in October 1835, and the Alamo, which fell in March 1836. It passes Washington-on-the-Brazos, where the declaration of independence was signed while the Alamo was still under siege. Then San Jacinto, where eighteen minutes made a country.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The country lasted almost ten years, and Sam Houston was its first president; its capital moved to Austin in 1839. It joined the Union in 1845, and within a year the United States and Mexico were at war over where Texas ended. The Rio Grande became the line.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Texas left the Union in 1861 to join the Confederacy, in a war over slavery, and heard of freedom late, in Galveston on June 19, 1865. The order was read by a Union general about two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation. Juneteenth began there and is now a national holiday.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The last miles are cattle country that walked its herds north to the railroads in Kansas from 1867, until railroads reached Texas and barbed wire fenced the open range. Then cotton, then, at Spindletop in 1901, oil more than a hundred feet in the air, and money from oil on state land for schools.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The highway ends in a city that did not exist when the road began. Six flags have flown over the land beneath it, and a seventh thing, the skyline, is newer than any of them. A driver who knows the story reads the road like a book, one chapter a mile.
description: "The land under the highway", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Four flashlights.
description: The title of the story "Four flashlights", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Priya had one job at the campout: tell her friend across the field how many marshmallows to bring back from the car. The number was ten. She had no phone, no paper, and the field was too wide to shout across. All she had was a row of four flashlights on the fence post.
description: "Four flashlights", paragraph 1 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She tried flashing one light ten times. Her friend counted eight, then lost track when a moth flew past. She tried again. Nine. The marshmallows were not getting any closer.
description: "Four flashlights", paragraph 2 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she stopped counting flashes and started using places. She gave each flashlight a value, left to right: 8, 4, 2 and 1. A light that was on meant count me. A light that was off meant skip me. To send ten, she turned on the 8 and the 2 and left the other two dark. Her friend added the lit ones, 8 plus 2, and held up ten fingers. No counting, no moths, one look.
description: "Four flashlights", paragraph 3 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her friend asked about the biggest number, and Priya lit all four: 8, 4, 2 and 1, which is fifteen. A fifth flashlight worth 16 would reach thirty-one, because every new light doubles what the row can say.
description: "Four flashlights", paragraph 4 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That is binary. Every place is a switch that is on or off, a 1 or a 0. You read the number by adding the values of the places that are on. Priya's four flashlights could say any number from 0 to 15. Your phone has billions of switches. Every photo, song and message on it is a very long row of lights that are on or off.
description: "Four flashlights", paragraph 5 of 5: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] One piece at a time.
description: The title of the story "One piece at a time", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai sent his cousin a photo and it arrived in a second, and he pictured the whole picture flying across the country in one piece. His aunt, who worked at the post office, said it had gone as a thousand envelopes.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The internet cuts a message into packets, small pieces, each with the destination address on it and a number saying which piece it is. The packets take whatever routes are open, arrive in any order, and get put back together by the number.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Along the way, machines called routers read each envelope's address and pass it one step closer, the way sorting offices pass mail from city to city. No single router knows the whole route. Each one only knows the next step.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] And the address is a number, not a name. When Kai typed his cousin's site, a directory called DNS turned the name into the number address, the way a phone book turns a name into a phone number. Then the envelopes went out.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] When an envelope goes missing, the receiving computer notices a gap in the numbers and asks for that piece again. And when the address bar shows a small lock, the pieces travel sealed, scrambled so that anyone who opens an envelope along the way sees nonsense.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Messages travel as addressed packets that can take different routes and arrive out of order. DNS turns names into number addresses. A photo is a thousand envelopes that know how to line up.
description: "One piece at a time", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The message that said now.
description: The title of the story "The message that said now", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The message said her account would be closed unless she clicked the link now. Rosa's thumb was already moving. Her father asked one question: who wants you to hurry?
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Hurry is the tell. Someone who wants you not to think will tell you there is no time to. Rosa put the phone down and went to the real site herself, typing the address, and her account was fine.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Three habits, her father said. Long passwords, four random words beat one clever one. A second proof, so a stolen password alone opens nothing. And never through the link: go to the site yourself. The message that says now is the one that can wait.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Why four words? Each word added multiplies the guesses an attacker needs. A computer can try enormous numbers of short passwords quickly, but four random words from a big dictionary make so many combinations that guessing takes far longer than anyone would wait.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her father kept his in a password manager, a locked vault that remembers a different long password for every site. Then one stolen password opens only one door.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Privacy was the last habit. A photo of a new house with the street sign behind it tells strangers where you live. Before posting, Rosa started asking who could see it and what it gave away.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Long passwords, a second proof, and never through the link. The message that says now is the one to slow down for, and a post is worth a second look before it goes.
description: "The message that said now", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The message across the ocean.
description: The title of the story "The message across the ocean", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The photo was a sunset on a beach in Portugal, sent to a cousin in Texas. It did not travel as a photo. It was cut into packets, a few thousand of them, each stamped with an address that was a number.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each packet took whatever route was open: an undersea cable, a switch in London, a tower outside Dallas. Routers along the way read the address and passed each packet one step closer, the way sorting offices pass mail. The packets arrived out of order and were put back together in the right one.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Two packets never arrived at all. The cousin's computer noticed the gaps in the numbers and asked for those pieces again, and they came a moment later by a different road. Nobody saw it happen. The whole trip took less than a second.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The cousin's name for the site was words, but the address the packets used was numbers. A directory called DNS had turned one into the other before the first packet left. The little lock in the address bar meant every packet traveled sealed, scrambled for anyone who might open it along the way.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Underneath everything, the sunset was ones and zeros. Every tiny dot of color was a set of numbers. Every number was a row of switches, on and off, in places worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and on up. The orange of the sky was just a long row of lights.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next morning a message arrived saying the account was locked and to click now. It even used the real company's colors. The cousin did not click. Hurry is the tell: whoever wants you not to think will tell you there is no time.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He went to the site the usual way, typing the address himself, entered the long password that was four unrelated words, and answered the code on his phone. His password manager filled in the password on the real site, as it always did. It would have filled in nothing on a fake one, which is one more reason to use one. He found nothing locked at all.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The sunset was still there. The scam was not. He sent the photo on to his grandmother in Ohio. It crossed the country the same way it had crossed the ocean, in a few thousand sealed envelopes that knew how to line up. She called within the minute to say it was beautiful.
description: "The message across the ocean", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two hills.
description: The title of the story "Two hills", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Owen rode his bike up two hills on the way to school. The first was easy. The second made his legs burn. He knew the second was steeper, but when his teacher asked how much steeper, he had nothing but a feeling in his legs.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He drew the two hills on graph paper and stared. Both went up. Both went across. Steep was somewhere in the relationship between the two, and he could not name it.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he counted. The steep hill rose two squares for every one square across. Two over one, slope two. The gentle hill rose two squares for every four across. Two over four, slope one half. Rise over run, and the bigger the number, the harder the climb.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On the way home both hills ran the other way. Going down, each line fell as it went across, so its slope was negative: minus two and minus one half. The flat stretch by the park rose nothing at all, a slope of zero.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Road signs use slope too. A sign warning of a 6 percent grade means the road rises or falls 6 feet for every 100 feet across. The steep line in Owen's drawing, at slope two, would be a 200 percent grade, so he admitted he had drawn his hill a little steeper than it was.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Slope is rise over run. In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is where the line crosses the y-axis. Owen's legs had known the answer all along; now the ruler could say it.
description: "Two hills", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Five folds.
description: The title of the story "Five folds", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Priya bet her brother that folding a sheet of paper five times would make ten layers. Five folds, two layers each, ten. It was obvious. Her brother said thirty-two and would not say why.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She folded once. Two layers. Twice. Four. Three times. Eight. That was not going up by two each time. It was doubling, and doubling ran away from her fast.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Five folds: two times two times two times two times two. Thirty-two layers. The exponent, the little five, was just counting how many times she had multiplied by two. Two to the fifth. Her brother had counted the folds, not the layers. Each fold doubled everything that came before it.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her brother showed her the shortcut. Two to the third times two to the second is two to the fifth, because three twos and two more twos make five twos. Eight times four is thirty-two either way.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he asked about zero folds: one sheet, one layer. Two to the zero is one, and so is any other number to the zero, except zero itself. Divide two to the fifth by two to the fifth and you get two to the zero, and anything divided by itself is one.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An exponent counts the multiplying. With the same base, add exponents to multiply and subtract them to divide. Five folds is thirty-two layers, and ten folds would be 1,024, if anyone could fold a sheet that many times.
description: "Five folds", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Forty-nine tiles.
description: The title of the story "Forty-nine tiles", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa had forty-nine tiles and one job: lay them in a square, no leftovers. She tried six across. One row short and some spare. She tried eight. Not enough tiles. The patio was hot and the tiles were heavy.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A square meant the same number across as down. So she needed a number that, times itself, made forty-nine. She had never thought of a number that way before.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Seven. Seven rows of seven is forty-nine. That is the square root: the number that, multiplied by itself, gives you the total. The perfect squares, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, are the tile counts that make tidy squares. Any other count leaves a leftover, and its root sits between two whole numbers.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her aunt asked about fifty tiles. No whole number times itself makes fifty, so the square root of fifty lies between seven and eight, just past seven: about 7.07. Rosa would have one tile left over, and a patio that could never be a perfect square. Seven times seven is 49; seven and a bit times itself is 50.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Some roots never come out even at all. The square root of two goes on forever without repeating, 1.41421 and on. Numbers like that are called irrational, and the ancient Greeks are said to have been upset to discover them.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A square root asks which number times itself gives this. Know the perfect squares by heart, and a root you cannot find exactly still lives between two that you can.
description: "Forty-nine tiles", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The rope with twelve knots.
description: The title of the story "The rope with twelve knots", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Mike was building his first deck alone. The boards were good, the posts were set, and the corner was wrong. He could feel it. Not by much. Just enough that every board after it would be a little more wrong than the last.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A square is a square only if its corner is exactly a right angle, and Mike had no tool big enough to check a corner that size. His square was eight inches long. The deck was twelve feet.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The old carpenter he worked for did not use a tool. He used a rope with knots tied at equal spaces, and he laid it out as a triangle: three spaces on one side, four on the next, five on the last. If the corner was true, the rope closed. If not, the fifth side came up short or long.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Three, four, five. It works because three squared plus four squared is nine plus sixteen, which is twenty-five, which is five squared. In a right triangle the two short sides squared always add up to the long side squared. Builders have used the knotted rope for centuries, and a Babylonian clay tablet almost four thousand years old lists number triples just like it.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Mike stretched the rope. It closed. He moved the post two fingers and it closed better.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The carpenter showed him a faster check with a tape measure. The deck was 12 feet by 16. If the corners were square, the diagonal would be 20 feet, because 144 plus 256 is 400, and 400 is 20 squared. Mike measured corner to corner: 20 feet exactly.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The deck is still standing. The rule works both ways: in a right triangle the short sides squared add up to the long side squared, and if they add up, the corner is square.
description: "The rope with twelve knots", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Sliding the point.
description: The title of the story "Sliding the point", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus had to copy the distance to the Sun into his notebook: 150,000,000 kilometers. By the fourth zero he had lost count. By the sixth he had written one too many, and the Sun was now ten times farther away.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Zeros were the problem. They looked alike, they were easy to drop, and nobody could tell at a glance whether a number had eight or nine.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher slid the decimal point. Move it eight places to the left and 150,000,000 becomes 1.5. Then write how far it moved: times ten to the eighth. 1.5 × 10⁸. Every digit that mattered was there, and the size lived in the exponent instead of a trail of zeros.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Small numbers work the same way in reverse. A red blood cell is about 0.000007 meters across. Slide the point six places to the right and write a negative exponent: 7 × 10⁻⁶ meters.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher gave him the nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri: about 40,000,000,000,000 kilometers away. Marcus wrote 4.0 × 10¹³ and did not have to count a single zero twice. Light from that star takes more than four years to reach us.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Scientific notation is a number from 1 to 10, times a power of ten. The exponent counts how many places the decimal point moved: left for a big number, right for a tiny one. It is how scientists write the very large and the very small without losing a zero.
description: "Sliding the point", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The taxi meter.
description: The title of the story "The taxi meter", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena watched the taxi meter tick and tried to guess the fare before it did. At three miles it read five dollars. At five miles, seven. She could not see the rule, but she could feel that there was one.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The meter had started at two dollars before the taxi moved an inch. Then it climbed. Every mile added the same amount. Two points were enough, if she could read them.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] From three to five miles, the fare rose two dollars. A dollar a mile. That was the slope, m. And the two dollars at the start, before any miles, was b, where the line began on the y-axis. Fare equals one times the miles plus two. y = mx + b.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Now she could beat the meter. Twelve miles would be twelve dollars plus two: fourteen. When they stopped at twelve miles, the meter read fourteen, and the driver asked how she knew. She showed him the two points on her napkin.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Not every rule makes a straight line. If the fare doubled every mile, the graph would curve upward like a ski jump, the way the layers did when a sheet of paper was folded. A linear function adds the same amount each step; it never multiplies.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A linear function is y = mx + b: m is the slope, the change for each step, and b is where the line starts. Two points on any straight line are enough to write its rule.
description: "The taxi meter", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] A circle, stacked.
description: The title of the story "A circle, stacked", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal needed the volume of a soup can for a science project, and the formula in the book looked like alphabet soup. Pi r squared h. He knew what the letters were. He had no idea why they were there.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He stacked coins on the counter instead. One coin was a flat circle. Ten coins was a short tower. The tower was just the circle, ten times over.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That was the can. The base was a circle, and its area was pi r squared. Stack that circle up the height of the can, h, and you have the whole can: pi r squared times h. Then he folded a paper cone with the same base and height and filled it three times to fill the can. A cone is a third.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then he did the numbers. The can was 8 centimeters across, so its radius was 4, and it was 11 centimeters tall. Pi times 4 times 4 is about 50.3, and times 11 is about 553 cubic centimeters. The label said 550 milliliters, and a cubic centimeter is a milliliter.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher added one more. A ball that just fits inside a can exactly as tall as it is wide holds two thirds of the can. Archimedes was so proud of finding that, the old writers say, that he asked for it to be carved on his tomb.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The volume of a cylinder is pi r squared times h, a circle stacked to its height. A cone with the same base and height holds exactly a third of it, and a ball that fits inside holds two thirds.
description: "A circle, stacked", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The treehouse.
description: The title of the story "The treehouse", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The treehouse needed a ramp for the wagon that carried the lumber. The builders worked in rise over run and settled on 1 to 4, one foot up for every four along. That is a slope of one quarter, the gentlest that fit between the tree and the fence. The ramp had to reach 3 feet up, so it ran 12 feet along.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The floor was a square of 49 tiles, seven by seven, because the square root of 49 is 7 and nobody wanted to cut tiles. When a neighbor offered 50, they said no thanks: the square root of 50 is about 7.07, and that one extra tile would have had nowhere to go.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They tested the rope for the ladder by doubling the weight each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 kilograms. Two to the fifth. Each test doubled the last, which is exactly what an exponent counts. The rope held at 32, and they stopped there, because the next step, 64, was more than the ladder would ever carry.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The brace was the hard part. A diagonal from the floor corner to the trunk had to be cut before anyone climbed: 6 feet along, 8 feet up, and the brace was the hypotenuse. Thirty-six plus sixty-four is a hundred, and the square root of 100 is exactly 10 feet. The lumber yard had a 10-foot board.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The lumber yard charged 20 dollars for delivery plus 3 dollars a board, and the price was a line on a graph. Twelve boards cost 56 dollars. The older builder wrote it as y = 3x + 20, and the younger one checked it at the counter.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The water barrel under the treehouse was a cylinder, 2 feet across and 3 feet tall. Pi times 1 squared times 3 is about 9.4 cubic feet, a little over 70 gallons, enough rain for the tomato plants below.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.
