text: [warm and natural] When it was done they counted the nails and wrote the total in scientific notation as a joke: 3.4 times ten to the second, three hundred and forty. Nobody had to count them twice, which is the whole point of scientific notation. They wrote it on the wall beside the date.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The wagon rolled up the ramp on the first try. Slope, squares, roots, exponents, a right triangle, a line and a cylinder: the treehouse was a whole year of math, and it held. The builders sat inside it until dark.
description: "The treehouse", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The car and the rain.
description: The title of the story "The car and the rain", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Marcus washed the car on Saturday and it rained on Sunday. His uncle said, that is what you get for washing it, and everyone laughed. Marcus laughed too. Then he thought about it on the bus and stopped laughing. Did washing the car really cause the rain?
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It felt true. It happened right after. But when he tried to explain how a wet car pulls clouds across the sky, he could not. The argument had a shape that looked like reasoning and a middle made of nothing.
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher had names for that. False cause: one thing came after another, so it must have been caused by it. Overgeneralizing: every dog I met bit me, so every dog bites. Attacking the person: you are only saying that because you are a kid. False choice: either we ban phones or nobody learns. Name the flaw, and the argument loses its grip.
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She added two more shapes. Everyone is doing it, so it must be right: the bandwagon. It is true because it is true, said a louder way: circular reasoning. Marcus started a list in the back of his notebook and caught three in one week of commercials.
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fix for false cause is one question: what else could explain it? It had rained on Sunday because a storm had been forecast all week, and the forecast came out before the car was washed.
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Flawed reasoning looks like reasoning until you name it. Overgeneralizing, false cause, attacking the person, false choice: shapes that fool people every day. Once you can see the shape, you cannot unsee it, and the washed car stops causing rain.
description: "The car and the rain", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The fire station.
description: The title of the story "The fire station", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The fire station in Priya's town burned down, and the whole town called it ironic. A month later Priya broke her arm the day before a swim meet, and her friend said that was ironic too. Priya was not sure both could be right.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Bad luck was everywhere. If every bad thing was irony, the word did not mean much. There had to be something more in the fire station than in her arm.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] There was a gap. A fire station is the one building that should never burn, so what happened stood against what everyone expected. That gap is irony. Her arm was just bad luck; nobody expects a broken arm to be impossible. The gap can sit between expected and actual. It can sit between what is said and what is meant, as in great weather in a storm. It can sit between what the audience knows and what the hero does not.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher gave the three gaps their names. The fire station is situational irony. Great weather in a storm is verbal irony. When the audience knows the villain is behind the door and the hero does not, that is dramatic irony.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Priya found dramatic irony in the next play they read. The audience knew the letter had been switched; the two friends on stage did not, and every kind word between them hurt to watch.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Irony is a gap: expected against actual, said against meant, known against unknown. Bad luck alone is not irony. The fire station qualifies. The arm, however sore, does not.
description: "The fire station", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] One word, one story.
description: The title of the story "One word, one story", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai would not share his dessert, and his sister said, do not be such a Scrooge. Kai had never read the book. He still knew exactly what she meant, and he gave her half.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] How did one word do that? She had not told a story. She had not even said what a Scrooge was. Kai looked it up later and found a short novel by Charles Dickens about a miser who counted coins while others went cold.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That is an allusion. A writer borrows a whole story in a few words and trusts the reader to bring the rest. Scrooge means stingy, an Achilles' heel means the one weak spot, a Trojan horse means a gift that hides a trap. Know where the word points, and you know what the writer meant.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Allusions come from everywhere people share stories. A small team beating a giant one is a David and Goliath game, from the Bible. Starting a trouble that lets loose many more is opening Pandora's box, from a Greek myth.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An allusion only works if the reader knows the story. Kai called his friend a Hamlet for taking ten minutes to choose a sandwich, and his friend just stared. Kai laughed and explained, and later he read the play himself.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An allusion borrows a whole story in a few words. When a word seems to carry more weight than it should, ask where it points, and read that story too. Writers pack their sentences with other people's books.
description: "One word, one story", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The mirror.
description: The title of the story "The mirror", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa summarized an article that argued the park should close at dusk. Her summary said the article unfortunately argued the park should close at dusk. Her teacher circled one word.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Unfortunately. Rosa had not meant to put herself in the summary. But there she was, in one adverb, disagreeing with an article that had not asked her opinion.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A summary is a mirror, her teacher said, not a review. Say what the text says, in neutral words. The article argues that the park should close at dusk, for safety. That is all. No liked, no hated, no unfortunately. Watch for the single words that let an opinion back in: sadly, of course, so-called, only. And keep the article's reasons: fewer accidents after dark, and fewer complaints from neighbors.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Verbs can lean too. The article argues, states or reports. It does not rant, admit or whine. Rosa had once written that an author admitted something, and her teacher asked whether the author had confessed or simply said it.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher gave her a test for fairness. Would the person who wrote the article agree that her summary said what they meant? And would someone who disagreed with it agree too? If both would sign it, the mirror is clean. Rosa tried it on her next summary, and both her parents signed.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] An objective summary says what the text says in neutral words and leaves your opinion out. The dangerous words are the small ones. A mirror does not sigh.
description: "The mirror", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Outside the frame.
description: The title of the story "Outside the frame", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] A pamphlet came through Theo's door: vote for her. Should, must, best, on every line. Theo could tell it wanted him to do something. His mother asked what it wanted him not to see.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Not to see? It was a page of words. Everything on it was there to read. Theo read it twice and found no lie on it anywhere.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The lean was not in what the page said. It was in what it left out. Should and must told him the purpose: to persuade. Then he drew a frame around the pamphlet and asked what lived outside it. The costs. Not one number, anywhere on the page. Bias is the shape of the frame.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His mother pointed to the small print at the bottom: paid for by the campaign. A text that comes from the side it praises has a reason to lean. That does not make it false. It makes it worth checking.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So Theo found the city's voter guide, which listed the plan and its costs side by side, and a newspaper story that quoted both candidates. The costs were there after all: a new park, paid for over ten years. The pamphlet had told the truth, and only half of it.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Every text has a purpose: to inform, to persuade or to entertain. A bias is a lean you can see in what a text leaves out and in who is speaking. Read the page, then read the empty space around it, then read another source.
description: "Outside the frame", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] One tune, two songs.
description: The title of the story "One tune, two songs", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Lena read a long novel about two brothers and, the same week, a one-page fable about two foxes. Her teacher asked what they had in common. Nothing, Lena said. One had cars and a hospital. The other had a hen.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she thought about how each ended. The brother who told the truth lost a friend and kept his brother. The fox who told the truth lost the hen and kept the den. Different stories. Same shape at the end.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A theme is not a topic. It is a sentence about what a story says. Both stories said that honesty costs something and is worth it. The novel showed it over three hundred pages. The fable said it outright in a moral at the bottom. Two songs, one tune.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher warned her about one-word answers. Honesty is a topic, not a theme. A theme is a whole sentence someone could agree with or argue against: honesty costs something and is worth it.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Lena backed it up the way a lawyer would, with one piece of evidence from each text: the brother who kept his brother, the fox who kept the den. A theme you can prove from two very different stories is one worth believing.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A theme is a sentence about what a story says about life, and very different texts can share one. A fable states its theme as a moral; a novel makes you find it. Look at what each character paid, and what they kept.
description: "One tune, two songs", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The fire station that burned down.
description: The title of the story "The fire station that burned down", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The town paper had a bad week and the class read every word of it. The fire station had burned down, which the paper called ironic, and it was: the one building that should never burn. That was situational irony, a gap between what anyone would expect and what happened.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The mayor's statement said the town had been unlucky, and the class caught the flawed reasoning in one line. Two fires in a month did not mean the town was cursed, only that two fires had happened. They asked the question that undoes false cause: what else could explain it?
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The editorial called the fire chief a Scrooge for cutting the budget, and the class had to know the old story to feel the sting. An allusion only works on readers who know what it points to. Half the class knew Dickens. The other half looked it up and understood exactly what the editorial wanted them to feel.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They checked the editorial's purpose next. Should, must and shameful were on every line: it wanted to persuade. And the frame left something out. Not one sentence said what had actually started the fire. It named a villain before it named a cause, which should have been the first warning.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then came the hardest assignment: an objective summary of the whole week, a mirror, not a review. Three drafts had an opinion hiding in them, in words like sadly and so-called. The fourth said only what the paper said, in verbs like reported and stated.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The next week the paper ran a correction. The station had not burned because of the budget; an old heater had failed. The class, who had summarized without judging, had nothing to take back. The columnist who had called the chief a Scrooge did.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Their teacher asked for one last thing: a theme that ran through the whole week. The class argued, and settled on a sentence: people reach for a villain before they reach for the facts, and the facts usually arrive a week later. It was a sentence someone could argue with, which is what made it a theme and not a topic.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They pinned the correction beside the editorial on the class board. The correction was smaller, on page six, and it was the page that mattered most. A careful reader learns to wait for page six, and to read the first page with that in mind.
description: "The fire station that burned down", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The balloon on the wall.
description: The title of the story "The balloon on the wall", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] At a birthday party, a boy rubbed a balloon on his hair, pressed it to the wall, and let go. It stayed. The room went quiet. Then everybody tried it.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Nothing was glued. Nothing was wet. A balloon that had been ordinary a second ago now clung to the wall like it belonged there.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Inside every atom is a small, heavy center, the nucleus, made of protons and neutrons, wrapped in a cloud of tiny, light electrons. The nucleus never moves in a game like this. But the outer electrons are loosely held, and rubbing the balloon scraped some of them off the hair and onto the rubber. Now the balloon carried extra electrons, a negative charge, and the wall, with its charges nudged apart, pulled it in.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] If the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a marble on the center spot, and the electrons a haze in the farthest seats. Almost all the atom's mass is in that marble. Almost all the rest is empty space.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The number of protons is what makes an atom the element it is: six for carbon, seventy-nine for gold. Electrons can come and go. Protons stay put.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Neutrons can vary. Most carbon atoms have six, but a few have eight. That kind, carbon-14, slowly breaks down over thousands of years, which is how scientists date old bones and wood. Same element, different weight: an isotope.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Almost everything you can touch, push, or stick to a wall is the outside of atoms shaking hands. The inside is a fortress nobody at the party ever reached.
description: "The balloon on the wall", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The cart that would not start.
description: The title of the story "The cart that would not start", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] The truck was broken, so Savanah had to get the feed to the barn by cart. Six sacks. She put her shoulder to it and pushed. Nothing.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 1 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] She pushed harder. It rocked and stopped. It felt personal, like the cart had decided.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 2 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It had not decided anything. A thing at rest stays at rest until a force moves it, and a heavy thing needs a bigger force, because force equals mass times acceleration. Six sacks of feed have a lot of mass, and at a standstill the friction in the wheels and the soft dirt holds a load hardest of all. Her first shove was fighting all of it at once.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 3 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So she stopped fighting and started leaning, one long steady push. The cart crept, then rolled, then wanted to keep rolling, which is the other half of the same law: a thing in motion stays in motion. At the barn door she had to lean the other way to stop it.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 4 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Every push she gave the cart, the cart gave back to her hands, exactly as hard. And every push her boots gave the road, backward, the road gave her, forward. That is the third law: push on the world and the world pushes back exactly as hard.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 5 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her cousin, who liked numbers, worked it out that night. The loaded cart was about 300 kilograms. A steady push of 150 newtons, beyond what friction took, would speed it up by half a meter per second, every second: 150 divided by 300. Twice the push, twice the speed-up.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 6 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Savanah left the farm a few years later for the city. She still moves heavy things the same way: one steady force, and let the motion do the rest.
description: "The cart that would not start", paragraph 7 of 7: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Fold it, burn it.
description: The title of the story "Fold it, burn it", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo folded a sheet of paper into a plane, then flattened it out again. Same paper, a few creases. Then, at the campfire, he let a scrap catch the flame. It curled, went black, and became ash and smoke. He could not fold it back.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Both were changes. Why could one be undone and the other could not? The paper had gone somewhere, and it was not coming back.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Folding was a physical change. The paper was still paper, just a different shape. Burning was a chemical change. The paper's atoms had rearranged into new substances, ash and gases, and no atom was created or lost. The paper was not gone. It was everywhere, in a form no fold could reach.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher listed the signs that give a chemical change away: a new color, bubbles of a new gas, heat or light, or a solid appearing out of a liquid. The burning scrap had shown three of them at once: a black color, smoke, and heat with light.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] In class they mixed baking soda and vinegar inside a sealed plastic bag on a scale. The bag puffed up with carbon dioxide, but the scale did not move. Every atom was still in the bag, just arranged into new substances.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change does not. In every reaction, atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed. Fold it and it is still paper. Burn it and it is something else.
description: "Fold it, burn it", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Boxes inside boxes.
description: The title of the story "Boxes inside boxes", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Nadia found a set of nesting boxes in the attic. Inside the biggest was a smaller one, and inside that a smaller one, down to a tiny box with a blue marble in it. Her uncle said, that is where we live.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The marble was the Earth, he said. Nadia laughed. Then she asked what the next box was, and the next, and stopped laughing somewhere around the fourth.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The moon circles the Earth. The Earth and its neighbors circle the sun: the solar system. The sun is one star among hundreds of billions in a galaxy. The galaxy is one among billions in the universe. Each layer sits inside the next, and the distances are so vast that astronomers measure them by how far light travels in a year.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her uncle gave her the numbers. Light from the Sun reaches the Earth in about eight minutes. Light from the nearest star after the Sun takes more than four years. A light-year, the distance light travels in a year, is about 9.5 trillion kilometers.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Our galaxy, the Milky Way, is about 100,000 light-years across, and its stars are the faint band you can see across a dark sky. The nearest big galaxy, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away, so the light we see from it left long before the first modern humans walked the Earth.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Moon, planet, solar system, galaxy, universe: each is inside the next. Distances are measured in light-years, because kilometers run out of zeros. The marble is small, and it is home.
description: "Boxes inside boxes", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The walk on a graph.
description: The title of the story "The walk on a graph", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Kai timed his walk to school and marked how far he had gone every minute. Then he plotted it: time across, distance up. He expected a straight line. Instead the line had a flat bit, a gentle stretch and a steep jump at the end.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The flat part puzzled him. Time kept passing, but the distance did not move. Had he stopped? He thought back. He had stopped to tie his shoe.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That was it. On a distance-time graph, flat means standing still. A gentle slope means moving slowly, the stroll past the park. A steep slope means moving fast, the sprint for the bell. The slope is the speed. And the whole trip's average speed was the total distance over the total time, one gentler line from start to finish.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He worked out the numbers. The whole trip was 1,200 meters in 15 minutes, an average of 80 meters a minute. The last sprint covered 200 meters in a single minute, which is why that part of the line stood up so steeply.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher showed him one more shape. When he sped up little by little, the line did not jump from gentle to steep; it curved, bending upward as it went. A curve on a distance-time graph means the speed is changing, and that is acceleration.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] On a distance-time graph, flat is still, sloped is moving, steeper is faster, and a curve is speeding up or slowing down. The slope is the speed, and average speed is the whole distance over the whole time. A walk becomes a line, and the line remembers the shoe.
description: "The walk on a graph", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The laundry pile.
description: The title of the story "The laundry pile", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Diego was looking for the shirt he had worn on Monday. It was Friday. The pile of laundry on his floor was tall, and Monday was nowhere near the top.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He started digging. Thursday, Wednesday, Tuesday. Each shirt was under the one that came after it. Monday was at the bottom, because it had gone in first, and everything since had piled on top.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Rock layers work the same way. Mud and sand settle one layer on top of another, year after year, so the deepest layer is the oldest. A fossil buried deep is older than one near the surface, and the layer around it, sand or mud or shells, says what the place was like when that creature lived.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Where did the mud and sand come from? Weathering, his teacher said: rain, ice and roots crack rock into smaller and smaller pieces. Rivers and wind carry the pieces away, which is erosion, and drop them somewhere else in a new layer, which is deposition.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A creature buried quickly in that mud can become a fossil, as minerals from the water slowly take the place of its shell or bone. The limestone hills around Austin were once the floor of a shallow sea, and people still find fossil shells in them.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Layers pile up over time, so deeper is older, unless the Earth has folded or overturned them. Fossils and the layers around them tell what a place was like and when. A cliff is a laundry pile that took a million years.
description: "The laundry pile", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The night sky over the quarry.
description: The title of the story "The night sky over the quarry", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] They drove to the quarry because the sky was darkest there. The quarry walls were the first lesson: layers, the oldest at the bottom, and a fossil shell halfway up that had been sea floor long ago. Weathering had cracked the rock face, and rain had washed its sand into a fan at the bottom.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The telescope went up on the flat ground. The first thing in it was the moon, whose light takes a little over a second to reach us. Then Jupiter, whose light had taken about forty minutes to arrive, and then a faint smudge that was the Andromeda galaxy, whose light had left it two and a half million years ago.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] While they waited for full dark, the physics teacher let a marble roll down the quarry ramp and timed it with a stopwatch. On the distance-time graph the line curved upward: faster every second, which is acceleration. At the bottom, on the flat, it rolled on until the gravel stopped it. A thing in motion stays in motion until a force acts.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then she pushed two balls across the flat ground, a marble and a heavy steel ball. To make the steel ball speed up as quickly as the marble, she had to push much harder: force equals mass times acceleration. When the steel ball hit the wall, the wall pushed back and it bounced. That was the third law, in one clack.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Someone asked what the marble was made of, and the talk went smaller. Every atom in it had a tiny, heavy nucleus of protons and neutrons, wrapped in electrons, and it was mostly empty space. The number of protons made each atom the element it was.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The campfire was the next lesson: wood and air becoming ash and smoke and heat, a chemical change, nothing you could fold back. The atoms were only rearranged, not destroyed. The carbon in the smoke had been in the tree, and before that in the air, and before that it was made inside a star.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] One of them pointed at a bright moving dot: a satellite. It crossed the whole sky in a few minutes because it was so close, while the stars behind it hardly moved at all. Near things race and far things wait, which is a lesson about distance too.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Everyone looked up again. The quarry rock, the marble, the smoke and the smudge of Andromeda were all made of the same kinds of atoms, arranged differently. The scale of it was the point.
description: "The night sky over the quarry", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] A fight worth picking.
description: The title of the story "A fight worth picking", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Sam's first thesis was dogs are pets. His teacher asked who would disagree. Sam thought about it. Nobody. Not one person on Earth would argue with him, and that, she said, was the problem.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A thesis that everyone agrees with is a topic wearing a thesis costume. There was nothing to prove and nowhere for the essay to go.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He tried again. Dogs make better pets than cats for busy families. Now someone would argue. His cousin would argue right now. And once he had a claim someone could fight, the reasons lined up under it on their own: dogs get you outside, dogs fit a schedule, dogs guard the house. The outline wrote itself.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher pushed once more: a strong thesis also says why. Dogs make better pets than cats for busy families because they build a routine. Now the because pointed at the reasons before he had even listed them.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Under each reason in the outline went a piece of evidence and a note about the other side: cats are cheaper, some would say. He gave that a line too, and planned his answer. The outline now held the whole essay on one page. When he sat down to write, every paragraph already knew its job.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Write the thesis first, then list the reasons under it. A good thesis is one someone could disagree with, because an essay is a fight worth picking, and a fight needs another side.
description: "A fight worth picking", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The missing sentence.
description: The title of the story "The missing sentence", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Ana wrote to the city. Claim: the town needs a safer crossing at Oak and Third. Evidence: twelve near-misses this year, counted by the crossing guard. She was proud of the number. The city wrote back and asked what the number had to do with a crossing.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Ana was furious. The connection was obvious. Twelve near-misses meant danger, and a crossing fixed danger. But she had not written that sentence. She had assumed it.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That sentence has a name: the warrant. It says why the evidence counts for the claim. Twelve near-misses mean that twelve times someone was nearly hurt, and a crossing that makes drivers stop would cut that number. Claim, evidence, warrant.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The warrant also told her what to ask for. On a busy road, a traffic engineer told her, plain painted stripes alone do little; flashing lights that drivers can see make them far more likely to stop. Ana changed her claim to match her warrant.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her teacher added one more habit: pick evidence a stranger can check. The crossing guard's count was good. A photo of the corner at rush hour was better still. She sent it all again, and the city sent a crew to put up a crossing with flashing lights.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A paragraph that proves something has three parts: the claim, the evidence, and the warrant that says why the evidence counts. The warrant is the sentence most often missing, because the writer already believes it.
description: "The missing sentence", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Body first.
description: The title of the story "Body first", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Diego stared at a blank page for twenty minutes trying to write his introduction. He could not introduce an essay he had not written. Every opening sentence promised something he did not have yet, and he deleted each one.
description: "Body first", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His teacher told him to skip it. Write the body first. Diego thought that was cheating. Essays started at the top.
description: "Body first", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] They are read from the top. They are not built from it. He wrote three body paragraphs, one reason each, with evidence and a warrant. Then the introduction was easy: it promised exactly what the body delivered, with the thesis at the end of it. The conclusion looked back at the three reasons and said the thesis again in fresh words. Five paragraphs, one skeleton.
description: "Body first", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The introduction also needed a hook, a first line to make a reader lean in. Diego used a question his cousin had asked him, and the thesis came at the end of the paragraph, where a reader expected it.
description: "Body first", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] A five-paragraph essay is an introduction with the thesis, three body paragraphs and a conclusion that looks back. Write the body first, then the introduction that fits it. Nobody builds a house starting with the roof.

text: [warm] Frederick builds the essay.
description: The title of the story "Frederick builds the essay", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Frederick was thirteen and had a jar of pond water on his desk and a thesis nobody could ignore: the pond behind the school was healthier than the county said. A topic is something nobody argues with; a thesis is a fight worth picking. The county's website called the pond impaired, and Frederick thought it was wrong.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] His outline had three reasons, and one of them, that the pond looked pretty, did not hold the thesis up, so it went. A weak reason does not just fail to help; it gives the other side something easy to knock down. He replaced it with the reason he could prove.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The paragraph that proved it had a claim, evidence and the sentence most writers skip: the warrant. Claim: the pond is healthy. Evidence: fourteen kinds of insect larvae in one jar, counted under the microscope his dad had finally let him use alone, including mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies. He counted twice, and his dad counted once more to be sure.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Warrant: mayflies, stoneflies and caddisflies are sensitive to pollution and are among the first to disappear from dirty water. So finding all three, among so many kinds, is a sign the water is clean. The evidence counted because the warrant said why.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He named the other side too. Some would say one jar is one sample, and it was. So his conclusion asked the county to test the pond properly, at several spots and in more than one season, instead of claiming more than a jar could prove.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] He built the body first, three paragraphs with one reason each, and then the introduction that fit it. For the hook he used a question from his little sister: why do the bugs in our pond have tails? The thesis came at the end of that first paragraph, where a reader expected it.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The five-paragraph essay went to the county office with a photograph of the jar. The conclusion said the thesis again in the light of what was shown. He read it aloud to his dad twice and cut every sentence that made him stumble.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The county sent someone to look. Frederick was there, in a lab coat two sizes too big, and the someone was impressed. The county tested the pond that spring at four spots, and the next year's report called it healthy. Frederick kept the jar, and the essay, and the county letter, in the same drawer.
description: "Frederick builds the essay", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Why, how, and what may not.
description: The title of the story "Why, how, and what may not", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] On the class trip, Maya stood in front of three framed documents and could not tell them apart. Old paper, fancy writing, the same few names at the bottom. Why did a country need three?
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her guide asked her three questions instead. Why did the colonies leave? How does the government work? What may the government never do? Maya could not answer any of them, but she noticed they were different questions.
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each document answered one. The Declaration of 1776 said why: governments exist for the people, and this one had failed them. The Constitution of 1787 said how: three branches, and a Congress where big and small states share power under the Great Compromise. The Bill of Rights of 1791 said what may never be done: speech, worship, a fair trial, untouched.
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Her guide added a fourth paper that was not on the wall. Before the Constitution came the Articles of Confederation, in force from 1781. They made a government so weak it could not even collect taxes to pay its soldiers. The Constitution was the second try.
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The three branches keep watch on one another. Congress writes the laws, the president can veto them, Congress can override the veto with two thirds of each house, and the courts can strike down a law that breaks the Constitution. Checks and balances, the guide called it.
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The Declaration says why, the Constitution says how, and the Bill of Rights says what may never be done. Three questions, three answers, and a country runs on all of them at once.
description: "Why, how, and what may not", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Learning to drive.
description: The title of the story "Learning to drive", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal got his learner's permit the week his class started the early republic, and his teacher said the two had a lot in common. A new country in 1789 was a driver with a brand-new license and no idea where the road went.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal did not see it. A country was not a car. But then he thought about his own first weeks: learning the habits, going farther than felt safe, a scare, and then finally being allowed to carry passengers.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] That was the order. Washington set the habits: two terms, then go home. Jefferson went farther, buying Louisiana in 1803 and doubling the map. The War of 1812 was the scare that made a loose collection of states feel like one nation. And in Jackson's time, states dropped their property rules and many more ordinary white men gained the vote.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark west in 1804 to see what he had bought, and Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, helped guide the way. In 1803 the Supreme Court also claimed a power the Constitution never spelled out: to strike down laws that break it.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Jamal's teacher made sure the lesson had its other side. The vote widened only for white men; women, enslaved people and most free Black men were still shut out. And under Jackson, the Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced the Cherokee and other nations from their homelands, on the road later called the Trail of Tears.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Washington set the habits, Jefferson doubled the land, the War of 1812 made a nation, and Jackson widened the vote for some while driving others from their land. A republic learns to drive the way a teenager does, and it can hurt people on the road.
description: "Learning to drive", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] The coin toss.
description: The title of the story "The coin toss", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Rosa noticed something strange in the chapter. Every time the country added a state, the whole nation held its breath. Why did one more state matter so much?
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Because each new state was a coin toss: slave or free. Every state sent senators, and whichever side had more senators could make the laws. The map was a scoreboard, and both sides counted every square.
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] So they made deals. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 kept the score even. The Compromise of 1850 bought a few more years. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 let settlers vote and turned Kansas into a battlefield. Then the Dred Scott decision said the score could not be kept at all, and in 1860 Lincoln won without a single southern state. The tosses were over.
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The Compromise of 1850 also carried the Fugitive Slave Act, which forced people in free states to help return those who had escaped. Many Northerners who had looked away from slavery now had to face it, and a novel, Uncle Tom's Cabin, made millions more feel it in 1852.
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The score on the map was about people. By 1860 nearly four million people were enslaved in the United States. When Lincoln was elected, South Carolina left the Union in December 1860, and other states soon followed.
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Each new state asked slave or free, and the compromises of 1820, 1850 and 1854 each bought less time than the last. Dred Scott and Lincoln's election ended the bargaining. A country can only put off a question about human freedom for so long.
description: "The coin toss", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Three promises.
description: The title of the story "Three promises", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] Theo read the three amendments in a row and thought the story was over. The 13th ended slavery. The 14th made everyone born here a citizen, with equal protection of the laws. The 15th said no one could be denied the vote because of race; women would wait until 1920. Three promises, all in writing, by 1870. What was left to fight about?
description: "Three promises", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] For a few years the promises held. Freed people opened schools and churches, and Black men voted and served in office. In 1870 Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black United States senator.
description: "Three promises", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] Then Theo turned the page to 1877 and the soldiers went home from the South. Within a few years, the same states that had signed the promises found ways around them: poll taxes, literacy tests, laws that split every town in two. The promises stayed on the page and left the streets.
description: "Three promises", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It took nearly a century to bring them back. The marches, the courts and the laws of the 1950s and 1960s did not write new promises. They forced the country to keep the three it already had. Theo's grandmother had been at one of those marches, carrying a sign with three numbers on it.
description: "Three promises", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The laws finally closed the loopholes. The 24th Amendment of 1964 banned poll taxes in federal elections, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended the literacy tests.
description: "Three promises", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments promised freedom, citizenship and the vote; after 1877 the promise was broken for decades, and the civil rights movement made the country keep it. A promise on paper is the beginning of a story, not the end.
description: "Three promises", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Four papers on the wall.
description: The title of the story "Four papers on the wall", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm and natural] On the wall of the house hang four papers. The first is a copy of the Declaration of 1776, which says why the colonies left: governments exist for the people, and this one had failed them.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The second is the Constitution of 1787, which says how the country runs. It sets up three branches, each able to stop the others, and a Congress where big and small states share power. Checks and balances keep any one of them from running the whole road. It was the second try; the Articles of Confederation before it could not even collect taxes.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The third is the Bill of Rights of 1791, the fence around the government: speech, worship, a fair trial, untouched. The grandmother who framed them says the three papers answer why, how and what may never be done.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The fourth paper is an old land deed from Missouri, land that had been part of the Louisiana Purchase, when a president bought a territory that doubled the country. A great-great-great-grandfather went west into it. The family's history runs through the early republic: two terms and go home, and a war in 1812 the country survived.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] It runs through the hard parts too. The widened vote of the 1830s was for white men only, and the same years forced the Cherokee and other nations off their land. Then came the slow arithmetic of new states, slave or free, and the compromises of 1820, 1850 and 1854 that kept the count even until 1860 broke it.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] There is a fifth paper in a drawer, a letter from 1870. A son who had fought for the Union writes that three promises have now been made. No more slavery; everyone born here a citizen; no one denied the vote because of race. He had seen the first one ratified the winter he came home.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The letter is hopeful, and the handwriting is careful, as if he meant it to be kept. The family knows what came next. The soldiers left the South in 1877, and poll taxes and literacy tests took the vote away again for most of a century. It took the laws of 1964 and 1965 to win it back.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm and natural] The grandmother keeps the letter in the drawer, not on the wall. The papers on the wall are what the country promised. The letter is about how long the promises took to keep, and she says that is the part worth reading twice.
description: "Four papers on the wall", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, natural voice.

text: [warm] Two sides of the bed.
description: The title of the story "Two sides of the bed", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] Owen's room had socks on both sides of the bed, and his math homework had x on both sides of the equals sign. 5x + 3 = 2x + 15. He had solved plenty of equations with x on one side. This one felt like it was fighting back.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] He tried subtracting 3, then got stuck staring at 5x and 2x on opposite sides, like two piles of laundry with a bed in between. Nothing he knew told him which pile to touch first.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] His sister told him to clean the room. Gather every sock on one side. Take 2x from both sides: 3x + 3 = 15. Now gather the numbers on the other side. Take 3 from both: 3x = 12. Divide by 3: x = 4. He put 4 back into the original, and both sides said 23.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The next one had parentheses: 3(x + 2) = 2x + 10. His sister said to empty the parentheses first, the way you empty pockets before laundry: 3x + 6 = 2x + 10. Take 2x from both sides and 6 from both sides, and x = 4 again.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Then she showed him two strange ones. x + 1 = x + 2 cleans up to 1 = 2, which is never true, so it has no solution at all. 2x + 2 = 2(x + 1) cleans up to 2 = 2, which is always true, so every number works.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Whatever the shape of the equation, the moves are the same. Clear any parentheses, gather every x on one side and every number on the other, then undo what is left and check. A room and an equation both clean up the same way.
description: "Two sides of the bed", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] The honest machine.
description: The title of the story "The honest machine", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] The vending machine outside the gym was the most honest thing at Lena's school. Press 3, get a pretzel. Every single time. Press 3 again, another pretzel. Never a candy bar, never nothing, never two.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Her teacher called it a function, and Lena thought that was an odd name for a snack machine. Then he showed her one with a rule inside: press 1, get 3. Press 2, get 5. Press 3, get 7. Lena could not see the machine's insides, but she could see its habit.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The rule was f(x) = 2x + 1. Press 3 and the machine doubles it and adds one: f(3) = 7. One input, one output, always the same. If pressing 3 ever gave two different answers, it would not be a function. It would be a broken machine.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Lena asked about the machine by the library, where buttons 3 and 4 both gave pretzels. That was still a function, her teacher said. Two inputs may share an output. What a function may never do is give two outputs for one input.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] He drew the rule as a graph, a straight line, and showed her the test: run a vertical line anywhere across it. If the line ever crosses the graph twice, one input has two outputs, and it is not a function.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] A function gives one output for each input, every time. f(3) means the rule applied to 3. When you can trust a machine the way Lena trusts the pretzel button, you are looking at a function.
description: "The honest machine", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] Two clues.
description: The title of the story "Two clues", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] The gift had a number lock, and Marcus's uncle gave him two clues on two cards. Two numbers add to 5. Their difference is 1. Marcus tried the first clue alone and found too many answers: 0 and 5, 1 and 4, 2 and 3.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The second clue alone was no better: 4 and 3, 7 and 6, a hundred and ninety-nine. One clue narrowed the world. It did not pin it down.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] He used them together. From the first card, the second number was 5 minus the first. He put that into the second clue: the first number minus, in parentheses, 5 minus the first, equals 1. Opening the parentheses flips the minus inside to a plus, so two of the first number, minus 5, make 1. Two of the first are 6, and the first number is 3. The second was 2, and the lock opened.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] His uncle showed him a quicker way. Stack the clues: x plus y is 5, x minus y is 1. Add them, and the ys cancel: 2x is 6, so x is 3. Adding equations to cancel one unknown is called elimination.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Then he drew both clues as lines on graph paper. Each line held every pair that fit one card. They crossed at one point, 3 and 2, the only pair on both lines. The answer to a system is where the lines meet.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] A system of equations is two clues about the same unknowns. Substitute one into the other, or add them to cancel an unknown, solve, then check the pair in both. One clue narrows; two clues decide.
description: "Two clues", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] Un-multiplying.
description: The title of the story "Un-multiplying", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] Priya could multiply (x + 2) by (x + 3) and get x² + 5x + 6 without thinking. Then the homework handed her x² + 5x + 6 and asked where it came from. Going backward felt like un-baking a cake.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] She drew the rectangle. Its area was x² + 5x + 6, and its sides had to be x plus something and x plus something else. The somethings had to multiply to 6, the corner piece. And they had to add to 5, the strip along the middle.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3. So x² + 5x + 6 = (x + 2)(x + 3). And once it was two factors, a new door opened: if the whole thing equals zero, one of the factors must be zero, so x is either minus 2 or minus 3.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Her teacher gave her one with a minus: x² − x − 6. Two numbers that multiply to minus 6 and add to minus 1: minus 3 and 2. So it is (x − 3)(x + 2), and she checked by multiplying it back out.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Then a shortcut with no middle at all: x² − 9. There is no x term, so the two numbers must cancel each other: 3 and minus 3. x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), a pattern called the difference of squares.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] To factor, find two numbers that multiply to c and add to b. If a product is zero, one of the factors is zero, which is how a factored equation gives up its answers. Un-multiplying is baking in reverse.
description: "Un-multiplying", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] The rumor.
description: The title of the story "The rumor", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] Diego told two friends a rumor at first period. By lunch the whole school knew. He had told exactly two people. How could two become six hundred by noon?
description: "The rumor", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] His math teacher asked him to count. He told two. Each of them told two: four. Then eight, then sixteen. Diego assumed the rumor grew by a couple of people every round, and by ten rounds that would be twenty or so. Not six hundred.
description: "The rumor", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] But it was not adding two each round. It was doubling. Two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two. After ten rounds, over a thousand. Adding the same amount each step is linear and climbs like stairs. Multiplying by the same amount each step is exponential and climbs like a rocket.
description: "The rumor", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] His teacher wrote it as a power. In round n, the number of new listeners is 2 to the nth. Round ten is 2 to the tenth: 1,024 people hearing it in that round alone, more than the whole school.
description: "The rumor", paragraph 4 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Things can shrink the same way. A medicine that halves in the blood every six hours goes 100 milligrams, then 50, then 25: exponential decay. And money grows like the rumor: 100 dollars earning 7 percent a year doubles in about ten years, then doubles again.
description: "The rumor", paragraph 5 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Adding the same amount each step is linear growth. Multiplying by the same amount is exponential growth, and it runs away from every straight line eventually. A rumor is exponential. So is a savings account, given time.
description: "The rumor", paragraph 6 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] Frederick and the culture flask.
description: The title of the story "Frederick and the culture flask", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] Frederick had been given a corner of a real lab for the summer, a flask of yeast and a rule: measure everything. At fourteen, he was the youngest person in the building by eight years. The yeast doubled every ninety minutes, and by the second day he had learned the difference between adding and multiplying the hard way.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 1 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Ten rounds of adding two cells to one would have reached twenty-one; ten rounds of doubling reached 1,024. Exponential, said the graduate student, and drew the curve that starts slow and then leaves every straight line behind. Frederick wrote it as 2 to the n and pinned it over the bench.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 2 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The growth depended on the warmth of the incubator. Put in a temperature, out came a growth rate, and the same temperature never gave two answers: a function, a vending machine that never lied. Too cold and the yeast barely grew; too hot and it died. Frederick graphed it and found the one temperature where it grew fastest.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 3 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The flask budget was a system. One supplier charged 300 dollars plus 10 a flask; another charged 20 a flask and nothing else. Frederick set 300 + 10x equal to 20x and got x = 30. Below thirty flasks the second supplier was cheaper, and above thirty the first.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 4 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] One morning the log held a puzzle. Two shelves had the same number of dishes: the first held 5 racks of x dishes plus 3 loose ones, the second 2 racks plus 15 loose. Frederick gathered the xs on one side, 3x = 12, and got 4 dishes a rack. Both shelves held 23.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 5 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The last week he needed the sides of a rectangular tray whose area was x² + 5x + 6 square inches. He factored it into (x + 2)(x + 3) and found the sides from the area. He checked it by multiplying back out, the way he checked everything now.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 6 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] In August the yeast ran out of sugar, and the curve that had climbed like a rocket bent over and flattened. Nothing grows exponentially forever; the food runs out first. The graduate student called it the most important graph of the summer, because it was the one that explained all the others.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 7 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The lab kept his notebook when the summer ended. He kept the habit: everything measured, everything written down, and the curve always drawn. The graduate student wrote him a letter for the next summer's program.
description: "Frederick and the culture flask", paragraph 8 of 8: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm] Three ways to sell a bicycle.
description: The title of the story "Three ways to sell a bicycle", said warmly, as a title is read aloud.

text: [warm, conversational] Priya was selling her old bicycle at the garage sale and had three pitches ready. Trust me, I have ridden it for years. Imagine the wind on your face on the first warm day of spring. It costs a third of a new one and the frame is aluminum, so it will last for years. The first buyer walked away from all three.
description: "Three ways to sell a bicycle", paragraph 1 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] Her brother said she had used every appeal in the book and had no idea what any of them was for. Priya said they were just sentences. He said each one was asking the buyer to trust a different thing.
description: "Three ways to sell a bicycle", paragraph 2 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

text: [warm, conversational] The first was ethos: trust me, because I know. The second was pathos: feel this, because feeling moves people. The third was logos: here is the reasoning and the numbers. None was better than the others. The question was whether the appeal fit the claim, and a buyer asking whether the brakes worked did not need the wind on his face.
description: "Three ways to sell a bicycle", paragraph 3 of 6: a warm, conversational voice that never talks down.

The bracket just before each sound's symbols tells Eleven what the sound should be (Mikey, pass MX). If a take reads a bracket aloud or sounds like a sound effect, delete that take and run the generator again, which makes only what is missing; if the new take fails too, delete it as well and run ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=... node tools/audio-generate.mjs with the voices you used before and --only sound-u --no-goals (pasting into ElevenLabs, leave out each bracket before a sound). If no take says it right, record it yourself and turn it into the lesson voice with ElevenLabs' Voice Changer (EARMARKS A41).

text: One excited fan's loud two-finger whistle at a ball game, close by, on a single breath: it swoops up to a bright, high note, holds, then slides down and fades as the breath runs out. About one second, one whistle, no crowd noise, no voices, no music.
description: One fan's two-finger whistle on a single breath, about a second, swelling and then fading as a real breath runs out (Mikey, of the app's own: "It should be drawn out a bit more and slightly change the amplitude of the whistle sound to sound natural as if a real breath was required."). It plays between the cheer's sayings, so pick the take with one clear whistle and nothing behind it.

text: About forty people clapping and cheering for a child in a school gym, warm and happy: claps, cheers and a whistle or two burst out together right away, then fade away at the end. About two and a half seconds, no music, no spoken words.
description: About forty people clapping and cheering in a school gym for two and a half seconds, fading out at the end, after the cheer's last saying. Pick the take whose claps sound like real hands (Mikey, of the app's own: "the clapping sounds like static"), starting at once, with no music and no words.
